## SUBJECT: CJCS EXECUTE ORDER SER 014-26 — OPERATION SILENT FATHOM

### REFERENCES

- (a) 10 U.S.C. § 164 (Combatant commander command authority)
- (b) 10 U.S.C. § 162; standing Title 10 authorities for forward presence and support to allies and partners
- (c) North Atlantic (Washington) Treaty, 4 April 1949 — Article 4 (consultation)
- (d) US–Norway Supplementary Defense Cooperation Agreement (SDCA), 16 April 2021 (access, basing, and overflight)
- (e) UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Articles 58, 87, 112–115 (submarine cables; high seas and EEZ freedoms; flag-state jurisdiction)
- (f) Svalbard (Spitsbergen) Treaty, 9 February 1920 (Norwegian sovereignty; demilitarization regime)
- (g) Joint Publication 5-0 (Joint Planning); CJCSM 3130.02 (linked-order chain)
- (h) Joint Publication 3-0 (Joint Operations); JP 3-32 (Joint Maritime Operations)
- (i) CJCSI 3121.01B (Standing Rules of Engagement / Standing Rules for the Use of Force for US Forces)
- (j) GEF 2026 / JSCP — USEUCOM campaign and crisis-response planning guidance
- (k) Kingdom of Norway request for Allied support, transmitted via Embassy Oslo, 13 JAN 26

---

### 1. SITUATION

#### (a) General

Between 05 and 13 January 2026, three subsea telecommunications/data cables — the twin Svalbard Link (SVL-1/SVL-2, Longyearbyen–Harstad), the trans-Atlantic Boreal Connect (Norway–Iceland–North America), and the coastal Nordkapp Data Link — and one segment of the Arctic Bridge high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) power interconnector were damaged in near-simultaneous incidents across the Norwegian and Barents Seas. The damage was coincident with sustained GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing that degraded navigation across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches. A Russian-flagged hydrographic/survey vessel (GS Pomor) and two shadow-fleet merchants (MV Arktika Star, MV Kola Trader) operated in or near the affected cable corridors during the window, each with extended, unexplained AIS gaps. Damage to this critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) degraded — but did not sever — connectivity that includes allied space-ground, communications-transport, and financial-clearing data dependent on the affected routes. Attribution is plausible but not conclusive.

On 13 January, the Kingdom of Norway requested Allied support and requested consultations under Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty (reference (c)). Article 5 has not been invoked. The North Atlantic Council has convened Article 4 consultations; the United States supports those consultations through the Department of State and the US National Military Representative at SHAPE.

The President and the Secretary of Defense have directed USEUCOM to conduct mission analysis and develop options to protect critical undersea infrastructure, deter further sabotage, and enable attribution of the incidents — explicitly below the threshold of armed conflict.

#### (b) Enemy

The Russian Federation, through the Northern Fleet (HQ Severomorsk, Kola Peninsula) and its deniable deep-sea survey capability (Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research, GUGI-analog), possesses the platforms, seabed knowledge, EW assets, and demonstrated method to conduct deniable interference with seabed infrastructure across the operating area. Russian Northern Fleet EW units on the Kola Peninsula are the assessed source of the GPS/PNT jamming and AIS-spoofing footprint. Russian state media and a coordinated inauthentic network are advancing an attribution-denial narrative ("trawler/anchor accident," "NATO false flag"). Adversary **capability is assessed with high confidence; intent and conclusive attribution are assessed with low confidence** — the deliberate use of deniable means is itself consistent with an intent to act below the collective-defense threshold. See USEUCOM J2 products (`02_Regional_Intel_Summary.md`, `03_Adversary_OOB.md`).

#### (c) Friendly

USEUCOM is the supported combatant command. The Department of State leads US diplomacy and supports the NAC Article 4 process; Embassy Oslo (Chief of Mission, Hon. Patricia Donnelly) is the in-country focal point. The DOJ/FBI lead the US attribution and protected-infrastructure investigation; DHS/CISA lead CUI dependency analysis. USSPACECOM, USCYBERCOM, and USTRANSCOM are supporting combatant commands. NATO acts through the North Atlantic Council, NATO MARCOM's Critical Undersea Infrastructure Coordination Cell (Northwood), and Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 (SNMG1); the United Kingdom and the Kingdom of Norway contribute maritime and seabed-surveillance capability. COMUSEUCOM is dual-hatted as SACEUR; this order directs the US national chain only and does not direct or imply action in the NATO chain.

#### (d) Civil Considerations

The affected CUI carries allied and civil space-ground links from the Svalbard Satellite Station and a portion of allied communications-transport and financial-clearing data; the loss of redundancy when one cable of a redundant pair is damaged raises the consequence of any further cut. Commercial cable operators, the HVDC interconnector operator, and a contracted cable-repair ship govern the restoration timeline and are central, non-force stakeholders. The polar-night environment — near-continuous darkness, sea state 4–6, icing, and an intermittent ice edge in the northern Barents — constrains surface, air, and repair operations.

#### (e) Assumptions

- The Kingdom of Norway will continue to request and consent to US and Allied support as host/lead.
- Russia will continue to prefer deniable, sub-threshold pressure to overt confrontation, and will posture to exploit attribution ambiguity in the information environment.
- Conclusive, releasable attribution will require fusion of vessel-track, EW-geolocation, and seabed/acoustic-forensic reporting and will not be available at the outset.
- Allies converge on the need to deter and to develop attribution but differ on the evidentiary threshold for public attribution and on the level of response that competition permits.
- Access, basing, and overflight in Norway are available under reference (d).

### 2. MISSION

When directed, USEUCOM, in coordination with NATO Allies and the Kingdom of Norway, conducts mission analysis and develops options to protect critical undersea infrastructure, deter further sabotage of subsea infrastructure, and enable attribution of the incidents in the Norwegian and Barents Seas, below the threshold of armed conflict, in order to restore the security of critical undersea infrastructure, preserve freedom of navigation, and reassure Allies.

### 3. EXECUTION

#### (a) National-Level Commander's Intent

Protect the critical undersea infrastructure on which Allied security depends, deter the next act of sabotage, and build the attribution picture that enables a coordinated Alliance political response — without handing Moscow the escalation it would exploit. The military instrument supports a State-led, NATO-framed effort: visible, lawful presence; surveillance and protection; and disciplined collection. Develop a deny–attribute–signal option set that deters repetition while remaining demonstrably below the armed-conflict threshold and consistent with the law of the sea. Reassure Norway and the exposed Allies; preserve Allied unity and escalation control throughout.

#### (b) Concept (national direction)

- **Phase 0 (Shape) — ongoing:** ISR, presence, interagency and Allied coordination; support to the NAC Article 4 consultations.
- **Phase I (Set / Deter):** flow the apportioned maritime and ISR force forward; establish a subsurface-inclusive maritime domain-awareness picture; integrate with the NATO MARCOM CUI Cell and the Norwegian Joint Headquarters; establish PNT-resilient operations with USSPACECOM.
- **Phase II (Protect / Attribute):** surveil and protect CUI; escort cable-repair operations; detect, track, and shadow suspect vessels; conduct seabed/acoustic forensics in support of attribution; develop deterrent-signaling options for decision.
- **Phase III (Transition):** as restoration and attribution mature, transition CUI-resilience and forensic lines to civil, Allied, and interagency leads; preserve a residual deterrent posture as directed.

#### (c) Authorities Granted

- CDR USEUCOM is delegated authority for crisis-response planning and execution within this order, references (a)–(k), and the SROE/SRUF at reference (i).
- US role and access derive from (i) the Kingdom of Norway's request for Allied support (reference (k)); (ii) US Title 10 support-to-ally and forward-presence authorities (reference (b)); and (iii) the US–Norway SDCA (reference (d)). No new self-defense trigger is invoked.
- USEUCOM is authorized to coordinate directly with USSPACECOM, USCYBERCOM, and USTRANSCOM for supporting effects and with the Department of State, DOJ/FBI, and DHS/CISA for the attribution and CUI-dependency lines.

#### (d) National-Level Restraints and Constraints

The following are directed and are not waivable below the National Command Authority:

- Operate below the threshold of armed conflict at all times.
- **Do not invoke or imply NATO Article 5.** US action supports the Article 4 consultative process and Norway as host/lead; this order directs the US national chain only.
- **No kinetic action against Russian state vessels.** Interaction with suspect or Russian state vessels is limited to lawful detection, tracking, shadowing, and presence.
- **No entry into Russian territorial waters.**
- **No boarding or seizure of any vessel in international waters absent a positive legal determination and a separate grant of authority.** Cable damage in the high seas and the Norwegian EEZ sits under flag-state jurisdiction and the limited enforcement regime of reference (e); the binding constraint is legal-jurisdictional.
- Comply with UNCLOS (reference (e)) and the Svalbard Treaty regime (reference (f)), including the demilitarization nuance constraining posture around the archipelago.
- **No public attribution release without National Command Authority and NATO coordination.** Contest, do not amplify, adversary deniability narratives.
- **RETAINED AT THE NCA:** approval of any deterrent action with offensive cyber effect; any use of force beyond unit self-defense; and any change to the posture or restraints above. CDR USEUCOM is the senior military planning authority and may plan, posture, and rehearse within the restraints of this order.

#### (e) Tasks

**Supported Command**

- **CDR USEUCOM:** Execute Operation SILENT FATHOM mission analysis. Publish the USEUCOM Linked EXORD NLT 140600Z JAN 26 and direct component orders. Designate the maritime component supported. Integrate the Department of State (Embassy Oslo / EUR), DOJ/FBI (attribution), DHS/CISA (CUI dependency), the NATO MARCOM CUI Cell, and the Norwegian Joint Headquarters. Develop the deny–attribute–signal option set and the deterrent-signaling recommendations for NCA/NATO decision. Manage escalation and Allied unity throughout.

**Supporting Commands**

- **CDR USSPACECOM:** Provide space domain awareness and PNT support; characterize the GPS/PNT jamming footprint; deconflict degraded-PNT effects on friendly maritime and air operations across the EUCOM/NORTHCOM/SPACECOM seam; support alternate-navigation measures for the maritime force.
- **CDR USCYBERCOM:** Provide technical attribution support in coordination with the FBI; coordinate any defensive and (NCA-retained) offensive cyberspace planning related to the information and EW activity.
- **CDR USTRANSCOM:** Provide strategic and intratheater lift to flow and sustain the apportioned force into the High North; coordinate movement under degraded-PNT conditions.
- **CDR USNORTHCOM (coordinating):** Coordinate the Arctic-approaches and homeland-PNT seam with USEUCOM and USSPACECOM.

**Interagency (coordination)**

- **DoS:** Lead US diplomacy; support the NAC Article 4 process; Embassy Oslo is the in-country focal point; manage attribution-release diplomacy.
- **DOJ/FBI:** Lead the US attribution and protected-infrastructure investigation.
- **DHS/CISA:** Lead CUI dependency analysis.

#### (f) Coordinating Instructions

- **Execution authority for sensitive lines** (offensive cyber effect; force beyond self-defense; public attribution release) is NCA-retained per §3(d). Report readiness; do not execute without separate order.
- **ROE/RUF** per reference (i) and the SILENT FATHOM ROE Supplement (`11_Annexes.md` Annex A). Inherent right of unit self-defense always applies.
- **Escalation management.** Calibrate presence and signaling to deter without manufacturing confrontation. Immediate report on indications of further sabotage and on movement of the second survey vessel (GS Ladoga) toward the Bear Island Gap corridor (CCIRs, `13_CCIRs.md`).
- **Legal determination.** USEUCOM, with OSD/General Counsel and the Department of State, will obtain a determination on interdiction authority in international waters and the Norwegian EEZ before any action contemplating visit, board, or diversion.
- **PNT deconfliction.** Coordinate degraded-PNT effects continuously with USSPACECOM.
- **Classification/releasability** for Allied sharing per `11_Annexes.md` Annex A and the disclosure guidance.

### 4. SUSTAINMENT / LOGISTICS

USTRANSCOM coordinates strategic and intratheater lift to flow and sustain the apportioned maritime, ISR, and forensic capability into the High North, accounting for degraded-PNT navigation and the polar-night/weather constraints. Forward access, basing, and overflight in Norway (including Evenes) are coordinated under reference (d). Sustainment of high-demand, low-density ocean-surveillance and undersea-ISR enablers is prioritized against standing theater demand.

### 5. COMMAND AND SIGNAL

- **Command.** SecDef exercises authority through CJCS to CDR USEUCOM (supported). USSPACECOM, USCYBERCOM, and USTRANSCOM are supporting. Supported/supporting relationships per §3(e). NCA retains the authorities at §3(d). COMUSEUCOM's NATO (SACEUR) hat is distinct from this US national order.
- **Signal.** USEUCOM is the supported-command reporting authority. Daily SITREP to the Joint Staff (J3); immediate reports on CCIR triggers. Standard reporting per the USEUCOM order.

### ANNEXES REFERENCED

- A — OPLAW / ROE Supplement (`11_Annexes.md` Annex A)
- B — Cyber / EW (`11_Annexes.md` Annex B)
- C — Information (`11_Annexes.md` Annex C)
- D — Climatology / Astronomical (`11_Annexes.md` Annex D)

### ACKNOWLEDGE.

CJCS SENDS.

text:
# JIPOE Brief — Operation SILENT FATHOM

UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

**Product Type:** Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment (Executive Brief; per JP 2-01.3)
**Briefing Date:** 140700Z JAN 26
**Briefed by / to:** USEUCOM J2 to COMUSEUCOM and the maritime-component planning staff (NAVEUR-6F)
**Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

---

## [Slide 1] Title

Operation SILENT FATHOM — JIPOE Executive Brief. AOR: USEUCOM / European High North. AOI: Norwegian and Barents Seas, the Svalbard approaches and Longyearbyen landing, the Boreal Connect trans-Atlantic corridor, the Finnmark coast, and the Bear Island Gap corridor. NORTHCOM (Arctic approaches), SPACECOM (PNT/SDA), and CYBERCOM (attribution support) are supporting seams. As of 140600Z JAN 26.

## [Slide 2] Step 1 — Define the Operational Environment

- **Joint OE.** A maritime/subsea competition environment in the European High North: a NATO Ally (Norway) whose critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) has sustained four near-simultaneous faults in nine days; the Russian Northern Fleet and its deniable seabed-survey directorate; a shadow-fleet and EW/PNT apparatus; commercial cable and HVDC operators and a contracted cable-repair ship; and an Alliance split on attribution thresholds. The contest is deliberately sub-threshold — below the level of armed conflict and short of any Article 5 trigger.
- **Area of Operations.** The Norwegian Sea and Barents Sea high seas and the Norwegian EEZ; the Svalbard approaches (Cut Site A, vcnty 76.5N 014.0E) under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty regime; the Boreal Connect corridor (Cut Site B, vcnty 67.5N 002.0E); the Finnmark coastal belt; forward operating from Evenes, with Reitan/Bodø (FOH) and Vardø (E-tjenesten) as the principal Norwegian nodes.
- **Area of Interest.** The Kola Peninsula (Severomorsk; Northern Fleet and EW garrisons); the GIUK–Bear Gap; the Bear Island Gap corridor (the DP-1 named area); and the trans-Atlantic and Svalbard data-transport paths whose dependencies extend well beyond the theater.
- **Domains.** The contest is principally **maritime and subsurface**, with the **electromagnetic spectrum** actively contested (GPS/PNT jamming, AIS spoofing). Cyberspace and space are **supporting** rather than the decisive fight — space provides PNT and surveillance that the adversary degrades locally; the seabed, not the network, is the decisive terrain. This is a CUI-protection and attribution problem, not a force-on-force campaign.

## [Slide 3] Step 2 — Environmental Effects on Operations

- **Polar-night climatology.** Mid-January polar night above the Arctic Circle: near-continuous darkness, sea state 4–6, persistent superstructure icing, and an intermittent ice edge in the northern Barents. Severe-weather windows constrain surface, air, and — critically — cable-repair operations, narrowing the periods in which protection and forensics can occur and lengthening restoration timelines.
- **EMS / PNT environment.** Sustained Kola-based GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing degrade navigation across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, peaking 11 JAN. The footprint affects friendly receivers as well as civil and adversary ones; degraded PNT is simultaneously an indicator to be characterized and a constraint on the forces conducting protection and seabed forensics.
- **Undersea acoustic conditions.** Polar-front and marginal-ice-zone gradients, seasonal layering, and shallow-shelf reverberation complicate the passive-acoustic and seabed-forensic picture; they raise the difficulty of localizing a subsurface contact (e.g., B-90 Vologda) and of distinguishing a deliberate seabed act from an anchor- or trawl-induced fault.
- **Jurisdictional geography.** The AO straddles Norwegian internal/territorial waters, the Norwegian EEZ, and high seas; the Svalbard Treaty regime overlays the northern approaches. The faults at Cut Site A and Cut Site B lie in waters where enforcement authority over cable damage is legally constrained — a binding feature of the environment, not merely a legal footnote (see Annexes, OPLAW).

## [Slide 4] Step 3 — Evaluate the Adversary

**Capabilities (HIGH confidence).**
- **Northern Fleet (HQ Severomorsk; CDR ADM Viktor Sorokin, RuN).** Concentrated surface, subsurface, and EW capability on the Kola Peninsula from which all observed activity is most plausibly staged.
- **GUGI-analog (Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research).** Deniable seabed/deep-submergence survey capability: survey vessels GS Pomor and GS Ladoga and special-mission host submarine B-90 Vologda, assessed able to locate, survey, and interfere with seabed infrastructure at the depths involved.
- **Shadow fleet.** MV Arktika Star (crude tanker) and MV Kola Trader (bulk carrier), both flags of convenience, providing accident-plausible, deniable proximity to the corridors.
- **EW / PNT units.** Kola-based Tobol-/Murmansk-BN-analog systems generating the GPS/PNT jamming and AIS-spoofing footprint.
- **Information apparatus.** State media and a coordinated inauthentic network advancing an attribution-denial narrative.
- **Seabed-sabotage TTPs (assessed).** Survey/loiter under AIS gaps; ROV or deep-submergence interference at the seabed; mechanisms (anchor drag, cable damage) chosen for accident-plausibility; EW activity that may mask or coincide with a seabed act.

**Intent (LOW confidence — the central problem).** Whether the campaign is meant to coerce Norway and the Alliance, condition the environment for future leverage, or probe Allied response thresholds is unresolved. The deliberate use of deniable means is itself consistent with an intent to stay below the collective-defense threshold.

**Attribution assessment.** J2 assesses **HIGH confidence** that Russia possesses the capability and is the **probable responsible party** for the pattern of incidents. J2 holds **LOW–MODERATE confidence** on conclusive **state-direction** attribution (directed act vs. deniable proxy/shadow-fleet action at state behest vs., in any single case, a genuine accident) and **LOW confidence on intent**. No single reporting stream resolves the gap; it is named as PIR-2.

**Centers of gravity (initial).** *Adversary COG (assessed):* the deniability of the means — the AIS-dark survey/shadow-fleet model, accident-plausible mechanisms, and EW masking that together hold attribution below the threshold of confident, attributable state action. *Friendly COG (initial):* the maritime force's ability to develop attribution and protect CUI and repair operations while controlling escalation, dependent on a subsurface-inclusive domain-awareness picture, PNT resilience, and Allied/interagency coherence.

## [Slide 5] Step 4 — Determine Adversary Courses of Action

**COA 1 — Continued Deniable, Sub-Threshold Sabotage (MOST LIKELY; moderate confidence).**
Russia continues paced, attribution-ambiguous interference against additional corridors — most plausibly the Bear Island Gap corridor as GS Ladoga transits — using survey/shadow-fleet platforms under AIS gaps and intermittent EW, calibrated to stay below the armed-conflict threshold and to exploit the genuine ambiguity of cable faults in these waters.
*Indicators:* GS Ladoga track converging on the Bear Island Gap corridor (NAI Bear-Island-Gap / DP-1); renewed AIS gaps by survey or shadow-fleet vessels near a corridor; localized GPS/PNT jamming coincident with a new fault; sustained attribution-denial messaging.

**COA 2 — Escalatory / Coercive Incident (MOST DANGEROUS; low–moderate confidence).**
Russia escalates against a higher-value target or stages a coercive incident: a deliberate cut of the residual Svalbard fiber (SVL-1) to fully isolate Longyearbyen/SvalSat, a more consequential strike on the Boreal Connect trans-Atlantic transport, or an at-sea harassment/unsafe-intercept of a repair or escorting unit to impose costs and test Alliance unity around Svalbard.
*Indicators:* GUGI-analog or shadow-fleet positioning on SVL-1 or the Boreal Connect main path; B-90 Vologda subsurface activity near a corridor; surge or repositioning of Northern Fleet surface combatants toward the Svalbard approaches; aggressive close-aboard maneuvering or targeting-radar illumination of friendly/repair units; sharpened coercive state messaging.

## [Slide 6] Indications & Warning Matrix (extract)

| Indicator | Associated COA | Collection (NAI / asset) | Reports to |
|-----------|----------------|--------------------------|------------|
| GS Ladoga track converging on Bear Island Gap | COA 1 (DP-1 trigger) | NAI Bear-Island-Gap; P-8A / MQ-9 / SSN / space | CDR (immediate) |
| New AIS gap by survey / shadow-fleet vessel near a corridor | COA 1/2 | Corridor NAIs; commercial AIS / EO-SAR / MPA | J2 / JOC |
| GPS/PNT jamming coincident with a new fault | COA 1/2 | Finnmark / Svalbard EMS NAIs; SPACECOM / E-tjenesten | J2 / SPACECOM cell |
| B-90 Vologda subsurface activity near a corridor | COA 2 | Corridor NAIs; USNS Cascadia (T-AGOS) / SSN | CDR (immediate) |
| Northern Fleet surface surge toward Svalbard approaches | COA 2 | GIUK–Bear / Svalbard NAIs; MPA / space | CDR (immediate) |

Full matrix in `13_CCIRs.md` and `15_Event_Template_NAI_Matrix.xlsx`.

## [Slide 7] Confidence Assessment

- Russian capability: **HIGH** (Northern Fleet, GUGI-analog, EW/PNT, shadow fleet).
- Probable Russian responsibility for the pattern: **HIGH** (probable; not conclusive).
- Conclusive state-direction attribution per incident: **LOW–MODERATE** — the binding analytic gap (PIR-2).
- Adversary intent: **LOW**.
- GS Ladoga next-target intent: **LOW–MODERATE** (track suggestive, purpose unconfirmed; PIR-3).
- Jamming extent / effect on friendly ops: **MODERATE** (footprint observed, full intent uncertain; PIR-4).

**Key intelligence gaps:** (1) state-direction vs. deniable proxy vs. accident per incident; (2) GS Ladoga next-target indication against the Bear Island Gap corridor; (3) the subsurface picture — B-90 Vologda location and any deployed seabed payloads; (4) full characterization of the GPS/PNT jamming; (5) the precise military-communications and financial-clearing dependency on each affected cable and the realistic restoration timeline.

## [Slide 8] Implications for JIPOE Consumers

- Treat **attribution as an objective in its own right**, not an assumption; protection and seabed forensics are mutually reinforcing collection that close the PIR-2 gap.
- Plan **COA-robust** across continued sub-threshold sabotage and an escalatory/coercive incident — do not optimize only to the most-likely COA.
- Wire the **GS Ladoga / Bear Island Gap** indication to DP-1 and a CCIR; it is the time-sensitive branch.
- Resource **PNT resilience and EMS deconfliction** continuously against the jamming, across the EUCOM / NORTHCOM / SPACECOM seam.
- Manage **escalation** throughout: the deniability that frustrates attribution also caps the permissible response — the approach must deter repetition without crossing the Article 5 / armed-conflict threshold.

title: Annexes
text:
# Annexes — Operation SILENT FATHOM

UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

**Product Type:** Planning Annex Compilation (supporting the linked-order chain and CIPG)
**Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

---

## Annex A — OPLAW / Legal

**Legal basis for US role.**
- No new self-defense trigger is invoked. US entry and role rest on: (a) the Kingdom of Norway's request for Allied support; (b) NATO Washington Treaty **Article 4** consultations requested by Norway — **Article 5 is deliberately not invoked** (sub-threshold); (c) the US–Norway Supplementary Defense Cooperation Agreement (SDCA 2021) for access and basing; and (d) US Title 10 support-to-ally / forward maritime presence.

**Submarine-cable regime (UNCLOS).**
- UNCLOS **Art. 113** requires each state to make it a punishable offense for a vessel flying its flag, or a person subject to its jurisdiction, to break or injure a submarine cable willfully or by culpable negligence.
- **Art. 114** addresses liability of cable owners to one another; **Art. 115** provides for indemnity of vessels that sacrifice gear to avoid injuring a cable. The regime is principally one of flag-state penalty and inter-owner liability, not third-state enforcement.
- Enforcement therefore runs principally through **flag-state jurisdiction**. There is **no general coastal-state or third-state authority to board, search, seize, or divert a foreign-flagged vessel on the high seas or in the EEZ for cable damage** absent flag-state consent, a treaty basis, or another recognized exception.
- **Consequence.** For the faults at Cut Site A (Svalbard approaches) and Cut Site B (Norwegian Sea high seas), and for activity in the Norwegian EEZ, **US/Allied enforcement authority over cable damage in international waters is limited**. The binding constraint on interdiction is legal/jurisdictional, not military, and it persists even where the responsible vessel is identified.

**Svalbard Treaty regime.**
- The 1920 Svalbard Treaty confirms Norwegian sovereignty over the archipelago while granting treaty-party nationals equal economic access. Art. 9 constrains the use of the archipelago for "warlike purposes" and is the source of the demilitarization nuance that bounds military posture in and around Svalbard.
- Operations near the Svalbard approaches and the Longyearbyen landing — including any escort of repair operations on SVL — must account for this regime and for Russia's standing readiness to characterize Allied activity there as militarization. It is a deliberate legal seam, not a settled permission; coordinate posture with Norway as the sovereign and with the legal-determination track below.

**ROE / RUF summary (SILENT FATHOM ROE Supplement to CJCSI 3121.01B).**
- Inherent right of **unit and individual self-defense** always applies, including defense of accompanied repair and partner units.
- Posture toward Russian state vessels is **defensive**; **no kinetic action against Russian state vessels** and **no entry into Russian territorial waters**.
- **No boarding, seizure, or diversion of vessels in international waters absent a positive legal determination and granted authority.** Shadowing, querying on bridge-to-bridge, overt presence, and persistent ISR are permitted within standing guidance.
- All operations remain **below the threshold of armed conflict.** **Do not invoke or imply NATO Article 5.**
- Coordinate with Norway as host/lead and through the NAC consultative process; comply with UNCLOS and the Svalbard Treaty regime.
- **No public attribution release without NCA and NATO coordination.**

**Open decision item.** The **interdiction-authority determination** — whether, and on what basis, friendly forces may interdict GS Ladoga or a shadow-fleet vessel approaching the Bear Island Gap corridor in international waters / the Norwegian EEZ — is an **unresolved legal question** referred for determination. It is recorded as FFIR-2 and is a precondition for any action beyond shadowing at DP-1.

**Releasability.** Releasable to Norway and overt Allied contributors (UK, NATO MARCOM CUI Cell, SNMG1) on the CUI-protection and repair-escort lines per disclosure guidance; attribution-support and interdiction-option legal analysis held more closely pending the determination above.

## Annex B — Cyber / EW / Spectrum

- **GPS/PNT jamming picture.** Sustained Kola-based GPS/PNT jamming and AIS spoofing degrade navigation across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches, peaking 11 JAN coincident with the Nordkapp Data Link faults. Source is assessed as Northern Fleet EW units on the Kola Peninsula (Tobol-/Murmansk-BN-analog). The footprint affects friendly, civil, and adversary receivers alike; full characterization of extent, pattern, and effect is a collection priority (PIR-4).
- **EMS / PNT management.** Establish PNT-resilient maritime operations and alternate-navigation measures (inertial, celestial, eLORAN-type and visual backups) in coordination with **USSPACECOM** (PNT / space-domain awareness).
- **Multi-CCMD deconfliction.** Deconflict friendly EMS use and counter-EW measures across the EUCOM / NORTHCOM / SPACECOM seam; manage spectrum per JP 3-85. Degraded PNT is a planning constraint on maritime, air, and repair operations — including precision station-keeping for seabed forensics — not only an intelligence indicator (FFIR-4).
- **Defensive cyberspace operations (DCO).** Protect maritime-force networks, ISR feeds, and the JOC; treat commercial cable-landing and operator networks as both an intelligence opportunity and an OPSEC risk.
- **Cyber attribution support.** Coordinate attribution-support arrangements with **USCYBERCOM** (supporting CCMD) and, on the protected-infrastructure line, with DOJ/FBI; offensive cyberspace options are NCA-retained.
- **Geolocation feed.** Cyber/EW geolocation of the jamming source contributes to the broader attribution problem (PIR-2) and is synchronized with the Information annex and seabed/acoustic forensics.

## Annex C — Information / IO

- **Adversary narrative.** Russian state media and a coordinated inauthentic network advance an attribution-denial narrative on two complementary lines: (1) that the faults are routine "trawler/anchor accidents" in busy fishing grounds, and (2) that any Allied investigation is a "NATO false-flag" pretext to militarize the Arctic. The narrative exploits the genuine ambiguity of cable faults and raises the evidentiary bar the Alliance must clear before any public attribution.
- **Effect on the operation.** The denial narrative is calibrated to the same deniability the adversary relies on physically; it converts the attribution gap (PIR-2) into an information-environment vulnerability and pressures Allied cohesion, where members already differ on naming Russia publicly.
- **Counter-messaging / PA posture.** Lead with accurate, first-with-the-truth messaging on infrastructure security, freedom of navigation, and Allied reassurance; expose the pattern with releasable information while avoiding over-claiming attribution.
- **Attribution-release discipline.** **No public attribution release without NCA and NATO coordination**; messaging must not outrun the assessed confidence (probable Russian responsibility; not yet conclusive on state direction).
- **OIE / MISO and MILDEC.** Counter the denial narrative to Norwegian, Allied, and regional audiences in coordination with DoS (Embassy Oslo / EUR) and NATO strategic communication; MILDEC supports escalation-control and option ambiguity within authorities; coordinate with OPSEC and Annex B.
- Attribution of the influence activity itself is **moderate confidence**.

## Annex D — Climatology

- **Polar night.** Mid-January, near-continuous darkness above the Arctic Circle; at Longyearbyen the sun remains below the horizon throughout the period, with only brief civil twilight farther south along Finnmark. Limited natural illumination is favorable for low-signature work but degrades EO ISR and at-sea recovery; detailed BMNT/EENT and twilight tables maintained by theater METOC.
- **Sea state.** Sea state 4–6 prevailing across the Norwegian and Barents Seas, higher in passing low-pressure systems; the higher sea states limit small-boat, RHIB, and over-the-side ROV operations and degrade towed-array and seabed-survey precision.
- **Icing.** Recurrent superstructure and topside **icing** in the cold polar air mass — a sustainment, flight-deck, deck-handling, and small-boat constraint that compounds the sea-state limits.
- **Ice edge.** Intermittent marginal ice zone in the northern Barents and near the Svalbard approaches; the edge position shifts with wind and current and constrains the northern operating area and any approach to Cut Site A.
- **Operating windows.** Severe-weather windows recur on a multi-day cycle and constrain surface, air, and especially cable-repair operations, lengthening restoration timelines and narrowing the periods available for protection and forensics. Astronomical and sea-state detail supports `06_Critical_Geography.md`.

## Annex E — Time / Date & Critical-Undersea-Infrastructure Dependency

- **Reference conventions.** All times Zulu (Z) unless noted; mainland Norway local = Z+1 (CET). DTG format DDHHMMZ MON YY; geographic references in lat/long (WGS-84) and named features per `06_Critical_Geography.md`.
- **STARTEX:** 140600Z JAN 26.
- **Incident arc (pre-STARTEX, framing the analysis):** 07 JAN — SVL-2 severed at Cut Site A (Svalbard approaches); 09 JAN — Boreal Connect partial fault at Cut Site B (Norwegian Sea); 11 JAN — Nordkapp Data Link intermittent faults coincident with the jamming peak; 12 JAN — Arctic Bridge HVDC protective trip / suspected anchor-drag damage; 13 JAN — GS Ladoga departs the Kola area toward the Bear Island Gap corridor.
- **CUI dependency note (factual).** The affected infrastructure carries more than civilian internet traffic. **SVL** (twin Svalbard Link, Longyearbyen–Harstad) transports Svalbard Satellite Station ground links and a portion of **allied military-communications transport**; **Boreal Connect** (Norway–Iceland–North America) likewise carries **allied military-communications transport and financial-clearing data**. SVL-2 is severed; **SVL-1 carries the residual Svalbard connectivity**, so the redundancy lost on the Svalbard pair raises the consequence of any further cut. These dependencies inform CUI-restoration prioritization (FFIR-1) and operational risk; the full picture is developed in `05_Country_Fact_Sheet.md` and `16_OSINT_Bundle.md`.

title: CIPG
text:
# Commander's Initial Planning Guidance (CIPG) — Operation SILENT FATHOM

UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

**Product Type:** Commander's Initial Planning Guidance (per JP 5-0)
**Commander:** GEN Marcus T. Hale, USA — COMUSEUCOM (acting in US national capacity)
**Issued to:** Commander, NAVEUR-6F (supported maritime commander); Commander, SOCEUR; USEUCOM staff
**Date:** 140900Z JAN 26
**Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

> I am dual-hatted as SACEUR. This guidance is issued in my **US national** capacity. Coordination with the NATO chain runs through the NAC consultative process and MARCOM; keep the two lanes deconflicted and do not let our national planning outrun Allied political consensus.

---

## 1. Operational Design

### 1.1 The Problem
Over nine days an adversary has degraded four pieces of critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) in the Norwegian and Barents Seas and laid a coincident GPS/PNT-jamming and AIS-spoofing footprint across Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches. The acts are deliberate, plausibly Russian state-directed, and deliberately deniable — executed by survey vessels and shadow-fleet merchants operating in international waters and a contested legal regime, paced and packaged to stay below the armed-conflict threshold. **The central tension is this: we must deter and, where we can, defend against further sabotage and reassure Norway and the Allies, without handing Moscow the escalation it is courting and without ambiguously implying Article 5.** Too forceful a posture invites a confrontation we are not authorized to seek; too little invites repetition. Our task is to find the operating space in between — to deny, attribute, and signal below the threshold.

### 1.2 Operational Approach
Establish a subsurface-inclusive maritime domain awareness picture over the cable corridors; protect the highest-dependency CUI and the cable-repair effort by presence and escort; develop attribution to a confidence sufficient to enable a coordinated Allied political response; and signal resolve through calibrated, reversible presence rather than force. We lead with Norway as host and lead, operate inside the NAC consultative framework, and set conditions to transition CUI security back to Allied and commercial stewardship. We compete in the information environment to deny the adversary an uncontested attribution-denial narrative.

### 1.3 Lines of Effort
- **LOE 1 — Protect CUI.** *Main effort initially.* Surveillance and protective presence over the cable/interconnector corridors; escort and protect cable-repair operations; prioritize by **military-communications dependency**, not by cable length or commercial value.
- **LOE 2 — Attribute.** Fuse vessel tracks, AIS gaps, EW geolocation, and seabed/acoustic forensics — in support of CYBERCOM and FBI — to close the gap between observed activity and state direction.
- **LOE 3 — Deter & Signal.** Calibrated, reversible presence and declaratory measures; shadowing of adversary survey vessels; deterrent signaling options that support, not pre-empt, Article 4 consultations.
- **LOE 4 — Reassure Allies.** Visible commitment to Norwegian sovereignty and Allied unity; integrate UK, SNMG1, and Nordic partners; preserve cohesion across divergent Allied attribution and response thresholds.

### 1.4 Decisive Points
- A subsurface-inclusive MDA picture sufficient to cue protection and forensics in the corridors.
- A legal determination on interdiction authority in international waters and the Norwegian EEZ (gates what we may do to adversary vessels).
- Attribution developed to a confidence that can underwrite a coordinated NATO political response.
- Cable-repair of the highest-dependency segment escorted and completed.
- PNT-resilient maritime operations sustained in the jamming footprint.

### 1.5 Termination / End-State Criteria (initial — deliberately incomplete)
Planners will treat these as a starting point requiring staff development and higher-headquarters clarification:
- Further sabotage **deterred or defeated** — the threshold that distinguishes "deterred" from merely "no incident this week" is **undefined and must be staffed against a defined observation window.**
- Attribution developed to a confidence "sufficient to support a coordinated NATO political response" — **the confidence standard, and who certifies it, is not specified and must be coordinated with the NAC track and the interagency.**
- CUI restoration **enabled and prioritized by military dependency** — restoration is a commercial/Allied function; **the conditions under which the military protection effort transitions off are not yet defined.**
- Allied unity and Norwegian sovereignty reassured **— the measure of "reassured" is left to higher direction.**
- Escalation controlled and kept below the Article 5 / armed-conflict threshold.

The relationship between these military criteria and the **political** end-state of the Article 4 process is intentionally left to higher direction. Identify the gaps; do not assume them closed.

## 2. Initial Commander's Intent

**Purpose.** Protect the undersea infrastructure the Alliance depends on, deny the adversary further low-cost sabotage, and help build the attribution case that lets NATO respond as one — all while keeping this crisis below the threshold of armed conflict.

**Method.** Surge a subsurface-inclusive surveillance picture over the corridors; protect the highest-dependency CUI and the repair ship by presence and escort; shadow and document adversary survey and shadow-fleet activity; fuse the forensic and intelligence picture to attribute; and signal resolve through reversible presence calibrated to support the Article 4 track. Lead with Norway; operate inside the NAC framework and UNCLOS; obtain the legal determination before we contemplate any action against vessels.

**End-State.** Further sabotage deterred or defeated; attribution sufficient to enable a coordinated NATO political response; the highest-dependency CUI restored or on a clear restoration path; Norwegian sovereignty and Allied unity reassured; escalation controlled below the Article 5 threshold; the force postured to transition CUI security to Allied and commercial leads.

## 3. Joint Function Planning Guidance

- **Command and Control.** Designate NAVEUR-6F the supported maritime commander; SOCEUR supporting. Stand up a CUI coordination construct that ties the US national effort to the **NATO MARCOM Critical Undersea Infrastructure Cell (Northwood)** and the **Norwegian Joint HQ (Reitan/Bodø)** without blurring the US/NATO chains — I am dual-hatted, but this plan is national. Establish the **SPACECOM PNT deconfliction** link and the **CYBERCOM** attribution-support link as standing supporting-CCMD relationships, and coordinate the NORTHCOM Arctic-approaches seam. Integrate Norwegian, UK, SNMG1, and interagency (DoS Embassy Oslo, DOJ/FBI, DHS/CISA) liaison. Publish the battle rhythm and the CCIR immediate-report flow early.
- **Intelligence.** Main intelligence problem is **attribution** (PIR-2) and **warning of the next attack** (PIR-1, PIR-3). Build a subsurface-inclusive MDA picture; fuse US, E-tjenesten (Vardø), and OSINT reporting. Treat ISR as a scarce, weather- and PNT-constrained resource and publish the collection plan (`13_CCIRs.md`). Stand up an attribution working cell with CYBERCOM and FBI; characterize the gap between deniable proxy activity and state direction rather than overstating it.
- **Fires.** Predominantly **non-kinetic and informational** — presence, shadowing, declaratory signaling, and information effects. **No kinetic action against Russian state vessels; no offensive fires.** Kinetic fires are constrained to unit self-defense under the ROE Supplement. Hold any escalatory option for NCA decision. The fires fight here is escalation control, not target servicing.
- **Movement and Maneuver.** Forward-employ TF-65 surface and CTF-67 maritime patrol into the High North; sequence presence to cover the highest-dependency corridors and the repair-ship track first. Plan subsurface maneuver (SSN) for the ISR/seabed task. Do not enter Russian territorial waters; respect the Svalbard Treaty demilitarization nuance in posture around the archipelago.
- **Protection.** Force protection in a **PNT-degraded, EW-contested** environment: assume degraded GPS and spoofed AIS in the operating area and plan alternate navigation and EMCON accordingly. Layered protection for the repair ship and escorts. **Protect the CUI itself** as a protection task — prioritized by military dependency — and protect the integrity of our own positioning, navigation, and timing.
- **Sustainment.** This is a **polar-night, Arctic** sustainment problem: near-continuous darkness, sea state 4–6, icing, and an intermittent ice edge constrain replenishment, aviation, and forward basing. Sustain forward operations from Evenes and Norwegian host-nation support under the SDCA; plan for weather-driven windows and cold-weather readiness as limiting factors, not afterthoughts.
- **Information.** Compete actively. PA-led, first-with-the-truth messaging; counter the adversary attribution-denial narrative ("trawler/anchor accident," "NATO false flag") in coordination with DoS and the NATO information effort. **No public attribution release without NCA and NATO coordination.** Synchronize OIE/MISO, EW/EMSO, and cyber planning; protect the deterrent-signaling effort with tight PA-OPSEC coordination.

## 4. Branches and Sequels to Develop
- **Branch A — GS Ladoga targets the Bear Island Gap corridor:** intercept/shadow/divert decision package (DP-1); presence reinforcement; legal triggers for any vessel action.
- **Branch B — Additional sabotage during repair:** surge escort to the repair ship (DP-2); reprioritize CUI protection by dependency.
- **Branch C — Attribution matures to coordination threshold:** escalate Article 4 toward a coordinated deterrent signal (DP-3); release-authority and NATO synchronization.
- **Branch D — PNT degradation expands / affects air ISR:** activate counter-PNT and alternate-navigation measures (DP-5); SPACECOM deconfliction.
- **Sequel — Transition:** hand CUI security to Allied and commercial leads; redeploy; sustain the attribution and information follow-through.

## 5. CCIRs (initial — refined in 13_CCIRs.md)
- **PIR-1:** Will Russia conduct additional sabotage against CUI within the next 14 days, and against which corridor?
- **PIR-2:** What is the assessed attribution confidence linking the damage to Russian STATE direction versus deniable proxy action?
- **PIR-3:** Is GS Ladoga positioning to target the Bear Island Gap corridor?
- **PIR-4:** What is the extent and pattern of GPS/PNT jamming and its effect on friendly maritime and air operations?
- **FFIR-1:** Status of CUI — what is down, restoration timelines, military-communications dependency impact.
- **FFIR-2:** Legal determination on interdiction authority in international waters / Norwegian EEZ.
- **FFIR-3:** Allied force availability and ROE alignment (SNMG1, Norway, UK RFA Proteus).
- **FFIR-4:** PNT resilience / alternate-navigation status for the maritime force.

## 6. Coalition / Partner Considerations
Norway is host and lead; we support, we do not supplant. Integrate UK (RFA Proteus seabed-warfare role), SNMG1, and the MARCOM CUI Cell; bring Finland and Sweden in as NATO members per their national arrangements. Expect **divergent Allied thresholds** for attribution and response — preserve cohesion and do not outrun consensus. Coordinate commercial cable operators and the repair-ship schedule as non-force stakeholders. Coordinate releasability through the NAC and the interagency.

## 7. Strategic Communication Themes
Allied infrastructure and Norwegian sovereignty are protected; this is a measured, lawful, Allied response below the threshold of conflict; escalation is Moscow's choice, not ours; attribution will be established deliberately and credibly, not asserted. Synchronize with DoS, Embassy Oslo, and the NATO information effort; counter the "accident / false flag" narrative with consistent, verifiable action.

title: Running Estimates
text:
# Running Estimates — Operation SILENT FATHOM

UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

**Product Type:** Pre-Mission-Analysis Staff Running Estimates (by joint function, per JP 5-0)
**As of:** 141100Z JAN 26
**Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

> Each estimate: current running assessment • key shortfalls / limiting factors • running risk. Analytic judgments throughout; to be refined through mission analysis.

---

## 1. Command and Control (C2)

- **Running assessment.** NAVEUR-6F is designated supported maritime commander; SOCEUR supporting; TF-65 (surface) and CTF-67 (MPA) forward-employed to the High North. The architecture is workable, but it carries an unusual coordination load: the US national chain runs parallel to the NATO chain through a dual-hatted COMUSEUCOM/SACEUR, and the effort depends on three external coordination links — the **NATO MARCOM CUI Cell (Northwood)**, the **Norwegian Joint HQ (Reitan/Bodø)**, and the supporting CCMDs (**SPACECOM** for PNT deconfliction, **CYBERCOM** for attribution, with a **NORTHCOM** Arctic-approaches seam). Liaison with Norway, UK, SNMG1, and the interagency is forming.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** The US/NATO chain seam is the principal C2 risk: national planning could outrun NAC consensus, or be read as implying Article 5. Multi-CCMD coordination (EUCOM/NORTHCOM/SPACECOM/CYBERCOM) adds latency to PNT and attribution decisions. Comms in the High North are themselves degraded by the same CUI damage and jamming this operation is meant to counter.
- **Running risk.** MODERATE-HIGH. Mitigated by early publication of supported/supporting relationships, a CCIR immediate-report flow, and a standing CUI coordination construct that keeps the national and NATO lanes deconflicted.

## 2. Intelligence

- **Running assessment.** Adversary capability is well understood; **intent and, above all, attribution are the binding gaps.** No single source resolves whether the damage was state-directed or deniable-proxy action (PIR-2); the picture must be fused from vessel tracks, AIS gaps, EW geolocation, seabed/acoustic forensics, E-tjenesten reporting, and OSINT. Warning of the next attack (PIR-1/PIR-3) and characterization of the jamming (PIR-4) compete for the same scarce collection.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** **Arctic ISR coverage** is thin and weather/polar-night constrained; **PNT degradation** corrupts the sensors and platforms we would use to build the picture; subsurface MDA over the corridors is immature; attribution is inherently uncertain against a deniability-designed adversary; collection assets (P-8, T-AGOS, SSN, RQ-4/MQ-9) are over-subscribed across corridor-watch, forensics, and PNT-characterization tasks.
- **Running risk.** HIGH. Mitigated by a daily collection-deconfliction board, a CYBERCOM/FBI attribution working cell, and disciplined characterization of the attribution gap rather than over-claiming.

## 3. Fires

- **Running assessment.** This is a **non-kinetic and informational** fight: presence, shadowing, declaratory signaling, and information effects. Kinetic fires are constrained to unit self-defense; there is no offensive-fires role and an explicit restraint against kinetic action against Russian state vessels. The "fires" problem is escalation control — calibrating reversible signals that deter without provoking.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** Positive ID and intent characterization in cluttered, AIS-spoofed traffic are difficult, raising the risk of a self-defense engagement that escalates. Any action above self-defense is NCA-retained, so the menu of usable effects is narrow and slow. Signaling effectiveness is hard to measure.
- **Running risk.** MODERATE. Mitigated by tight ROE discipline, a non-lethal-effects synchronization with Information, and contingency packages held for NCA decision (Branches A/C).

## 4. Movement and Maneuver

- **Running assessment.** Forward presence is building with TF-65 surface combatants, CTF-67 MPA from Evenes, USNS Cascadia, and USS Cheyenne, alongside Norwegian, UK, and SNMG1 units. The maneuver problem is covering multiple dispersed corridors (Svalbard approaches, Norwegian Sea, Finnmark coast, Bear Island Gap) and the repair-ship track simultaneously, across long Arctic distances.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** **Escort capacity is the pressure point:** the allocated surface force is thin against the apportioned task, and committing escorts to the repair ship (DP-2) trades off against corridor presence and the Ladoga decision (DP-1). Severe-weather windows, sea state 4–6, icing, and the intermittent ice edge constrain surface and air maneuver. The Svalbard Treaty demilitarization nuance and the restraint on entering Russian territorial waters bound maneuver geography.
- **Running risk.** MODERATE-HIGH. Mitigated by sequencing presence to the highest-dependency corridors first, integrating Allied hulls (RFA Proteus, SNMG1, Norwegian units), and reserving the SSN for the subsurface ISR/forensics task.

## 5. Protection

- **Running assessment.** The force must operate in a **PNT-degraded, EW-contested** environment — degraded GPS and spoofed AIS are assumed in the operating area. Protection spans three objects: the force, the cable-repair effort, and the **CUI itself** (prioritized by military-communications dependency). Force-protection posture is being set for a contested-navigation environment.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** **PNT degradation** affects navigation safety, sensor performance, and GPS-timing-dependent systems; alternate-navigation fits and procedures are uneven across the force (FFIR-4). Protecting dispersed seabed infrastructure with limited hulls is infeasible everywhere at once, forcing dependency-based prioritization. Polar-night and icing degrade lookout, aviation, and small-boat operations.
- **Running risk.** HIGH (driven by PNT). Mitigated by alternate-navigation activation (DP-5), EMCON discipline, layered repair-ship protection, and dependency-prioritized CUI coverage.

## 6. Sustainment

- **Running assessment.** Forward operations are sustained from Evenes and Norwegian host-nation support under the SDCA, with theater reach-back. The defining condition is the **Arctic polar-night** environment: near-continuous darkness, sea state 4–6, icing, and an intermittent ice edge in the northern Barents.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** **Polar-night sustainment** compresses replenishment, aviation, and fuel-handling into weather windows; cold-weather readiness, de-icing, and crew endurance are limiting, not incidental. Forward basing depth in the High North is shallow and host-nation-dependent. Long transit distances stress logistics responsiveness; the same CUI/PNT degradation complicates sustainment C2.
- **Running risk.** MODERATE. Mitigated by treating weather windows as a planning driver, leaning on Norwegian host-nation support, and building cold-weather readiness into force generation.

## 7. Information

- **Running assessment.** The information environment is **actively contested.** A Russian state-media and coordinated inauthentic-network effort is pushing an attribution-denial narrative ("trawler/anchor accident," "NATO false flag") to keep the incidents ambiguous and below the threshold. The friendly effort must contest this narrative, reassure Allies and the Norwegian public, and protect deterrent signaling.
- **Key shortfalls / limiting factors.** **No public attribution release is authorized without NCA and NATO coordination**, so the friendly narrative must compete while the attribution case is still maturing — a speed disadvantage against the adversary. Divergent Allied messaging thresholds risk incoherence. EW/EMSO contention with the jamming environment complicates the technical side of the IE.
- **Running risk.** MODERATE-HIGH. Mitigated by a PA-led first-with-the-truth posture synchronized with DoS and the NATO information effort, OIE/MISO counter-narrative, and tight PA-OPSEC coordination around signaling.

# OSINT Bundle — Operation SILENT FATHOM

UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

**Product Type:** Open-Source Intelligence Compilation (J2 OSINT cell)
**Compilation window:** 05 JAN – 13 JAN 26
**Source basis:** Wire/press reporting, commercial maritime (AIS) and flight-tracking aggregators, social-media monitoring, commercial satellite-imagery vendors, cable-operator and grid-operator public notices, and NGO/think-tank/academic assessment. All items are open-source; reliability and credibility are graded (Admiralty-style: source A–F / info 1–6). Entities are fictionalized for the synthetic frame.
**Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

> Caveat: OSINT here is indicative, not confirmatory. Several items are unverified social-media or partisan-media claims included precisely because they shape the information environment and public narrative. Cable and interconnector faults in these waters arise from genuine accidents as well as deliberate acts; grading reflects that ambiguity. No single item below establishes attribution.

---

## 1. Press / Wire Reporting

| # | Date | Item (summary) | Source (fictionalized) | Grade |
|---|------|----------------|------------------------|-------|
| P-1 | 07 JAN | "Svalbard internet and SvalSat data links disrupted; operator confirms one of two fiber cables faulted near Svalbard." | Norwegian national broadcaster | B2 |
| P-2 | 09 JAN | "Trans-Atlantic Boreal Connect cable reports partial outage; rerouting under way, operator cites 'external damage' under investigation." | International tech/telecom wire | B2 |
| P-3 | 11 JAN | "Navigation warnings issued for Finnmark coast amid widespread GPS disruption; Nordkapp fiber faults reported." | Regional maritime-affairs outlet | B2 |
| P-4 | 12 JAN | "Power link in the Norwegian Sea trips offline; grid operator points to suspected anchor damage." | European energy-sector outlet | B3 |
| P-5 | 12 JAN | "Norway summons Russian envoy, signals NATO consultations over 'pattern' of subsea incidents." | Major international outlet (Oslo dateline) | A2 |
| P-6 | 12 JAN | Russian state media: "Western hysteria over cables; faults are routine trawler and anchor accidents in busy fishing grounds." | Russian state broadcaster | C4 |
| P-7 | 13 JAN | "Analysts question coincidence of four infrastructure faults in nine days; attribution remains unproven." | International wire | B2 |
| P-8 | 13 JAN | Russian state media: "NATO seeks pretext to militarize the Arctic; 'false-flag' over cables alleged." | Russian state-aligned outlet | C5 |
| P-9 | 13 JAN | "Cable-repair vessel chartered; operator warns weather and polar night may push restoration timelines into weeks." | Telecom-industry trade press | B2 |
| P-10 | 13 JAN | "Finland and Sweden back Norway's call for consultations; Allies said to differ on naming Russia publicly." | European wire (Brussels dateline) | B2 |

## 2. Maritime (AIS) and Flight Tracking

| # | Date | Observation | Source | Grade |
|---|------|-------------|--------|-------|
| M-1 | 05–07 JAN | Russian-flagged survey vessel GS Pomor departs Kola area; AIS shows an extended gap bracketing the SVL-2 fault timeframe in the Svalbard approaches. | Commercial AIS aggregator | B3 |
| M-2 | 08–09 JAN | Shadow-fleet bulk carrier MV Kola Trader (flag of convenience) tracks near the Boreal Connect corridor with a multi-hour AIS gap over the relevant segment. | Commercial AIS / ship-spotter | C3 |
| M-3 | 11–12 JAN | Crude tanker MV Arktika Star (flag of convenience) transits the Norwegian Sea near the Arctic Bridge HVDC corridor; AIS gap of ~24h in the preceding day. | Commercial AIS aggregator | C3 |
| M-4 | 06–11 JAN | Persistent AIS position anomalies / "spoofed" tracks clustered over Finnmark and the Svalbard approaches — consistent with deliberate AIS spoofing rather than receiver outage. | Commercial AIS integrity monitor | B2 |
| M-5 | 13 JAN | Second Russian survey vessel GS Ladoga departs Kola area on a northwesterly track; projected course consistent with transit toward the Bear Island Gap area. | Commercial AIS / ship-spotter | C3 |
| F-1 | 06–11 JAN | Civil flight-tracking shows GNSS-jamming flags and position-integrity warnings over Finnmark/Barents airspace, peaking 11 JAN. | Flight-tracking aggregator | B2 |

## 3. Commercial Satellite Imagery (described)

| # | Date | Observation | Source | Grade |
|---|------|-------------|--------|-------|
| I-1 | 06 JAN | EO/SAR pass places a vessel matching GS Pomor's profile loitering in the Svalbard approaches near the SVL corridor, station-keeping pattern. | Commercial EO/SAR vendor | C2 |
| I-2 | 08 JAN | Imagery of GS Pomor with deck arrangement (stern A-frame / handling gear) consistent with seabed survey or ROV launch-and-recovery operations. | Commercial EO vendor | C2 |
| I-3 | 11 JAN | SAR-derived vessel detections near the HVDC corridor where one track corresponds to an AIS-dark contact (no correlating AIS). | Commercial SAR vendor | C3 |
| I-4 | 13 JAN | Imagery confirms GS Ladoga underway from the Kola area; heading northwest. | Commercial EO vendor | C2 |
| I-5 | 09 JAN | EO pass near the Boreal Connect corridor places a bulk-carrier-profile vessel consistent with MV Kola Trader; no correlating AIS for part of the timeframe. | Commercial EO vendor | C3 |

## 4. Social-Media Monitoring (information environment)

| # | Date | Theme | Notes | Grade |
|---|------|-------|-------|-------|
| S-1 | 12–13 JAN | "#JustAnAnchor / accident" narrative | Rapid, partly inorganic amplification of the trawler/anchor-accident framing; clusters link to Russian state-aligned and inauthentic accounts. | C4 |
| S-2 | 12–13 JAN | "#NATOFalseFlag" narrative | Coordinated push alleging NATO staged the incidents to justify Arctic militarization; attribution of the network moderate. | C4 |
| S-3 | 11–13 JAN | Mariner/aviator reports of GPS loss along Finnmark | Geotagged user reports corroborate the jamming footprint and timeline (F-1, M-4); some aggregated/recycled. | C2 |
| S-4 | 13 JAN | Open-source-analyst threads correlating GS Pomor track to fault sites | Independent enthusiasts publishing AIS-gap timelines; useful but unverified and prone to over-claiming. | D3 |

## 5. NGO / Think-Tank / Academic Assessment

| # | Date | Assessment (summary) | Source | Grade |
|---|------|----------------------|--------|-------|
| T-1 | 13 JAN | "Four subsea incidents in nine days exceeds the baseline accident rate for the region, but coincidence cannot be ruled out for any single event." (Captures the attribution ambiguity.) | Seabed-security research institute | A2 |
| T-2 | 12 JAN | "Russia's deep-sea research directorate has the demonstrated capability to locate and interfere with seabed cables; capability is not the same as proven intent." | Naval/maritime studies center | A2 |
| T-3 | 13 JAN | "CUI vulnerability assessment: redundant cable pairs mask risk — losing one fiber of a pair removes resilience and raises the stakes of a second cut." | Critical-infrastructure think tank | B2 |
| T-4 | 12 JAN | "Shadow-fleet vessels increasingly implicated in seabed incidents worldwide; flag-of-convenience structures complicate jurisdiction and attribution." | Maritime-affairs think tank | B2 |
| T-5 | 13 JAN | "Svalbard's connectivity and SvalSat ground-link dependence make the archipelago a high-leverage, low-attribution target." | Polar/Arctic studies academic | B2 |

## 6. OSINT Implications (for the analyst)

- OSINT **supports** but does not confirm a deliberate, state-directed campaign: vessel proximity, AIS gaps, AIS spoofing, and the above-baseline incident rate (M-1/M-2/M-3/M-5, I-1/I-2/I-3, T-1) are suggestive, while shadow-fleet structures and accident-plausible mechanisms (anchor drag) leave a deniability seam open (T-4, P-4/P-6).
- Imagery (I-2, I-3) places a Pomor-profile vessel in survey/ROV-capable configuration and an AIS-dark contact near a corridor — the closest open-source approach to a deliberate-act indicator, still short of attribution.
- The information environment shows **coordinated inorganic amplification** of two competing deniability narratives — "accident" (S-1) and "NATO false flag" (S-2) — designed to raise the evidentiary bar; handle PA/OIE accordingly and do not amplify either frame.
- M-5 / I-4 (GS Ladoga toward the Bear Island Gap area) is the most operationally time-sensitive item and should be wired directly to the next-target PIR and the associated decision point.
- All graded items feed the I&W matrix and NAI set (`02_Regional_Intel_Summary.md`, `13_CCIRs.md`, `15_Event_Template_NAI_Matrix.xlsx`); none, on its own, meets the threshold for a confirmed or attributable report.

title: Strategic Context
text:
UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

# 01 — STRATEGIC CONTEXT

**Product type:** USCENTCOM J5 compilation of national and theater strategic guidance excerpts. **From:** USCENTCOM J5 (Plans), Strategy Division. **DTG of issue:** 150300Z MAR 2026. **Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E).

> Abridged extracts from national strategy, Department of Defense direction, and theater strategy as they bear on northeast Syria. Extracts are compiled for planning use and are not the controlling documents.

## 1. National Security Strategy (relevant excerpts)

National strategy identifies the countering of Iranian malign influence across the region as an enduring objective, with specific reference to denying Iran a contiguous ground line of communication ("land bridge") from Iranian territory through Iraq and Syria toward the Mediterranean littoral. National strategy directs the prevention of the reconstitution of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) and the protection of gains achieved against it. National strategy emphasizes the use of partners and economy-of-force approaches, and the avoidance of large-scale, open-ended United States ground commitments.

## 2. National Defense Strategy (relevant direction)

Department strategy directs the imposition of cost on Iranian-backed consolidation in eastern Syria through partnered and irregular approaches, **without escalation to overt armed conflict** with the Syrian regime or with Iran. Department strategy designates the eastern Syria effort as a supporting effort within the broader theater campaign, to be resourced accordingly, and directs that the introduction of United States forces into ground combat in Syria is **not authorized** under this line of effort.

## 3. National Military Strategy / CJCS direction (relevant direction)

Military strategy directs combatant commands to develop options that achieve campaign objectives below the threshold of armed conflict, with explicit attention to authorities, attribution management, and escalation control. Support to vetted irregular forces conducting authorized unconventional warfare is to be conducted under Section 1202 (FY2018 National Defense Authorization Act); activities exceeding that authority are to be referred for separate authorization. All support to partner forces is conditioned on completion of human-rights (Leahy) vetting.

## 4. Theater strategy and commander's strategic estimate (excerpts)

The USCENTCOM theater strategy assesses the loss of partner-held terrain in the middle Euphrates valley as a reversal of counter-ISIS gains and as an enabler of Iranian land-bridge consolidation. The commander's strategic estimate assesses that an indigenous resistance — the Azadî Resistance Council (ARC) — retains latent capability in the Jazira but has been displaced and isolated from external resupply by recent Iranian-backed proxy action.

The theater strategy sets the desired conditions as: a viable indigenous capability able to coerce and disrupt regime and Iranian-backed proxy activity in the Jazira; a stalled consolidation in the middle Euphrates valley; and a minimized United States advisory footprint maintained below the threshold of overt armed conflict. The estimate notes that apportioned forces for the eastern Syria supporting effort are limited, that intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance and lift are shared theater assets prioritized against higher-priority requirements elsewhere in the area of responsibility, and that force closure for this line of effort is therefore time-phased and lift-dependent.

## 5. Authorities summary (planning-relevant)

- **Section 1202, FY2018 NDAA** — support to irregular forces, groups, or individuals conducting authorized unconventional warfare by United States special operations forces. Governing authority for this line of effort.

- **Title 10 / Title 50 boundary** — activities exceeding Section 1202, including activities properly characterized as covert action, require separate Title 50 or interagency authorization. The characterization of specific activities is a determination required of the command.

- **Leahy vetting** — provision of any assistance to partner units or individuals is conditioned on completion of human-rights vetting.

- **Absence of host-nation consent** — no status-of-forces or host-nation agreement covers United States activity in Syrian sovereign territory; the legal predicate rests on national authorities.

## 6. DIME integration

**Diplomatic.** Regional coordination is constrained: a North Atlantic Treaty Organization ally (Türkiye) opposes support to the ARC and denies northern access; host-nation consent is absent; cross-border access through Iraqi territory is tacit and politically reversible. Diplomatic effort is oriented on preserving Iraqi tolerance and managing allied friction.

**Informational.** The regime, Iranian-backed elements, and the Russian presence sustain a contested information environment in which United States and partner activity is subject to disinformation and pre-emptive attribution narratives. Information effort is oriented on exposing the Iranian and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps hand and countering disinformation, within deniability discipline.

**Military.** The military contribution is an unconventional-warfare supporting effort executed through SOCCENT, by, with, and through the ARC, below the threshold of overt armed conflict, and deconflicted with Russian forces present in theater.

**Economic.** Critical infrastructure in the operational environment — the Euphrates dams supplying power and water, and eastern hydrocarbon production — bears on the legitimacy and revenue of any actor controlling the valley and is a civil-vulnerability consideration.

## 7. Strategic risk framing

National and theater guidance accept the risk inherent in a partnered, deniable approach in a denied area, in exchange for avoiding a direct United States–regime or United States–Iran armed conflict. The strategic-risk emphasis is on attribution management, escalation control, and the human-rights legitimacy of the partner. Mission analysis admits no single right answer; the commander decides, grounded in doctrine.

title: Regional Intel Summary
text:
UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

# 02 — REGIONAL INTELLIGENCE SUMMARY

**Product type:** USPACOM J2 higher-headquarters intelligence background. **From:** USPACOM **DTG of issue:** 150400Z MAR 2026. **Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E).

> This summary provides the higher-headquarters intelligence background and escalation history for the mission-analysis staff. Assessments are stated at confidence; attribution of the Iranian directing hand is a cross-source assessment, not an open-source finding.

## 1. Strategic setting

Northeast Syria has remained a contested seam since the territorial defeat of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS). The Syrian regime, lacking the regular manpower to administer the eastern governorates, has come to rely on Iranian-backed proxy manpower to extend control. Iran's enduring strategic objective in the area is the securing of a contiguous ground line of communication — the "land bridge" — from Iranian territory through Iraq and Syria toward the Mediterranean littoral. The middle Euphrates valley is the decisive terrain for that line of communication, and partner-held ground in the Jazira has been the principal obstacle to its completion.

## 2. Road to war — escalation arc (preceding 90 days)

- **D-90 to D-60.** Iranian-backed proxy militias (principally Liwa al-Sadiq) reinforce in the western and middle Euphrates valley under cover of regime "counter-terrorism" framing. Advisory activity attributed to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps–Quds Force element (the Ansar Advisory Group) increases coordination among proxy formations.

- **D-60 to D-30.** Proxy forces conduct probing actions against Azadî Resistance Council (ARC) forward positions and interdict secondary supply movements along route BADGER. Regime intelligence activity against the ARC underground in Hasakah and Qamishli intensifies.

- **D-30 to D-7.** Proxy forces mass within indirect-fire range of the Tel Roj salient. Regional information channels pre-position an attribution narrative framing any escalation as a domestic counter-terrorism operation and accusing external powers of destabilization.

- **D-Day (150600Z MAR 2026).** Iranian-backed proxy forces seize the Tel Roj junction, sever route BADGER — the ARC's principal external support corridor — and displace the Roj Brigades from forward positions in the Tel Roj pocket, isolating the guerrilla force from external resupply.

## 3. Character of the offensive

The consolidation is led by Iranian-backed proxy militias — principally Liwa al-Sadiq, reinforced, with elements of Saraya Khorasan — operating alongside but distinct from Syrian regime regular formations. The proxy character of the lead echelon is assessed with moderate confidence and resolves only by cross-reading signals and human reporting against the adversary order of battle (document 03); surface and open-source reporting attribute the action to regime regulars. The Ansar Advisory Group is assessed to provide command, enabling, and indirect-fire coordination; its hand is concealed to preserve Iranian deniability. Employment of proxies in the lead is assessed as a deliberate measure to keep Iranian direction below the threshold of attributable state action.

## 4. Partner force — Azadî Resistance Council

The ARC is a Kurdish-led umbrella movement with Arab tribal affiliates of variable reliability. It is organized consistent with a doctrinal resistance:

- **Underground (Komel network).** Clandestine cells in the urban centers of Hasakah and Qamishli conducting intelligence, subversion, and early warning. Assessed penetrated by regime intelligence; communications security weak.

- **Auxiliary (Hêlîn network).** A clandestine support element providing logistics, safe houses, movement assistance, and early warning to the guerrilla force.

- **Guerrilla force (Roj Brigades).** The overt military arm, an estimated 2,500 fighters with limited heavy weapons, low ammunition stocks, and no organic sustainment independent of route BADGER.

Partner cohesion is assessed as adequate at present but degrading. Absent restoration of resupply, the Roj Brigades are assessed at risk of culmination or fragmentation within the near term — the binding planning timeline for any external support.

## 5. Population and terrain

The Jazira and the middle Euphrates valley present an ethnic-mosaic human terrain of Kurdish, Arab tribal, and minority communities. Partner legitimacy and freedom of movement vary by district: strong in Kurdish-majority districts of Hasakah and Qamishli, contested in Arab-majority districts along the Euphrates, where the ARC is viewed with suspicion and the population is more susceptible to regime and proxy influence. Internally displaced concentrations in Hasakah governorate add civil density and complicate the distinction between combatants and non-combatants.

## 6. Electronic and information environment

Adversary electronic warfare — attributed to proxy and Iranian-advisory systems and to Russian-enabled capability resident in theater — degrades Global Positioning System reception and tactical communications across the Euphrates valley. The information environment is contested by regime, Iranian, and Russian narratives, including a pre-emptive attribution narrative directed at United States and partner activity.

## 7. Residual ISIS threat

ISIS remnant cells persist in the Badia desert and exploit security vacuums. Diversion of regime and proxy attention toward a resistance buildup is assessed as a condition that could enable localized ISIS resurgence, with attendant risk to lines of communication and to the broader counter-ISIS gains the campaign seeks to protect.

## 8. External actors

- **Russia.** Maintains presence and air-defense coverage from Hmeimim air base; coverage extends over the Euphrates valley. A deconfliction mechanism exists; Russia is not a coordinating partner.

- **Türkiye.** Opposes the ARC, which Ankara assesses as linked to a designated terrorist organization, and denies cross-border access, overflight, and basing from the north.

- **Iraq.** Has not granted explicit consent for cross-border movement; tolerates low-visibility movement through the Rabia/Yaroubiya and al-Walid–al-Tanf area crossings, reversible under Iranian-aligned political pressure.

## 9. Assessment

The seizure of the Tel Roj junction is assessed as a deliberate, Iranian-enabled step to complete the land-bridge consolidation and to collapse the only viable indigenous resistance before it can be reinforced. The dominant unknowns are Iranian intent and the proxy reinforcement timeline, partner cohesion under pressure, and the trafficability of any restored or alternate corridor. The window in which external support can preserve the partner is assessed as narrow.
