**Enemy fires.** PRC has dense fires capability: PLAN ASCM (YJ-18 / YJ-12), submarine ASCM (YJ-18 / YJ-82), coastal-defense ASCM (YJ-12B mobile), and theater-range fires (PLA Rocket Force DF-21D / DF-26B). Outpost-based fires are within engagement envelope of much of the JOA. PRC has not initiated theater-strategic fires; PLARF DF-26B at baseline.

**Friendly fires.** US Navy: SM-6 / Tomahawk LACM / Tomahawk Block V anti-ship from CSG escorts and SSNs. US Air Force: AGM-158 JASSM-ER; AGM-158C LRASM (from B-1B / F-18 / F-15E); precision munitions from F-22 / F-35. USMC: HIMARS, NSM (Naval Strike Missile shore-based capability from 3d MEB). Coalition: Australian SM-6 / Tomahawk capability; UK Type 45 SM-6 / Sea Viper; Japanese SM-3 (BMD). Joint Targeting Cycle led by JTF J3 Fires Cell.

**Civilian considerations.** Pag-asa civilian population (~250); commercial maritime traffic; environmental sensitivities (coral reef / UNCLOS Art. 192 protections).

**Assumptions.** - ROE will permit engagement of declared hostile PRC forces on Pag-asa and engagement of Spratly outposts subject to proportionality. - No PRC mainland targeting absent Presidential release. - Precision munition inventory will be sufficient for sustained operations through D+30. - Collateral damage estimation tools / processes will operate in compressed timeline.

### 3.2 Mission (Fires)

Plan and execute joint and coalition fires to: (a) degrade PRC Spratly outpost air defense and ASCM capability; (b) suppress PRC fires during sea control and air superiority operations; (c) prepare and support amphibious restoration of Pag-asa; (d) protect coalition forces; (e) maintain disciplined non-escalation against PRC mainland.

### 3.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - US precision-strike capability significantly outclasses PRC defensive coverage at standoff range. - Multi-domain fires integration (sea / air / sub-surface). - Allied AAW destroyers (Australian Hobart-class; UK Type 45) provide additional SM-6 capacity.

**Limitations.** - Precision-munition stockpile is finite; sustained operations against hardened targets will deplete inventory. - HQ-9B / Type 366 / KJ-500 integrated PRC air defense imposes significant SEAD/DEAD requirement before strike operations are at acceptable risk. - Coral-reef and protected marine area considerations constrain targeting in some areas. - Coalition fires interoperability — particularly with Japanese forces in association — is constrained.

**Critical Issues.** - HPTL prioritization sequence — outpost air defense first (enables strike), then outpost ASCM (enables maritime maneuver), then PLAN South Sea Fleet combatants, then runway / HAS. - Collateral damage estimation discipline — strike approval must integrate civilian / coral reef / commercial traffic considerations. - Precision-munition inventory: AIM-120 / AIM-9X (air-to-air), SM-6 / SM-2 (air defense), Tomahawk / JASSM / LRASM (long-range strike). Coordinate with USSTRATCOM and CSAF for inventory management.

**Risks.** - HIGH: Precision-munition depletion under sustained operations. - MED: Civilian casualties at Pag-asa from fires (mitigated by strict proportionality discipline). - MED: PRC escalation in response to outpost engagement (mitigated by deliberate non-escalation discipline). - LOW: Coalition fires deconfliction failure.

### 3.4 Conclusions and Recommendations

Fires capability is sufficient for operational requirement subject to inventory management. Specific actions:

1.  **NLT N+3:** Establish JTF Fires Cell at JTF HQ; integrate USAF, USN, USMC, allied liaison.

2.  **NLT N+5:** Develop initial HPTL (J2 / J3 Fires).

3.  **NLT N+7:** Coordinate with CSAF / CSAF AFGSC / CNO for precision-munition surge.

4.  **NLT N+10:** Joint Targeting Cycle established; daily Targeting Working Group functioning.

5.  **Pre-D-Day:** CCDR personally approves HPTL; ROE adjudication for novel target sets.

6.  **Continuous:** Monitor precision-munition expenditure; submit RFFs as required.

## 4. Movement and Maneuver Running Estimate

**Lead:** USINDOPACOM J3 / J5; supported by USTRANSCOM, JFMCC, JFACC, JFLCC, MARFORPAC **As of:** 261800Z AUG 26

### 4.1 Situation and Considerations

**Higher HQ mission, intent, and concept.** Per CIPG: rapid coalition force closure into the Indo-Pacific; sea-control and air-superiority operations to enable amphibious restoration; protect FoN throughout.

**Enemy movement and maneuver.** PRC SAGs underway in SCS; SSN dispositions in SCS; PLAN amphibious shipping operating cycle Yulin↔Spratlys; PLAAF central-Spratly CAP. PLA Marine Corps reinforcement of Pag-asa ongoing.

**Friendly movement and maneuver.** Multi-domain coalition force closing into theater per 04_Coalition_OOB.md. Phase 0 shaping; Phase 1 sea-control + air-superiority; Phase 2 restoration; Phase 3 stabilization; Phase 4 transition.

**Civilian considerations.** Substantial commercial shipping continues in SCS at reduced volume (~70% of normal); commercial aviation deconflicted around JOA airspace; civilian fishing communities affected.

**Assumptions.** - Strategic lift availability sufficient for planned closure timeline. - Allied / partner basing remains available (Singapore, Australia, Japan, Philippines, Guam). - Bashi Channel, Mindoro Strait, Sibutu Passage remain transit-able. - Weather window (typhoon-free) of ≥5 days available for amphibious operations.

### 4.2 Mission (Movement and Maneuver)

Deploy, employ, and sustain coalition forces in the JOA with appropriate sequencing to enable sea control, air superiority, and amphibious restoration on the directed timeline, while preserving freedom of navigation in international waters and airspace.

### 4.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - USTRANSCOM strategic lift (AMC C-17 / C-5; MSC LMSR / T-AKE). - Self-deploying naval forces (CSGs, SAGs, ARGs, SSNs). - Rotational air mobility (Kadena, Andersen, Yokota, Hickam). - Philippine EDCA sites operational and accessible.

**Limitations.** - SPOD throughput at Philippine ports (Puerto Princesa, Subic, Manila) limited; Singapore primary. - APOD throughput at Clark and Antonio Bautista approaches saturation under sustained operations. - LMSR fleet on global commitment; prioritization required. - Coalition force closure subject to national authorization timelines. - Typhoon season may force force-flow disruption.

**Critical Issues.** - TPFDD (Time-Phased Force Deployment Data) discipline — particularly for sustainment-first sequencing. - SPOD throughput optimization — transload at Singapore to forward Philippine ports. - Coalition force-flow integration into TPFDD. - Airspace control authority establishment and FIR deconfliction.

**Risks.** - MED-HIGH: SPOD / APOD throughput bottlenecks delay D-Day. - MED: Typhoon force-flow disruption. - MED: PRC maritime interdiction of coalition transit (mitigated by sea-control phase). - LOW: Strategic lift availability shortfall.

### 4.4 Conclusions and Recommendations

Force-flow plan is achievable on planning timeline subject to SPOD / APOD throughput optimization. Specific actions:

1.  **Immediate:** Activate USTRANSCOM force-flow planning cell at JTF HQ.

2.  **NLT N+3:** TPFDD complete for first 30-day force flow.

3.  **NLT N+5:** SPOD / APOD throughput plan complete; transload to Philippine ports established.

4.  **NLT N+7:** Airspace control authority designated; FIR deconfliction established with Manila, Singapore FIRs.

5.  **NLT N+10:** Coalition force closure validated; TOA confirmed.

6.  **Continuous:** Daily force-closure tracking; typhoon-track monitoring; FoN operations continued.

## 5. Protection Running Estimate

**Lead:** USINDOPACOM J3 / J6 / J7 (Protection Cell); supported by FLTCYBERCOM, SOCPAC, USSPACECOM, USTRANSCOM **As of:** 261800Z AUG 26

### 5.1 Situation and Considerations

**Higher HQ mission, intent, and concept.** Per CIPG: dispersed force posture; integrated air and missile defense; submarine awareness; cyber / cable / SLOC protection; personnel protection and Personnel Recovery.

**Enemy threats.** PRC ASCM (sea / sub / air / land-based); PRC SAM (HQ-9B from outposts; long-range from mainland); PRC theater-range fires (PLARF DF-26B / DF-21D); PRC cyber (VOLT / SALT TYPHOON); PRC counter-space; PRC information operations / disinformation; PRC submarine forces. PRC has demonstrated willingness for asymmetric / deniable action.

**Friendly protection posture.** FPCON BRAVO theater-wide; FPCON CHARLIE at forward sites. Aegis BMD-capable Type 052D and 7th Fleet equivalents at sea; ground-based PATRIOT and THAAD coverage where positioned. FLTCYBERCOM CPTs (2) for DCO. SOCPAC PR capability. USSPACECOM space-domain awareness.

**Civilian considerations.** Substantial Philippine, US, and TCN civilians at risk; commercial traffic exposed; submarine cable users (telecommunications providers; internet routing) affected.

**Assumptions.** - PRC will not initiate strategic-escalation kinetic action against US forces (per MLCOA). - PRC cyber action will be persistent but at threshold below war-crime severity. - Submarine cable interdiction is a credible PRC option not yet activated. - Coalition force-protection cooperation will continue.

### 5.2 Mission (Protection)

Protect coalition forces, partner forces, critical infrastructure (C2, ISR, SPOD/APOD, submarine cables), and Philippine civilian populations against adversary threats across all domains; conduct effective Personnel Recovery; manage POW / detainee processes under international law.

### 5.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - Aegis BMD; PATRIOT; THAAD; integrated air and missile defense network. - Submarine awareness via P-8A, T-AGOS, SSN-on-SSN tracking. - Cyber defensive operations through FLTCYBERCOM CPTs and USCYBERCOM backstop. - Coalition force-protection cooperation (allied AAW destroyers add SM-6 capacity). - Personnel Recovery capability via SOCPAC, 129 RQS HH-60G.

**Limitations.** - DF-26B / DF-21D coverage from PLA Rocket Force at theater range; only Aegis BMD or specialized SSC capability defends. - PRC counter-space and PNT-denial may degrade BMD radar coverage. - Submarine cable protection is inherently limited — cables are vulnerable and prevention is hard. - Coalition CENTRIXS provisioning lag may delay full IAMD interoperability. - POW handling capacity in theater is modest; ICRC engagement critical.

**Critical Issues.** - AFP/PCG personnel detained at Pag-asa (~25 captured) require ICRC engagement and care for POW protection. - US citizens believed captured at Pag-asa (3 contractors) require diplomatic and ICRC engagement. - Pag-asa civilian population (~250) is at risk in any kinetic restoration; evacuation planning critical. - Cable disruption risk requires industry coordination and rapid-repair capability. - Force-protection at SPOD / APOD nodes (high-density US presence) is a force-protection challenge.

**Risks.** - HIGH: Detained personnel mistreatment (mitigated by ICRC engagement and PRC accountability statements). - MED-HIGH: Successful PRC ASCM engagement of US/coalition surface combatant. - MED: Pag-asa civilian casualties during restoration. - MED: Submarine cable disruption. - MED: Cyber action against critical infrastructure (financial, energy, transportation). - LOW: PRC PLARF kinetic action against forward bases.

### 5.4 Conclusions and Recommendations

Protection posture is achievable but requires sustained discipline. Specific actions:

1.  **Immediate:** ICRC liaison established for detained AFP/PCG and US-citizen personnel.

2.  **NLT N+3:** JTF PR Center established at WESCOM Puerto Princesa.

3.  **NLT N+5:** Coalition IAMD architecture established; SM-6 / SM-3 inventory consolidated.

4.  **NLT N+5:** Coordinate with submarine cable industry partners for rapid-repair capability pre-positioning.

5.  **NLT N+7:** Pag-asa civilian evacuation plan complete; AFP / PCG coordination via BCC.

6.  **Continuous:** FLTCYBERCOM CPT DCO; cyber threat hunting; FPCON management.

## 6. Sustainment Running Estimate

**Lead:** USINDOPACOM J4; supported by USTRANSCOM, MSC, DLA, COMMPSRON TWO/THREE, CTF 73, 8 TSC **As of:** 261800Z AUG 26

### 6.1 Situation and Considerations

**Higher HQ mission, intent, and concept.** Per CIPG: robust sustainment that does not break the strategic-lift system; SPOD prioritization (Singapore primary, Subic secondary, Cebu tertiary); APOD prioritization (Clark primary, Antonio Bautista secondary, Lal-lo / Mactan tertiary); prepositional stocks activation; host-nation support engaged.

**Enemy sustainment.** PRC sustains forward Spratly outposts and Pag-asa garrison via sea-line resupply from Hainan; sustained pattern of resupply ships and PAFMM logistics. PRC has interior lines and well-established forward logistic architecture.

**Friendly sustainment posture.** USTRANSCOM strategic lift planning underway; MSC sealift (LMSR, T-AKE, T-AO) committed; AMC airlift (C-17 / C-5 / KC-46) on rotational surge. Existing forward sustainment via CTF 73 / LOGFOR Singapore. Marine Prepositioning Squadron Two (Diego Garcia) and Three (Guam) available. EDCA sites in Philippines provide host-nation support.

**Civilian considerations.** Commercial supply chain affected by SCS war-risk premia (~300% surge); maritime insurance market under stress; commercial fuel and food security at SPODs.

**Assumptions.** - Strategic lift will be available for surge force flow. - Allied / partner host-nation support continues (Singapore, Philippines, Australia, Japan). - Commercial fuel and food supply chains continue at SPOD locations. - Marine Prepositioning Squadrons will be activated and lifted to forward areas.

### 6.2 Mission (Sustainment)

Provide and sustain personnel, equipment, supplies (Class I-IX), maintenance, medical, mortuary, transportation, and contracting support to coalition forces in the JOA throughout the operation, with sufficient redundancy to survive degraded conditions.

### 6.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - USTRANSCOM strategic lift sufficient for surge under current commitments. - Forward sustainment hub at Singapore (Sembawang / Changi / Paya Lebar / Tengah). - Marine Prepositioning Squadrons (MPS Two at Diego Garcia; MPS Three at Guam) provide pre-deployed equipment. - Multiple SPOD / APOD options through host-nation cooperation. - DLA / Defense Fuel Support Point capability.

**Limitations.** - Philippine SPODs (Puerto Princesa, Subic, Manila) have throughput limits; Singapore is primary. - APOD Clark / Antonio Bautista approach saturation under sustained operations. - LMSR fleet on global commitment; prioritization required against USFK / EUCOM / CENTCOM. - MCM capacity finite (4 hulls allocated, 2 in reserve); SCS approaches may require mine-clearing. - Coalition sustainment integration challenging (different fuel standards, food / messing standards, repair parts).

**Critical Issues.** - Singapore SPOD throughput will be the choke point under sustained operations. - Transload from Singapore to Subic / Cebu / Manila adds 24–48 hours to force flow. - Marine Prepositioning Squadron activation timeline — MPS Two from Diego Garcia is 7–10 days to JOA. - Medical capability — Role 3 afloat (USS *Tripoli*; HMAS *Adelaide* when in) and at Tripler / Guam; coalition coordination needed. - POW / detainee handling logistics — Geneva-compliant facilities required.

**Risks.** - HIGH: SPOD throughput bottleneck delays D-Day. - MED-HIGH: Precision-munition resupply (Class V) shortfall under sustained operations. - MED: LMSR availability shortfall against global commitments. - MED: Submarine cable disruption affecting logistics-supporting communications. - LOW: Fuel availability shortfall at SPODs.

### 6.4 Conclusions and Recommendations

Sustainment plan is achievable on planning timeline subject to throughput optimization and prepositioning activation. Specific actions:

1.  **Immediate:** Activate MPS Two and Three; commence lift planning.

2.  **Immediate:** USTRANSCOM joint planning cell at JTF HQ.

3.  **NLT N+3:** SPOD / APOD throughput plan complete.

4.  **NLT N+5:** Coalition sustainment integration cell established.

5.  **NLT N+5:** Precision-munition (Class V) inventory consolidated; surge production RFF submitted.

6.  **NLT N+7:** Role 3 medical capability validated; coalition medical coordination established.

7.  **NLT N+10:** Forward sustainment hub at Singapore at full operating capability.

8.  **Continuous:** Daily Class I / III / V / IX status; weekly sustainment forecast.

## 7. Information Running Estimate

**Lead:** USINDOPACOM J39 Information Operations; supported by J3 IO, J6, FLTCYBERCOM, USCYBERCOM, USSPACECOM, OSD-PA **As of:** 261800Z AUG 26

### 7.1 Situation and Considerations

**Higher HQ mission, intent, and concept.** Per CIPG: disciplined information operations integrated with kinetic action; counter PRC “lawful enforcement” narrative; preserve coalition narrative discipline; integrate EW; coordinate cyber.

**Enemy information operations.** PLA Information Support Force (post-2024 SSF reorganization) operates layered IO: state-controlled media (Xinhua, Global Times, CCTV); academic and legal-warfare publication; coordinated social media on Weibo / WeChat / TikTok / X; pre-staged content; AI-generated content; coordinated influence operations through PRC-aligned channels. PRC narrative is “lawful enforcement of PRC sovereign waters” with US framed as “external interference.”

**Friendly information posture.** OSD-PA (DOD), DOS R (State), partner Strategic Communications functions (UK Cabinet Office, AU OPM, JP MOFA, NZ DPMC), Philippine AFP / PCG Transparency Initiative. CSIS AMTI and partner think-tank network as supporting voice. Coalition counter-narrative integrated through liaison cells.

**Civilian considerations.** Civilian populations in PH / AU / JP / UK / US / PRC are key target audiences; diaspora populations are amplifiers; commercial information ecosystem (Big Tech platforms) operates outside government control.

**Assumptions.** - US-coalition strategic communications will retain factual high ground. - PRC will continue narrative effort with high tempo. - Allied government public communications will remain coordinated. - Commercial information platforms (Meta, X, TikTok, YouTube) will moderate at usual scale; major changes unlikely in operational window. - AI-generated disinformation will be prevalent; detection tools imperfect.

### 7.2 Mission (Information)

Through coordinated narrative alignment, counter-information operations, electronic warfare, and cyberspace operations, support CDR USINDOPACOM’s strategic objectives by: (a) maintaining factual coalition narrative dominance in English-language and partner-language spaces; (b) countering PRC “lawful enforcement” framing; (c) demonstrating coalition unity; (d) enabling kinetic action through information effects (deception, denial); (e) preserving operational security.

### 7.3 Analysis

**Capabilities.** - Coordinated coalition strategic communications. - Philippine AFP / PCG Transparency Initiative as factual rebuttal mechanism. - CSIS AMTI and partner think-tank network as third-party validators. - Cyberspace defensive capability (FLTCYBERCOM CPTs). - Electronic warfare capability (USAF E-EC; USN E-18G; USMC EA-6B / E-EC; allied EW units).

**Limitations.** - PRC narrative dominance in Mandarin-language space is structural. - AI-generated content detection is imperfect; disinformation prevalence will be high. - Coalition strategic-communications coordination has friction (different national agendas). - Offensive cyber against PRC infrastructure outside JOA requires Presidential release. - EW operations against PRC mainland sensors require Presidential release.

**Critical Issues.** - “Lawful enforcement” framing — needs continuous factual rebuttal grounded in PCA Award / UNCLOS. - Civilian-casualty narrative — every strike must be defensible; OPLAW review with IO coordination. - Coalition cohesion narrative — visible coalition unity matters more than messaging volume. - Counter-disinformation rapid-response — particularly against AI-generated content depicting purported AFP atrocities. - Operational security — protecting coalition force-flow patterns from PRC ISR / OSINT-collection.

**Risks.** - HIGH: AI-generated disinformation succeeds in shifting narrative on key incident. - MED: Coalition strategic-communications dissonance. - MED: PRC information escalation provoking US over-response. - MED: OPSEC compromise revealing force-flow patterns. - LOW: Loss of access to major commercial platforms.

### 7.4 Conclusions and Recommendations

Information posture is achievable with sustained discipline. Specific actions:

1.  **Immediate:** Establish JTF Information Operations Cell; integrate J39, J3 IO, J6, FLTCYBERCOM, USCYBERCOM, USSPACECOM, OSD-PA.

2.  **NLT N+3:** Coalition Strategic Communications Coordination Cell established.

3.  **NLT N+5:** Counter-disinformation rapid-response capability operational.

4.  **NLT N+5:** Daily IO Working Group functioning.

5.  **NLT N+7:** EW Working Group functioning; OCO RFI process to USCYBERCOM established.

6.  **Continuous:** Narrative monitoring; OPSEC discipline; coalition coordination; AI-content detection.

## 8. Cross-Functional Conclusions

Across the seven joint functions, the most binding constraints are:

1.  **Coalition force-flow timing** (Movement and Maneuver) — particularly SPOD throughput at Singapore and APOD throughput at Clark / Antonio Bautista.

2.  **Precision-munition inventory** (Fires + Sustainment) — sustainment must surge Class V; fires must conserve.

3.  **Cyber-pre-positioning risk** (C2 + Protection + Information) — DCO must be persistent; PACE must be exercised.

4.  **Strategic communications discipline** (Information) — narrative must hold under sustained PRC pressure.

5.  **POW / detainee handling** (Protection + OPLAW) — ICRC engagement is the lever; AFP/PCG and US-citizen accountability is the political dependency.

All seven functions can support CCDR planning intent on the directed timeline subject to identified RFFs and risk-management actions. Significant slip in any one function (particularly SPOD throughput or precision-munition surge) will cascade to D-Day timing.

1. (E) GENERAL. ON 22 AUGUST 2026 (220400L), PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA (PRC) FORCES CONDUCTED A DELIBERATE ARMED ATTACK ON PAG-ASA ISLAND, AN ISLAND TERRITORY UNDER PHILIPPINE JURISDICTION IN THE PACIFIC, KILLING 14 ARMED FORCES OF THE PHILIPPINES (AFP) AND PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD (PCG) PERSONNEL ASHORE AND 11 ADDITIONAL PCG PERSONNEL ABOARD THE PHILIPPINE PUBLIC VESSEL BRP TERESA MAGBANUA. THREE US CITIZENS ASSESSED CAPTURED. THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES HAS DETERMINED (REF C) THAT THE CONDITIONS OF ARTICLE V OF THE 1951 US-PHILIPPINES MUTUAL DEFENSE TREATY ARE SATISFIED. PER REF A, THE PRESIDENT HAS APPROVED COURSE OF ACTION TWO (COA-2 SHAPING-AND-NEGOTIATE) FROM THE USINDOPACOM TWO-COA DECISION BRIEF OF 041200ZSEP26.\
\
2. (E) ADVERSARY SITUATION. PRC RETAINS A REINFORCED BATTALION-EQUIVALENT GARRISON ON PAG-ASA ISLAND WITH ORGANIC AIR DEFENSE (HQ-17 / FN-16) AND ANTI-SHIP CAPABILITY. PLAN SOUTH SEA FLEET MAINTAINS SURFACE ACTION GROUP (ONE TYPE 055, TWO TYPE 052D, ASSOCIATED REPLENISHMENT) IN THE CENTRAL SPRATLY AREA. PLAAF MAINTAINS COMBAT AIR PATROL FROM YONGXING (WOODY ISLAND) AND FROM PRC-MILITARIZED FEATURES AT MISCHIEF, SUBI, AND FIERY CROSS. CCG AND PAFMM ELEMENTS REMAIN POSTURED FOR SUSTAINED GRAY-ZONE PRESENCE. PRC STRATEGIC POSTURE ASSESSED AS CALIBRATED DEFENSE WITH PRESERVED DIPLOMATIC OFF-RAMP; PRC HAS NOT INITIATED CROSS-STRAIT ACTION AND HAS NOT ELEVATED NUCLEAR POSTURE.\
\
3. (E) FRIENDLY SITUATION. PHILIPPINE AFP HAS DECLARED A STATE OF NATIONAL EMERGENCY AND FORMALLY REQUESTED COALITION MILITARY ASSISTANCE UNDER MDT ARTICLE IV. AUSTRALIA, JAPAN, UNITED KINGDOM, AND NEW ZEALAND HAVE FORMALIZED FORCE CONTRIBUTIONS. SINGAPORE, VIETNAM, INDONESIA, MALAYSIA, AND BRUNEI HAVE PROVIDED QUIET LOGISTICS, INTELLIGENCE, AND TRANSIT SUPPORT. USFK / CINCUNC RETAINS ALLOCATED FORCES FOR PENINSULAR DETERRENCE AT CURRENT LEVELS. KOREAN PENINSULA AND TAIWAN STRAIT ASSESSED STABLE BUT ELEVATED.\
\
4. (E) ASSUMPTIONS.\
\
A. (E) PRC WILL NOT INITIATE CROSS-STRAIT MILITARY ACTION DURING THE EXECUTION WINDOW.\
B. (E) PRC WILL NOT ELEVATE NUCLEAR POSTURE OR EMPLOY STRATEGIC WEAPONS.\
C. (E) RUSSIAN FEDERATION WILL NOT MATERIALLY INTERFERE WITH INDO-PACIFIC OPERATIONS BEYOND NOMINAL ISR PARTICIPATION.\
D. (E) THE STRAITS OF MALACCA, SUNDA, AND LOMBOK WILL REMAIN OPEN.\
E. (E) DPRK WILL NOT INITIATE PROVOCATION SUFFICIENT TO REQUIRE DRAW-DOWN OF USFK COMBAT POWER.\
F. (E) COALITION DOMESTIC POLITICAL SUPPORT WILL REMAIN SUFFICIENT THROUGH D+90.\
G. (E) PHILIPPINE GOVERNMENT WILL SUSTAIN PUBLIC CONSENT FOR COALITION OPERATIONS FROM PHILIPPINE TERRITORY.\
H. (E) USTRANSCOM STRATEGIC LIFT WILL SUPPORT PROJECTED FORCE FLOW WITHOUT MATERIAL DEGRADATION OF STANDING COMMITMENTS.\
\

5. (E) MISSION. EFFECTIVE ON RECEIPT OF THIS ORDER, USINDOPACOM (SUPPORTED) EXECUTES OPERATION PACIFIC HARRIER UNDER COA-2 (SHAPING-AND-NEGOTIATE) TO IMPOSE COST ON PRC AGGRESSION THROUGH CONTINUOUS ISR, FREEDOM-OF-NAVIGATION OPERATIONS, COALITION MARITIME AND AIR PRESENCE, AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE; TO DEMONSTRATE CREDIBLE COALITION CAPABILITY SUFFICIENT TO COMPEL PRC ACCEPTANCE OF A DIPLOMATIC OFF-RAMP RESTORING PHILIPPINE TERRITORIAL INTEGRITY; AND TO PRESERVE THE FORWARD POSTURE, OPTIONS, AND READINESS NECESSARY TO TRANSITION TO COA-1 (ISOLATE-AND-RESTORE) UPON DECISION BY THE PRESIDENT IF NEGOTIATION FAILS — IN ORDER TO RESTORE PHILIPPINE SOVEREIGNTY OVER THE PAG-ASA CLUSTER, DEFEND THE PHILIPPINES FROM ADDITIONAL ARMED ATTACK, DETER FURTHER PRC AGGRESSION IN THE SOUTH CHINA SEA, AND REINFORCE THE CREDIBILITY OF US INDO-PACIFIC ALLIANCES, CONSISTENT WITH ARTICLE IV OBLIGATIONS UNDER THE 1951 US-PHILIPPINES MUTUAL DEFENSE TREATY.\
\

6. (E) COMMANDER'S INTENT (CHAIRMAN). MY INTENT IS THAT WE PROSECUTE THIS OPERATION AS A DELIBERATE, DISCIPLINED COALITION CAMPAIGN OF PRESSURE — NOT A WAR OF ANNIHILATION — DESIGNED TO PRODUCE A NEGOTIATED RESTORATION OF PHILIPPINE SOVEREIGNTY ON FAVORABLE TERMS WHILE PRESERVING OUR CAPACITY TO ESCALATE IF NEGOTIATION FAILS. EVERY DEPLOYMENT, EVERY FONOP, EVERY ISR LINE, EVERY COALITION PORT CALL IS AN INSTRUMENT OF THE DIPLOMATIC EFFORT, NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR IT. WE WILL OPERATE AT A TEMPO THAT IS UNMISTAKABLY SERIOUS BUT THAT LEAVES THE PRC A FACE-SAVING EXIT. WE WILL NOT EXPAND THE CONFLICT BEYOND THE JOINT OPERATIONS AREA. WE WILL NOT TARGET THE PRC MAINLAND. WE WILL NOT BE THE FIRST TO ESCALATE INTO ATTRITION. WE WILL HOLD THE AMPHIBIOUS RESTORATION OPTION VISIBLE, READY, AND CREDIBLE — AND WE WILL EXECUTE IT IF AND ONLY IF DIRECTED BY THE PRESIDENT. THE END STATE IS RESTORED PHILIPPINE TERRITORIAL INTEGRITY OVER THE PAG-ASA CLUSTER, REINFORCED ALLIANCE CREDIBILITY, PRESERVED INDOPACOM POSTURE FOR CONTINUED KOREAN PENINSULA AND TAIWAN STRAIT DETERRENCE, AND A REGIONAL ORDER IN WHICH PRC RECOGNIZES THAT KINETIC SEIZURE OF DISPUTED FEATURES IS NOT A SUSTAINABLE INSTRUMENT OF POLICY.\
\
7. (E) CONCEPT OF OPERATIONS.\
\
A. (E) APPROVED COA. COA-2 (SHAPING-AND-NEGOTIATE) IS APPROVED AS THE PRIMARY COURSE OF ACTION. COA-1 (ISOLATE-AND-RESTORE) IS APPROVED AS THE ON-ORDER BRANCH UPON FAILURE OF NEGOTIATION. USINDOPACOM WILL MAINTAIN COA-1 AT A LEVEL OF READINESS SUCH THAT TRANSITION FROM COA-2 TO COA-1 IS EXECUTABLE WITHIN 96 HOURS OF DIRECTION.\
\
B. (E) MAIN EFFORT. THE PACIFIC HARRIER COALITION DEMONSTRATION AND PRESENCE CAMPAIGN IS THE INDOPACOM SUPPORTED MAIN EFFORT. CONTINUED USFK PENINSULAR DETERRENCE AND TAIWAN STRAIT STANDING DETERRENT POSTURE REMAIN INDOPACOM PRIORITY-OF-EFFORT TASKS NOT TO BE DEGRADED IN SUPPORT OF PACIFIC HARRIER.\
\
C. (E) PHASES. EXECUTION WILL BE CONDUCTED IN FIVE PHASES CONSISTENT WITH REF F:\
\
(1) (E) PHASE I — SHAPING AND POSTURE (ONGOING; CULMINATES D-DAY +14). RAPID FORCE CLOSURE; ESTABLISHMENT OF COALITION C2; ACTIVATION OF PHILIPPINE EDCA SITES; ESTABLISHMENT OF AIR BRIDGE TO ANTONIO BAUTISTA AB AND CLARK AB; ESTABLISHMENT OF MARITIME AND AIR PRESENCE PATTERN; INITIATION OF FONOP CADENCE.\
\
(2) (E) PHASE II — SUSTAINED PRESSURE (D+15 TO D+60). HIGH-VISIBILITY COALITION MARITIME AND AIR PRESENCE IN AND ADJACENT TO THE JOA; CONTINUOUS ISR ON PRC FORCES; FONOP CADENCE PER ANNEX C OF REF F; SYNCHRONIZATION WITH TREASURY-LED ECONOMIC PRESSURE MEASURES; SYNCHRONIZATION WITH DOS-LED ASEAN AND UN DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS; SYNCHRONIZATION WITH PHILIPPINE AFP/PCG TRANSPARENCY INITIATIVE; CONTINUOUS COA-1 RECONSTITUTION POSTURE.\
\
(3) (E) PHASE III — DECISION (D+60 TO D+90). ASSESSMENT OF DIPLOMATIC PROGRESS AGAINST TERMINATION CRITERIA; CCDR-LED RECOMMENDATION TO SECDEF AND CJCS NLT D+75 ON ONE OF: (A) CONTINUE COA-2; (B) TRANSITION TO COA-1; (C) INITIATE PHASE IV. AMPLIFICATION OF PRESSURE INSTRUMENTS AS DIRECTED.\
\
(4) (E) PHASE IV — STABILIZATION (D+90 ONWARD, AS DIRECTED). UPON ACHIEVEMENT OF NEGOTIATED OR COMPELLED PRC WITHDRAWAL, COALITION SUPPORT TO PHILIPPINE RE-OCCUPATION OF PAG-ASA; AFP/PCG REPATRIATION VIA ICRC; UNCLASSIFIED VERIFICATION REGIME; SUSTAINED COALITION DETERRENT PRESENCE.\
\
(5) (E) PHASE V — TRANSITION (CONDITIONS-BASED). REDEPLOYMENT OF COALITION SURGE FORCES; RESTORATION OF STANDING INDOPACOM POSTURE; PRESERVATION OF LONG-TERM EDCA POSTURE; TRANSITION TO STEADY-STATE COMPETITION.\
\
D. (E) LINES OF EFFORT. PER REF F, FOUR LINES OF EFFORT EXECUTED CONCURRENTLY:\
\
(1) (E) LOE 1 — SEA CONTROL AND AIR PRESENCE IN THE JOA. LIMITED TO ESTABLISHMENT OF SEA AND AIR CONTROL SUFFICIENT TO ENABLE PRESENCE AND PROTECT COALITION FORCES; KINETIC DEGRADATION OF PRC FORCES NOT AUTHORIZED EXCEPT IN SELF-DEFENSE OR AGAINST DECLARED HOSTILE FORCES ON PAG-ASA.\
\
(2) (E) LOE 2 — ISOLATION (NON-KINETIC) OF PRC SPRATLY OUTPOSTS. DEMONSTRATE COALITION CAPABILITY TO INTERDICT SEA-LINE RESUPPLY TO MISCHIEF, SUBI, FIERY CROSS BUT WITHOUT ACTUAL INTERDICTION ABSENT PRESIDENTIAL RELEASE. SUSTAINED ISR PRESSURE; OVERFLIGHT AS LEGAL; SUBMARINE PRESENCE.\
\
(3) (E) LOE 3 — RESTORATION READINESS. MAINTAIN AMPHIBIOUS RESTORATION OPTION AT 96-HOUR EXECUTABILITY THROUGHOUT PHASES II AND III. CONTINUOUS REHEARSAL, INTELLIGENCE PREPARATION, AND CIVILIAN-PROTECTION PLANNING.\
\
(4) (E) LOE 4 — DIPLOMATIC CONDITIONS FOR TERMINATION. MILITARY ACTIONS SYNCHRONIZED IN SUPPORT OF DOS-LED DIPLOMATIC EFFORT. JOINT STATE-DEFENSE TERMINATION FRAMEWORK PER REF K. INFORMATION OPERATIONS DIRECTED TO PRESERVING PRC OFF-RAMP CONSISTENT WITH RESTORED PHILIPPINE SOVEREIGNTY.\

## End-of-Order Notes (Non-MTF, <span class="mark">for synthetic-package use</span>)

This CJCS Execute Order transmits Presidential approval of COA-2 (Shaping-and-Negotiate) and SecDef execution authority to CDR USINDOPACOM as the supported CCDR. Key analytic features of this EXORD relative to the source-document package:

1.  **COA-2 selection imposes ROE constraints not present in the WARNORD.** Specifically, the standing authority under WARNORD para 9G(4) to engage the militarized Spratly outposts is rescinded for the duration of COA-2. This is a designed-in feature of the shaping-and-negotiate construct — kinetic action against the PRC operational center of gravity is held in reserve as the COA-1 branch.

2.  **COA-2 elevates the diplomatic effort above kinetic operations.** The military effort is explicitly characterized as an instrument of the State-led diplomatic effort (Para 6, Para 15). This is consistent with the CIPG framing that "every strike has a narrative" but in COA-2 the narrative dominates the strike.

3.  **COA-1 is preserved as the on-order branch with 96-hour executability.** This sustains the JTF's planning burden for both COAs throughout Phases I–III and creates a continuous reconstitution-posture reporting requirement (Para 19).

4.  **Phase III decision point is explicitly NLT D+75.** This is the operational analog to the political "off-ramp window" — if PRC has not accepted a negotiated withdrawal by D+75, the CCDR is required to recommend transition to COA-1 (or to Phase IV if conditions warrant).

5.  **Strategic notification criteria (Para 14) elevate select operational events to Pinnacle-level reporting.** Loss of a major surface combatant, submarine, or fixed-wing aircraft triggers OPREP-3 PINNACLE to CJCS regardless of escalation predicate.

6.  **Quiet-partner equities (VN / ID / MY / BX / SG) are preserved through DOS channels (Para 15D).** No public reflection in the EXORD; coordination is held within the country-team architecture.

7.  **The EXORD assumes the USINDOPACOM OPORD 26-09 (REF F) was published 052300ZSEP26 per the WARNORD-directed timeline.** A planner using this synthetic package can backstop with the OPORD as Reference F or treat it as a planning placeholder.

*End of CJCS EXORD — Operation PACIFIC HARRIER (COA-2 Shaping-and-Negotiate). For execution under the SecDef Execute Order of 081200ZSEP26.*

title: Strategic Context
text:
UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

# **STRATEGIC CONTEXT (SOUTHERN SHIELD)**

**DTG: 230400ZJUN2026**

*(E) This paper orients the Commander to the national and theater setting for Operation SOUTHERN SHIELD. It draws on historical background, recent events, the current situation, national strategy guidance, and CJCS WARNORD, but it does not substitute for those references.*

**1. (E) HISTORICAL BACKGROUND.**

1.  \(E\) Since Papua New Guinea’s independence (and United States formal recognition) in 1975, the 760 kilometer-long border between it and what is collectively called Indonesia’s West Papua region[^1] on New Guinea has been a focus for mutual suspicion. Using both diplomacy and intimidation, Indonesia has sought to prevent Papua New Guinea (PNG) from becoming a sanctuary for the Free Papua Movement separatists seeking either independence from Indonesia or reunification with the PNG side of New Guinea. PNG’s policy on the border situation is conditioned by fears of Indonesian expansionism and sympathy for West Papuan efforts to defend their cultural identity against “Indonesianization.”

2.  \(E\) West Papua, which Indonesia views as an intrinsic part of their country, was formally incorporated into Indonesia in 1969 following the Act of Free Choice plebiscite. Although there were accusations of widespread electoral fraud and voter suppression, 84 member states, including the United States and Australia, voted in favor for the UN to accept the result. As a result, a significant number of Papuans refused to accept the territories’ integration into Indonesia and formed the separatist armed insurgency group *Organisasi Papua Merdaka* (OPM, “Free Papua Movement”) which has waged an insurgency against Indonesian authorities to this day. Most of the Eastern Pacific islands, including neighboring Solomon Islands, have denounced the Act of Free Choice and/or support Papuan self-determination. The PNG government, while sympathetic to OPM, remains keenly aware of the economic and military imbalance between the two countries and offers no political support to OPM.[^2] The U.S. has not designated OPM as a foreign terrorist organization (FTO).

3.  \(E\) Talks to draw up a new agreement to regulate relations and define rights and obligations along the shared border between PNG and Indonesia culminated in the signing of the Treaty of Mutual Respect, Cooperation, and Friendship on October 27, 1986. (See “Treaty of Mutual Respect, Cooperation, and Friendship”) The Treaty was, in effect, a bi-lateral non-aggression pact in which Indonesia and PNG agreed to “avoid, reduce, and contain disputes or conflicts between their nations and settle any differences that may arise only by peaceful means” \[Article 2\], and they promised that “they shall not threaten or use force against each other \[Article 7\]. The treaty also provided a basis for building a lasting structure of peace and cooperation. The structure for peace was enhanced by the 1987 ASEAN decision to allow PNG to become the first non-ASEAN country to accede to the 1976 ASEAN Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, as a non-voting observer. Since 1992, member states of ASEAN have routinely blocked PNG’s accession to full ASEAN membership due to PNG’s membership in the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) as well as PNG’s challenges of political instability, crime, poor infrastructure, and lack of skilled labor.

4.  \(E\) The 1986 treaty left many issues unresolved. It did not resolve the problem of West Papuan refugees, fleeing insurgent violence, crossing into PNG. Additionally, PNG refused to agree to joint security operations in the border regions, while Indonesia avoided categorical assurance that its military would not cross the border in response to insurgent operations from PNG territory or in hot pursuit of OPM insurgents.

5.  \(E\) It is noteworthy that Indonesia has long supported PNG’s application to join ASEAN for regional stability reasons and security cooperation. It is likely that Indonesian support comes with a price: PNG admission to ASEAN requires PNG renunciation of any support for OPM as well as full security cooperation with Indonesia at the border to deny OPM any possibility of sanctuary in PNG territory. Politically, this would be difficult for the PNG government considering that the PNG people sympathize with the cause of OPM.

**2. (E) CURRENT STRATEGIC SITUATION.**

1.  \(E\) In February 2026, a recently armed wing of OPM calling itself the National Liberation Army (NLA) made a declaration of war against Indonesia. This followed unification of all various armed insurgent groups in West Papua. The NLA’s stated aim is to drive Indonesian forces out of West Papua and shut down operations of foreign companies exploiting New Guinea’s natural resources, for which indigenous peoples receive no benefit. This was followed by ~10,000 refugees fleeing the violence in West Papua and crossing the border into PNG, settling in the Komavi area. There are unconfirmed reports that large numbers of well-equipped insurgents crossed with them and have established numerous camps and weapons’ caches in the outlying hills on the PNG side.

2.  \(E\) Increasing reports of instability within West Papua and along the shared border are raising flags of alarm in Indonesia and PNG. Increasingly bold rebel action is likely to inspire a massive Indonesian military response. If Indonesia decides to invade Papuan territory to suppress OPM/NLA separatist activities, then the 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation signed by the U.S. and the government of PNG commits the U.S. to protect and secure U.S. personnel in PNG and thus, provides the U.S. the ability to cooperate in the defense of PNG territory from foreign invasion, IAW Article 5.[^3] This may involve a fight not only with West Papua’s insurgent NLA but Indonesia’s military as well. The political risk is that engaging in conflict on behalf of PNG may alienate Indonesia, which is an ASEAN partner to the U.S. Fighting the NLA risks alienating the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF)--many of which are supportive of U.S. policy in the Pacific – which supports OMP.

**3. (E) THE PRECIPITATING INCIDENTS TO CURRENT CRISIS.**

1.  \(E\) Regional violence has spread, with the flow of West Papua refugees increasing. Port Moresby, the capital of PNG, has been flooded by thousands of internally displaced persons (IDPs) fleeing the border. PNG in general and Port Moresby in particular are woefully equipped to handle this influx and have requested international assistance with this humanitarian crisis. USAID and several NGOs and International Organizations are flowing into Port Moresby and reporting an immediate need for food, shelter, clothing, and medical supplies. Due to the poor state of PNG infrastructure outside of the capital region, distribution of humanitarian supplies is expected to be a major problem.

2.  \(E\) USPACOM has received a report that Indonesia is continuing to fortify its outposts along the West Papua–PNG border, and now has an estimated 20,000 troops throughout West Papua, supported by at least two squadrons of attack aircraft (helicopters and fixed-wing). The Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assesses that Indonesian forces are preparing for a limited offensive into PNG to eliminate OPM/NLA strongholds and camps.

3.  The U.S. Department of State (DoS) has been consulting other regional powers, particularly Australia, regarding cooperation and assistance to prevent a regional war between Indonesia and PNG.

4.  The U.S. Ambassador in Port Moresby reports that the PNG Prime Minister is convinced that an Indonesian invasion of Papuan territory is imminent. The Prime Minister is requesting immediate U.S. and Australian intervention to deter such an attack, or, if an attack occurs, to assist in the defense of PNG. DoS has issued a travel advisory for PNG and encouraged the 2,000+ American citizens living in PNG to voluntarily leave for their own safety.

**4. (E) NATIONAL STRATEGY AND STRATEGIC DIRECTION.**

1.  \(E\) In the Pacific, China remains the key competitor of the United States. It is the strategy of the United States to cooperate and compete internationally from a position of strength in order to sustain peace in the Pacific. This strength is derived from America’s alliances and partnerships, which form a defensive perimeter around Eurasia.[^4] To that end, as the NSS directs, we will build, posture, and sustain a strong denial defense. We will also work closely with our allies such as Australia and partners such as Indonesia and Papua New Guinea to incentivize and enable them to do more for our collective defense, which is in U.S. interests. The Indo-Pacific will soon make up more than half of the global economy. The American people’s security, freedom, and prosperity are therefore directly linked to our ability to trade and engage from a position of strength in the Indo-Pacific. Were China—or anyone else, for that matter—to dominate this broad and crucial region, it would be able to effectively veto Americans’ access to the world’s economic center of gravity, with enduring implications for our nation’s economic prospects, including our ability to reindustrialize. That is why the NSS directs DoW, and thus USPACOM, to maintain a favorable balance of military power in the IndoPacific, including in New Guinea.

2.  \(E\) The President recently held a press conference on the growing crisis in New Guinea and stated that while the United States would pursue peaceful settlement of all regional disputes and does not wish to take sides in this dispute between Indonesia, OPM separatists, and PNG, the U.S. will honor the 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation with PNG. He strongly stated that protection of U.S. military personnel, contractors, citizens and their property is a top priority. Finally, the President emphasized that while the U.S. did not wish to get involved in the internal activities of either Indonesia or PNG, he would authorize military force to protect U.S. personnel and non-combatants, contain the situation to the immediate area, and to de-escalate the conflict.

    1.  \(E\) Diplomacy. DoS will seek to defuse the situation by offering a third-party state broker talks between Indonesia and PNG. New Zealand, which is a member of Pacific Islands Forum and a founding member of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) has committed to host these negotiations.

    2.  \(E\) Informational. The public position of the U.S. remains clear: this dispute will not be resolved through force of arms by Indonesia and PNG sovereignty must not be violated. Concurrently, the PNG government has a responsibility to regional stability to deny sanctuary to any armed insurgent or separatist groups.

    3.  \(E\) Military. Australia is a treaty ally of PNG and is obligated to use its military to defend the sovereignty of PNG: they will get involved militarily. While the U.S. is only obligated to protect U.S. citizens and their property, the President is willing to intervene with an expeditionary military force to ensure PNG sovereignty is not violated and that armed insurgent groups do not find illegitimate safe haven in PNG.

    4.  \(E\) Economics. U.S. tariffs on Indonesian exports to the U.S., worth \$45 billion, was recently dropped to 19%; the President will immediately raise tariffs to 100% should Indonesia violate PNG territory. PNG is heavily dependent upon U.S. mining machinery and petroleum products and the President has noted that an immediate sanction on these vital goods could be implemented should the PNG government balk at dealing with armed insurgent groups seeking safe haven on their side of the border.

3.  \(E\) The levers of national power, working together, will achieve the strategic endstate, which is to keep Indonesia and PNG as valuable cooperative partners in the region and avoid the possibility of armed conflict. As well, it will also strengthen the U.S. alliance with Australia, who will naturally take a leading role in strengthening PNG economically and militarily.

**5. (E) STRATEGIC RISK.**

1.  With Indonesia marshalling forces at the West Papuan/PNG border, there is limited time to achieve a diplomatic solution. Economic pressure, such as sanctions and tariffs, also require extended time to achieve the desired end. While Australia is both willing and able to deploy military forces to the West Papuan/PNG border, they will need time to alert and deploy sufficient forces capable of deterring or assisting PNG in repelling an Indonesian invasion. U.S. military forces can deploy sufficient military forces capable of repelling an Indonesian invasion, but this places U.S. military forces at risk of being perceived as taking sides in a regional dispute between U.S. regional partners, which would have a negative impact on U.S. interests in the Pacific and perhaps open the possibility of Chinese intervention on one side or the other, or even as a “peace-deal” broker, which is unacceptable to POTUS.

UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

[^1]: The West Papua region is made up of two Indonesian provinces - Papua province (formerly Irian Jaya) and West Papua province )formerly West Irian Jaya) - that together define the western half of the island of New Guinea (the eastern half constitutes the independent nation of Papua New Guinea). To avoid confusion, henceforth “West Papua” will refer to the region, not the province.

[^2]: OPM consists of three main elements: a disparate group of armed units each with limited territorial control with no single commander; several unarmed groups in the territory that conduct demonstrations and protests; and a small group of leaders based abroad that raise funds and awareness while striving for international support.

[^3]: See Treaty: [<u>https://www.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/63374-Papua-New-Guinea-Defense-08.16.2023.pdf</u>](https://www.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/63374-Papua-New-Guinea-Defense-08.16.2023.pdf)

[^4]: 2026 U.S. National Security Strategy, [<u>https://media.defense.gov/2026/Jan/23/2003864773/-1/-1/0/2026-national-defense-strategy.pdf</u>](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Jan/23/2003864773/-1/-1/0/2026-national-defense-strategy.pdf)

title: Regional Intel Summary
text: UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E) # DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE AGENCY - REGIONAL INTELLIGENCE SUMMARY (SOUTHERN SHIELD) **Product type:** Defense Intelligence Agency Strategic Intelligence Summary. **DTG of issue:** 220400Z JUN 2026. **Classification:** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E). > This summary provides the Strategic intelligence background and escalation history for the Geographic Combatant Commander. **1. (E) Strategic Setting (Papua New Guinea).** 1. \(E\) While PNG has sought to maintain good relations with its neighbours Australia, [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia), and the [Solomon Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Islands), tensions have emerged with Australia due to changes in aid, while regional conflicts have complicated relations with the Solomon Islands and Indonesia, due to the Bougainville independence movement and the West [Papua conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_conflict) respectively. The PNG government has recognised and supported Indonesia's control of neighbouring [Western New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_Guinea), the focus of the [Papua conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_conflict) where numerous human rights violations have reportedly been committed by the Indonesian security forces. Residents of PNG border communities, however, support West Papuan separatism and may cross the border for customary purposes or provide aid and shelter to West Papuan separatist groups, with whom they have cultural ties. Australia remains linked to PNG through institutional and cultural ties, and has remained the most consistent provider of foreign aid, as well as providing peacekeeping and security assistance. There are growing ties to China, mostly as a source of infrastructure investments. The strategic position of the country, linking Southeast Asia to the Pacific, has increased geopolitical interest in the 21st century. 2. PNG has been an observer state in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ([ASEAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASEAN)) since 1976, followed later by special observer status in 1981. It has filed its application for full membership status. PNG is a member of the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement), the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations), the [Pacific Islands Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islands_Forum), [APEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia-Pacific_Economic_Cooperation), and the United Nations. 3. \(E\) Since 2019, tensions between Indonesia and OPM have escalated. On 1 December 2018, an armed group with ties to OPM kidnapped 25 civilian construction workers in [Nduga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nduga_Regency) regency, Papua. The following day, the group killed [19 of the workers and a soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nduga_massacre).One of construction workers had allegedly photographed the group raising the Morning Star flag at an independence celebration - considered illegal acts by Indonesian authorities.The construction workers were building a part of the Trans Papua highway that aims to connect remote communities in Papua. In reprisals to obtain the massacred workers' bodies, the Indonesian military allegedly carried out airstrikes on at least four villages and used [white phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_phosphorus), a [chemical weapon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_weapon) banned by numerous countries and international organizations. This was however denied by the Indonesian government. Other significant incidents include: 1. (E) Protests involving thousands of participants demanding an independence referendum. In several locations, the protests have turned into general riots, resulting in the destruction of government buildings in [Wamena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wamena), [Sorong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorong) and [Jayapura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayapura). Clashes between protesters and counter-protesters and police resulted in injuries, with over 31 people killed from both the clashes and the rioting, mostly non-Papuan trapped when rioters burned houses. In response to the rioting, the [government of Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Indonesia) implemented an [internet blackout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_blackout) in the region. A [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters) reporter from the [Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta) bureau described the unrest as "Papua's most serious in years". 2. On 25 April 2021, Special Forces major-general [I Gusti Putu Danny Karya Nugraha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Gusti_Putu_Danny_Nugraha_Karya), head of the Papua intelligence agency, was killed when he was shot in the head while in an ambush in a heavily armed military convoy. 3. On 5 March 2022, Sebby Sambom, an OPM spokesperson supported the [2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine), claiming alleged similarity of Ukrainian police and military treatment of the Russian minority as *genocide* with Indonesian police and military treatment of Papuans. OPM claimed Russian government support of [pro-Russian separatists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_separatist_forces_in_Donbas) as justified, and claimed that both Indonesia and Ukraine are "capitalist puppets" of the United States. 4. On 7 February 2023, [Papuan separatists attacked and set fire to a plane, after taking the pilot and five passengers hostage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nduga_hostage_crisis). The passengers were soon released. The New Zealander pilot, Philip Mehrtens, remained in captivity until 21 September 2024.The flight was operated by Indonesian airline [Susi Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susi_Air) that operates flights in and out of Papua. OPM has claimed responsibility for the kidnapping and attack, stating that they would be targeting all foreigners as a part of their campaign. 5. On 3 April 2023, four Indonesian soldiers died and another five suffered gunshot injuries in an OPM attack led by [Egianus Kogoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egianus_Kogoya) in [Nduga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nduga_Regency), [Papua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_(province)). 6. On 11 February 2026, the pilot and co-pilot of a small commercial Smart Air plane were shot and killed during landing. Sambom claimed "the pilot was killed because this airline often carried Indonesian security forces throughout Papua". Another attack occurred on the same day that targeted a [Freeport Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeport_Indonesia) convoy, killing a soldier and injuring a Freeport employee and an officer. **2. (E) Escalation Arc (preceding 90 days).** 1. \(E\) In February 2026, after an armed wing of OPM calling itself the National Liberation Army (NLA) made a declaration of war against Indonesia, ~10,000 refugees fled the violence in West Papua and crossed the border into PNG, settling in the Komavi area, which lies along the Fly river just across the international border. There are unconfirmed reports that large numbers of well-equipped insurgents crossed with them and have established numerous camps and weapons’ caches in the outlying hills on the PNG side. 2. \(E\) Regional violence has spread, with the flow of West Papua refugees increasing. Port Moresby, the capital of PNG, has been flooded by thousands of internally displaced persons (IDPs) fleeing the border. Meanwhile, Indonesia is continuing to fortify its outposts along the West Papua–PNG border, and now has an estimated 20,000 troops throughout West Papua, supported by at least two squadrons of attack aircraft (helicopters and fixed-wing). DIA assesses that Indonesian forces are preparing for a limited offensive into PNG to eliminate OPM/NLA strongholds and camps. 3. \(E\) The U.S. Ambassador in Port Moresby reports that the PNG Prime Minister is convinced that an Indonesian invasion of Papuan territory is imminent. The Prime Minister is requesting immediate U.S. and Australian intervention to deter such an attack, or, if an invasion occurs, assistance in repelling the Indonesians. **3. (E) Strategic Environment (Relationships, Alliances, Frictions, Tensions).** 1. **(E) Combatants - Summary.** The U.S. maintains a partnered relationship with Indonesia and PNG. 1. \(E\) Indonesia: **Indonesia is a U.S. partner**[^1] and plays an essential role in the security architecture of the region. We maintain a robust defense relationship particularly in maritime security. The country straddles vital sea lanes and borders the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest trade routes, as well as the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Over the past 25 years, Indonesia has become a robust democracy, holding five direct presidential elections, each considered by international observers to have been largely free and fair. In the most recent, held in February 2024, Prabowo Subianto, a former defense minister who served as commander of the Indonesian military's special forces in the 1990s, was elected to succeed President Joko Widodo. Prabowo took office in October 2024 and is to serve a five-year term. The U.S.-Indonesia relationship has broadened over the past two decades, with closer military and counterterrorism cooperation and a range of new educational, environmental, and energy programs. Indonesia's foreign policy is guided by its historical role as a leader of the Non-Aligned Movement, and successive Indonesian governments have resisted aligning too closely with the United States or others, including the People's Republic of China. Indonesia is an active member in regional diplomatic institutions including the G-20 and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Some 87% of Indonesians are Muslim, with the vast majority subscribing to moderate, syncretic forms of Sunni Islam. While religious diversity is enshrined in the constitution, some observers express concern about growing political influence of conservative religious groups. Non-Sunni Muslims (such as people in West Papua) and other religious minorities have been targets of violence, and some conservative groups have organized mass demonstrations against non-Muslim politicians. Indonesia also has a history of violent extremism: several bombings in Jakarta and Bali targeted Westerners in the early 2000s, and smaller-scale attacks have occurred periodically. Indonesia desires to play a larger role in international economic and security issues, especially in New Guinea. 2. \(E\) Though sizeable for this region, Indonesian armed forces are occupied with “other internal issues” and in providing security around Jarkarta. Consequently, beyond the forces already in West Papua, not much additional reinforcement capability is expected to exist to support counterinsurgency action along the West Papua–PNG border. Indonesia’s three armed services–collectively called ABRI–consist of the army, navy, and air force. A second strike force command is the Special Forces Command (*Kopassus*). *Kopassus* personnel are identified by their distinctive red berets. These Special Forces units are trained in intelligence gathering, a variety of special operations techniques, sabotage, airborne insertion, and seaborne landings. ABRI also has a border security force which guards the international borders of Indonesia; this force is called *Kostrad Perbatasan* (Border Army Strategic Reserve Command). It guards the border between Indonesia and PNG. 1. \(E\) Indonesian Army. The Indonesian Army has about 300,000 personnel on active military duty and almost the same number to draw from its reserve. The Army forces are organized into 13 Military Area Commands (*Kodams*), or regional commands. The *Kodams* incorporate provincial and district commands, each with roughly 6 infantry battalions, sometimes a cavalry battalion, artillery, or engineers. 1. *(E) Kodam* XVII/Cenderawish is the military area command which oversees the entire West Papua region. It has been reported that the 6 infantry battalions (1,400 each/8,000 total) are based at Manokwari, Jaypura, and Sorong. Currently there are additional battalions at Tanah, Merah, Mappi, and Merauke respectively. 2. \(E\) Indonesian Naval Forces. The Indonesian Marine Corps has 3 brigades, the closest being at Surabaya on East Java, approximately 4 days away by amphibious ship (5 LPDs, 19 LSTs, 20 LCMs, and 20 LCVPs). 1. \(E\) Submarines. One CAKRA diesel-electric (German Type-209) at Jakarta. One CAKRA Type 209 is believed to be operating in the Arafura Sea. One NAGAPASA (South Korean Type 209) is at Surabaya naval base. 2. \(E\) Surface ships: 33 former Dutch, British, and home-grown frigates and corvettes of various classes. 3 Corvettes and 6 frigates are believed to be based in Manokwari Naval Base in West Papua. 3. \(E\) It is believed that the Indonesian Navy also has over 100 armed fast boats (80-100 tons) available for troop transport, relocation, or interdiction. 3. \(E\) Indonesian Air Force. The Air Force posses over 100 combat-capable aircraft including 26 U.S.-built F-16A A/B fighters. Additionally, the Air Force has 5 Su-27SK/SKM ground attack aircraft and 11 Su-30MK/MK2 fighter-bombers. Helicopters include 6 Mi-35P attack helicopters, 8 AH-64A Apaches, and 30 BAE Hawk light attack/trainer aircraft. 1. \(E\) It is assessed that a squadron of Su-30/F-16 A/B aircraft are stationed on West Papua at Jayapura Air Base, along with at least 4 Mi-35 helicopters supporting ABRI forces at Timika. 3. \(E\) Likely objectives of Indonesia: 1. \(E\) Destroy OPM/NSA sanctuary locations in West Papua and in the PNG border region. 2. \(E\) Avoid open conflict with the United States and Australia. 3. \(E\) Achieve acknowledged regional power dominance in the New Guinea and South Pacific island areas. 4. \(E\) **(Partner)** Papua New Guinea. Despite deep historical ties going back to WWII, from 1993-2022 there was little bi-lateral engagement between the U.S. and PNG except U.S. assistance in the removal of millions of UXOs left over from WWII, which remain a significant hazard to this day. Relations have expanded significantly since 2023, driven by Papua New Guinea's strategic location in the Indo-Pacific and U.S. efforts to counter growing Chinese influence in the region. The bilateral partnership focuses heavily on defense, maritime security, and economic development.[^2] 5. The armed forces are administratively integrated under the PNG Defence Force (PNGDF) and are equipped and trained almost entirely with Australian assistance. There are approximately 3,600 personnel in the PNGDF and service is entirely voluntary. 1. \(E\) Army. Ground forces consist of: 1. Army Command HQ with signals squadron at Port Moresby. 2. The Royal Pacific Islands Regiment (RPIR) with one battalion at Port Moresby and one battalion at Wewak. (3300 personnel total) 3. There are company size units at Vanimo and Kiunga. 4. One long-range reconnaissance/counter-terrorism unit. 5. One engineer battalion at Lae with EOD capability. 2. \(E\) Navy. The Maritime Operations Element is the naval branch of the PNGDF, being mainly a light patrol force responsible for defending local littorals. While capable of providing shore logistics to the Army, they are not capable of ‘blue-water’ operations. Australia has supplied the PNGDF with four Pacific-class patrol boats and three Balikpapan-class landing craft, also supplied by Australia. 3. \(E\) Air Force. The Air Operations Element is the air force branch of the PNGDF, operating a small number of light aircraft and rotary wing assets in support of Army operations. It operates one CAVA CN-235 utility aircraft, one leased Bell 412 and two leased Bell 212 helicopters, and two IAI ARAVA light STOL transport aircraft (20 pax or bulk cargo). 6. \(E\) Likely objectives of PNG: 1. \(E\) Defend PNG territory against both Indonesian aggression and OPM infiltration. 2. \(E\) Achieve a negotiated settlement with Indonesia regarding their common border. 7. \(E\) Free Papua Movement (OPM). OPM formed in 1965 as a separatist movement and began receiving funding from Libya in 1969. In the 1980s, OPM received training from the pro-communist, Maoist New People’s Army, which is a foreign terrorist group seeking to overthrow the Philippine government. After 9/11, OPM has created its own indigenous cadre to provide rudimentary training and arms to the various West Papuan disparate armed groups. It is estimated that OPM has between 2500-3000 committed members with at least 2,000 armed and organized into small insurgent groups. They are believed to be equipped with a variety of small arms, RPGs, and light mortars. 8. \(E\) Likely objective of OPM: West Papua region unification with PNG. 2. **(E)** The United States is allied or partnered with most nations of the South Pacific region and East Pacific islands. 1. \(E\) **(Ally)** Australia: In October 2025, Australia and PNG signed a mutual defense treaty that secured their mutual defence and security interests and affirmed that each would come to the other’s aid in defense of sovereignty.[^3] In addition, the U.S.-Australia alliance anchors peace and stability in the region. Australia plays a leading role in regional security, capacity-building efforts and addressing disaster response. Australia has procured high-tech U.S. platforms that will further increase interoperability. The Royal Australian Navy (RAN) is modern and interoperable with the USN, deploying two amphibious assault ships, three AEGIS-capable destroyers, and several dozen frigates, submarines, and multirole vessels. It is a certainty that Australia will honor their defense treaty with fellow commonwealth nation PNG and deploy forces to assist PNG in the defense of their sovereignty. 2. \(E\) **(Alliance)** AUKUS: AUKUS is a trilateral security pact between Australia, the UK, and the US, launched in September 2021. This is significant since PNG is a Commonwealth nation that recognizes UK Charles III as king, along with Australia. Its core focus is countering China's influence in the Indo-Pacific region through two "pillars", Nuclear-Powered Submarines and Advanced Capabilities. The U.S. has agreed to provide Australia Nuclear powered submarines to replace its aging fleet and Australia will provide submarine basing access in the near future. Pillar II has the allies collaborate on sharing military technology and expertise across six key technological areas: artificial intelligence and autonomy, quantum technologies, undersea robotics, hypersonic missiles, advanced cyber, and electronic warfare.The pact is designed to foster deep integration of the three nations' defense industrial bases. 3. \(E\) **(MN Partner)** East Pacific Islands (Oceana): Maintaining strategic influence in Oceania is becoming ever more important to U.S. national security. The provisions included in the Compacts of Free Association with the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, and the Republic of Palau are important mechanisms that guide the relationships, including U.S. obligations for their defense. In return, these agreements provide assured access to the three Compact Nations in a contingency situation. They also give the U.S. authority to grant or deny access to another nation’s military forces which allows the U.S. to maintain a clear strategic line of communication across the Pacific. 4. \(E\) **(Bi-Lateral)** Solomon Islands. The U.S. has strong historical ties to the Solomon Islands. Between 1942-44, the U.S.drove the Japanese out of the Solomon Islands in the largest, costliest, and most complex air/land/sea campaign in the Pacific War. Relations between the U.S. and the Solomon Islands have only recently warmed, however. Between 1993-2022, there was no U.S. embassy in the Solomon Islands; however, with Chinese growing influence in the region, in 2023 the embassy was re-opened in Honiara (Guadalcanal) and an Incentive Investment Agreement was signed soon after, boosting economic ties between the U.S. and the Solomon Islands. Both nations are parties to the U.S.-Pacific Islands Multilateral Tuna Fisheries Treaty. 5. \(E\) **(Multi-Lateral)** Pacific Islands Forum (PIF): Founded in 1971, PIF comprises 18 nations - most in the South and Eastern Pacific, including Australia and PNG. The U.S. actively engages with PIF to deepen strategic and economic ties. Recent high-level engagements include PIF leaders attending the U.S.–Pacific Investment Summit in Honolulu to unlock infrastructure investments and collaborate on climate resilience. 6. \(E\) **(Multi-Lateral)** ASEAN: The U.S. and ASEAN share the common principles of a rules-based order, respect for international law, and the peaceful resolution of disputes. The ten ASEAN member states continue to seek ways to improve multilateral security engagements and advance stability in the Indo-Asia-Pacific. UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

# SITUATIONAL MAP AND ENTITY RELATIONSHIP OVERLAY (SOUTHERN SHIELD)

**Product type:** Graphics and entities product — text rendering of a map series, gazetteer and overlay set. **Originator:** USPACOM J2, Camp H.M. Smith, HI. **DTG of issue:** 240600Z JUN 2026. **Classification:** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E).

**References.** A. CJCS Warning Order, 230500Z JUN 2026. B. Defense Intelligence Agency Regional Intelligence Summary (SOUTHERN SHIELD), 220400Z JUN 2026. C. Defense Intelligence Agency Country Fact Sheet (SOUTHERN SHIELD), 220400Z JUN 2026. D. Strategic Context (SOUTHERN SHIELD).

## 1. Scope

Text rendering of the graphics ordinarily carried on the theater situation map. Locations, entities and stated relationships only.

## 2. Map Series, Datum and Grid Conventions

| **Convention** | **Value** |
|:---|----|
| Horizontal datum | World Geodetic System 1984. All positions herein are WGS-84 |
| Vertical datum | Land, mean sea level; terrain in metres, heights in feet. Marine, lowest astronomical tide; soundings in metres |
| Operational series | Joint Operations Graphic (Air) 1:250,000, blocks SA 54, SB 53–55, SC 54–55, and adjoining Australian blocks SD 52–53 |
| Planning series | Operational Navigation Chart 1:1,000,000 and Tactical Pilotage Chart 1:500,000, same sheet blocks |
| Large scale | Topographic Line Map 1:50,000 for the Port Moresby, Lae and Daru approaches; upper Fly River coverage incomplete |
| Maritime series | Digital Nautical Chart libraries for the Gulf of Papua, Torres Strait, Arafura Sea and Bismarck Sea |
| Grid | Universal Transverse Mercator, MGRS. Grid zone designations covering the area are 52L, 53M, 54L, 54M, 55L, 55M |
| Coordinates and bearings | Degrees and minutes, latitude then longitude, to the nearest minute; position references, not survey control. Bearings true |
| Time | Date-time groups Zulu. Local time UTC+10 in Papua New Guinea, UTC+9 in the Indonesian provinces on New Guinea |
| Linear units | Nautical miles, air miles, kilometres and river miles as stated by the source; not converted between tables |

## 3. Gazetteer

Point positions are carried only where an aerodrome reference point is held. Entries marked "—" carry a relative position description; grid references for those are drawn from the sheets at paragraph 2.

| **Place** | **Country** | **Position (WGS-84)** | **Descriptive note** |
|:---|----|----|----|
| Komavi | Papua New Guinea | 05°42'S 141°08'E | Settlement area, upper Fly River catchment, Western Province. Unsealed grass and laterite airstrip. No road connection |
| Kiunga | Papua New Guinea | 06°07'S 141°17'E | River town on the Fly River, Western Province; head of navigation. Sealed airstrip; river wharf serving the Ok Tedi mine |
| Daru | Papua New Guinea | 09°05'S 143°12'E | Island town and administrative centre of Western Province, on the Torres Strait coast. Coastal wharf. Gravel airstrip, partially sealed |
| Lae / Nadzab | Papua New Guinea | 06°34'S 146°43'E (Nadzab) | Port city on the Huon Gulf; Lae Port handles about half of all Papua New Guinea international cargo. Nadzab is the asphalt airfield |
| Port Moresby / Jacksons | Papua New Guinea | 09°26'S 147°13'E (Jacksons) | National capital, southern coast on the Gulf of Papua. Motukea and Fairfax ports; Jacksons International airport |
| Vanimo | Papua New Guinea | 02°41'S 141°18'E | North-coast town near the northern terminus of the international border. Sealed airstrip |
| Wewak (Boram) | Papua New Guinea | 03°35'S 143°40'E | North-coast town on the Bismarck Sea. Boram airfield, sealed |
| Bougainville | Papua New Guinea | — | Island group east of the mainland. Autonomous region of Papua New Guinea; locus of an independence movement |
| Torres Strait | Papua New Guinea / Australia | — | Separates New Guinea from the Australian mainland; 90 miles at its closest point. Controlling depth about 12 m; mandatory pilotage, Prince of Wales Channel |
| Fly River | Papua New Guinea | — | Principal river of Western Province, navigable Daru to Kiunga; controlling depth 4.5 m wet season, 2.4 m June to November. Shallow-draft workboat only above Kiunga |
| Owen Stanley Range | Papua New Guinea | — | Dominates the eastern peninsula on a north-west to south-east axis; peaks of the central cordillera reach 16,000 ft |
| Jayapura / Sentani | Indonesia | 02°34'S 140°30'E (Sentani) | North-coast provincial capital near the international border. Sentani Air Base: asphalt, full military fuel, hardened revetments |
| Manokwari | Indonesia | — | North-coast city, Bird's Head peninsula. Manokwari Naval Base |
| Sorong | Indonesia | — | City and port at the western extremity of the New Guinea landmass |
| Timika | Indonesia | 04°32'S 136°53'E (Mozes Kilangin) | South-coast lowland town serving the Freeport Indonesia concession. Mozes Kilangin airport, asphalt |
| Merauke | Indonesia | — | Town in the far south-east of Indonesian New Guinea, on the Arafura Sea coastal plain |
| Mappi / Kepi | Indonesia | — | District and district centre, southern lowlands, inland of the Arafura Sea coast |
| Tanah Merah | Indonesia | — | Inland administrative centre, southern border region |
| Surabaya | Indonesia | — | Port city and naval base, East Java |
| Jakarta | Indonesia | — | National capital and naval base, north-west Java |
| RAAF Darwin | Australia | 12°25'S 130°53'E | Air force base and port city, Northern Territory, on the Timor Sea. Asphalt, full fuel, night-capable |
| RAAF Tindal | Australia | 14°31'S 132°23'E | Air force base, Northern Territory, inland south-east of Darwin. Asphalt, full fuel, night-capable |
| Townsville | Australia | — | Garrison city and port, north Queensland |
| Brisbane | Australia | — | Capital of Queensland; port and garrison city |

**Gazetteer entries: 24.**

## 4. Boundaries and Control Measures in Effect

Established by treaty, statute or administrative act and depicted on the base sheets. No joint operations area, fire support coordination measure or airspace control measure is depicted in this product.

| **Measure** | **Description** |
|:---|----|
| Indonesia–Papua New Guinea international border | 760 kilometres, running generally north to south across New Guinea from the north coast near Vanimo to the Arafura Sea coastal plain. Characterised in the references as porous and unsecured |
| Papua New Guinea provincial boundaries | Western Province is the largest by area and least dense, about 5 persons per square kilometre. The Autonomous Region of Bougainville carries its distinct annotation |
| Indonesian provincial and district boundaries | Kodam, Korem, Kodim and Koramil territorial boundaries on a separate layer |
| Torres Strait Protected Zone | Torres Strait Treaty, 1978, Australia–Papua New Guinea; protected zone and traditional-inhabitant movement. The treaty's separate seabed and fisheries jurisdiction lines are drawn as distinct lines, annotated not coincident |
| Territorial seas and contiguous zones | Territorial sea at 12 nautical miles from declared baselines for Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Australia; contiguous zone at 24 nautical miles where declared |
| Exclusive economic zones | 200 nautical miles from baselines, or the agreed median line where claims overlap in the Arafura Sea and Torres Strait approaches |
| Indonesian archipelagic baselines | Declared archipelagic sea lanes annotated, including approaches to the Lombok, Sunda and Malacca chokepoints |
| Navigational measures | Mandatory pilotage, Prince of Wales Channel. Recommended tracks through the Vitiaz and Dampier Straits north of Lae |

## 6. Entity Relationship Overlay

### 6.1 State to state

| **Parties** | **Nature** | **Instrument** | **Current state** |
|:---|----|----|----|
| United States — Indonesia | Partner | Defence relationship, maritime-security weighted | Active. Tariff on \$45 billion of Indonesian exports recently cut to 19 per cent, with stated Presidential intent to raise it to 100 per cent should Indonesia violate Papua New Guinea territory |
| United States — Papua New Guinea | Partner | 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation, Article 5 | In force. Commits the United States to protect and secure United States personnel in Papua New Guinea, and provides the ability to cooperate in the defence of its territory from foreign invasion |
| United States — Australia | Ally | Alliance | Active; Australia operates United States platforms |
| Australia — Papua New Guinea | Ally, treaty | Mutual defence treaty October 2025; Torres Strait Treaty 1978 | Both in force; each comes to the other's aid in defence of sovereignty. Australia assessed a certainty to honour it; equips and trains the Papua New Guinea Defence Force |
| Indonesia — Papua New Guinea | Treaty relationship, adversarial trend | Treaty of Mutual Respect, Cooperation and Friendship, 27 October 1986, Articles 2 and 7 | In force; both bound to settle differences only by peaceful means and not to threaten or use force. Unresolved: refugee status, joint border security operations, hot-pursuit assurance. Papua New Guinea recognises Indonesian control of West Papua |
| United Kingdom — Australia — United States | Ally, trilateral | AUKUS, September 2021 | Active. Pillar I nuclear-powered submarines; Pillar II advanced capabilities across six technology areas |
| United Kingdom — Papua New Guinea | Shared head of state | Commonwealth realm | Charles III recognised as king by Papua New Guinea and Australia |
| New Zealand — Indonesia and Papua New Guinea | Broker | Department of State-brokered talks | Committed to host |
| China — Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, United States | Economic partner; partner under Indonesian "active alignment"; United States competitor | Infrastructure investment in Papua New Guinea | Growing Papua New Guinea ties; Indonesia aligns closely with neither. Named in national strategy as the key Pacific competitor |
| United States — Solomon Islands | Partner | Incentive Investment Agreement 2023; Pacific Islands Tuna Fisheries Treaty | Embassy re-opened at Honiara 2023 after closure 1993–2022 |
| Solomon Islands — Papua New Guinea | Neighbour, strained | None | Complicated by the Bougainville independence movement |

### 6.2 Organizations

| West Papuan refugee concentration | Komavi area, Western Province | Approximately 10,000 persons arrived February 2026 across the international border. Prima facie refugees; Papua New Guinea is a 1951 Convention party with reservations. Unconfirmed reports state that well-equipped insurgents crossed with them |
| Internally displaced persons | Port Moresby | Thousands fleeing the border region. Papua New Guinea, and Port Moresby in particular, reported poorly equipped to receive the influx; international assistance requested |
| American citizens | Papua New Guinea, nationwide | 2,000-plus residents. Travel advisory issued, voluntary departure encouraged |
| Cross-border kinship groups | Komavi area, both sides of the international border | Awin and Yonggom language groups with kin ties across the border; residents cross for customary purposes |
