text:
UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

# Initial Staff Running Estimates by Joint Function — Operation SOUTHERN SHIELD

**Product type:** Initial staff running estimates, consolidated **Originator:** USPACOM staff directorates and special staff; consolidated by USPACOM J5, Camp H. M. Smith **DTG of issue / information as of:** 260200Z JUN 2026 **Update cadence:** Twice daily during crisis action planning; on material change thereafter **References:** CJCS Warning Order, 230500Z JUN 2026 · DIA Regional Intelligence Summary and DIA Country Fact Sheet — Papua New Guinea, both 220400Z JUN 2026 · US Force List for Planning · Strategic Context · 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation

**Document construct.** Estimates submitted on stand-up of the joint planning group, before issue of commander's planning guidance. Each section reports **Current posture**, **Data and holdings**, **Ongoing actions**, **Open items**.

## 1. J1 — Personnel

#### Current posture

Headquarters on 24-hour crisis action battle rhythm since 230600Z JUN 2026. A personnel cell is manned and a joint manning document is in construction. No joint task force is activated.

#### Data and holdings

- Headquarters assigned strength 1,247 against 1,312 authorized (95.0 percent). Draft joint manning document: 214 billets, 46 marked for individual augmentation from outside the theater; augmentees sourced, zero.

- Casualty reporting runs on the Defense Casualty Information Processing System, with notification a parent-service responsibility. No theater casualty assistance cell or mortuary affairs office is established.

- Accountability is by daily Joint Personnel Status Report at 0600L. Non-combatant accountability, where directed, runs on the Noncombatant Tracking System; no instance is activated for Papua New Guinea.

- United States citizens in Papua New Guinea: more than 2,000, concentrated in Port Moresby, Lae and the mining districts, with 1,180 traveller enrolment registrations. Embassy Port Moresby holds the consular population and evacuation planning report of record, dated 21 JUN 2026. A travel advisory is in effect and voluntary departure encouraged.

- Military personnel permanently assigned in country: 11, at the Office of Defense Cooperation and Defense Attaché Office, Port Moresby; Department of Defense contractors, 34.

#### Ongoing actions

Joint manning document first draft to J5 by 270000Z JUN 2026; augmentee sourcing coordination with service personnel commands; liaison billet identification.

#### Open items

Joint manning document validation, augmentee sourcing, casualty assistance cell manning and Noncombatant Tracking System activation — all pending.

## 2. J2 — Intelligence

#### Current posture

The Joint Intelligence Operations Center Pacific has been at continuous watch since 220600Z JUN 2026 and stood up an Indonesia–Papua New Guinea crisis cell at 230700Z JUN 2026. National intelligence agencies, with the USPACOM J2, have assessed that Indonesian forces are preparing for a limited offensive into Papua New Guinea to eliminate OPM and NLA strongholds and camps. No collection plan has been published.

#### Data and holdings

- **Apportioned collection.** CTF 76 / VP-16, six P-8A, Kadena, notice N. VUP-19, three MQ-4C, Andersen, notice N. FIWCPAC TF-501, Hawaii, notice N.

- **Collection tempo, week ending 250000Z JUN 2026.** Eleven P-8A sorties in the Arafura and Coral Sea areas averaging 8.2 hours on station; four MQ-4C sorties averaging 19.4 hours, orbits centred approximately 240 nautical miles south of the international border; national imagery averaging 3.1 targets per day against Western Province. Cloud base over the Fly headwaters is below 1,500 feet above ground level on approximately 60 percent of mornings.

- **Analytic capacity.** Six analysts on Indonesia, two on Papua New Guinea, one geospatial and one targeting analyst. No standing Western Province cell exists.

- **Liaison.** Defense Intelligence Agency, National Security Agency, National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and Australian Defence Intelligence Organisation representatives are resident at Camp H. M. Smith. No Papua New Guinea Defence Force liaison is resident.

- **Dissemination.** JWICS and SIPRNET to Camp H. M. Smith, Yokosuka and Hickam, and an accredited bilateral coalition network with Australia. No accredited releasable network exists with the Papua New Guinea Defence Force; release is by marked product and verbal briefing at the Defense Attaché Office, which holds no sensitive compartmented information facility.

#### Ongoing actions

Theater collection plan in drafting; Western Province geospatial baseline in compilation; requests for information to the Defense Intelligence Agency on the Indonesian order of battle and the reported Komavi camps.

#### Open items

Collection plan publication, Papua New Guinea Defence Force intelligence liaison, releasable network accreditation and linguist support — all pending.

## 3. J3 — Operations

#### Current posture

Crisis action posture since receipt of the CJCS Warning Order at 230500Z JUN 2026. A crisis action team is manned continuously, organised into current operations, future operations, fires, protection and an information coordination element. Components report readiness daily at 0400Z. Joint task force activation and commander designation have not been ordered.

#### Data and holdings

- **Force posture by notice to move**, per the US Force List for Planning. **N:** USS BLUE RIDGE and REAGAN CSG, Yokosuka; 31 MEU, Okinawa; one fleet oiler, Guam; six B-52 and VUP-19, Andersen; VP-16, Kadena; SOCPAC and TF-501, Hawaii. **N+1:** COMPHIBRON ELEVEN with four amphibious ships and Fleet Surgical Team Nine, Sasebo; 11 ABN 1BCT, Alaska. **N+2:** 35 AW and 12 C-130 of 374 AW / 36 AS, Misawa; 1 ASOS, Fort Lewis; two expeditionary fast transports, Saipan. **N+3 / N+4:** Combat Camera; 5 Mobile Public Affairs Detachment. **N+7:** NMCB FIVE, Okinawa; 1SFG; 5th PSYOP Battalion; 97th CA Battalion. **N+14:** HQ 25 INF DIV, 25 IN 1BCT and 84 EN BN, Hawaii. **N+90:** 7th PSYOP Group (USAR)(-), 364 CA Brigade HHC (USAR), 448 CA Battalion (USAR).

- **Alert status.** REAGAN CSG in port Yokosuka, sortie readiness reduced from 96 to 48 hours on 240000Z JUN 2026. TRIPOLI ARG alongside Sasebo in a maintenance availability. 31 MEU ashore on Okinawa.

- **Exercises and disposition.** Exercise OLGETA WARRIOR 26 with the Royal Pacific Islands Regiment at Igam Barracks, Lae, US element 62 personnel, redeployment scheduled 30 JUN 2026. Pacific Partnership 26 detachment, 41 personnel at Wewak, departure 04 JUL 2026. A planned Australian and Papua New Guinea Defence Force engineer exercise at Kiunga is deferred. No US exercise activity is scheduled in Western Province.

- **Current air and maritime activity.** Indonesian fighter activity from Sentani Air Base at Jayapura has risen from a baseline of four to six sorties per day to 12 to 16 since 18 JUN 2026, and Indonesian border outposts have been fortified. Armed fast boats are observed in the Arafura Sea at six to nine hulls per day. Australian maritime patrol aircraft fly daily from RAAF Darwin.

- **Watch organisation.** Joint operations centre director on duty continuously; battle captain on 12-hour shifts; component liaison desks manned; commander's update brief 1700L.

#### Ongoing actions

Daily readiness and notice-to-move reporting; deconfliction of exercise redeployment with commercial schedules at Nadzab and Jacksons International; coordination with the Australian Headquarters Joint Operations Command watch floor.

#### Open items

Joint task force activation order, component tasking, airspace control authority designation, disposition of the two exercise elements in country, and overflight and landing clearance renewals — all pending.

## 4. J4 — Logistics

#### Current posture

The logistics readiness cell is activated and a theater distribution picture is in compilation. No forward logistics node exists in country, and no US port or airfield survey has been conducted since 2024.

#### Data and holdings

**Airfields.** Papua New Guinea aerodrome register, updated 19 JUN 2026.

| **Field** | **Surface** | **LDA** | **Fuel** | **Night** | **Types recorded** | **MOG** | **Daylight throughput** |
|:---|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Jacksons International, Port Moresby | Asphalt | 2,750 m | JET A-1, commercial | Yes, ILS | C-17 / B767 | 3 wide-body | 400 short tons/day |
| Nadzab, Lae | Asphalt | 2,500 m | JET A-1, limited bulk | Yes, ILS Rwy 09 | C-17, weight restricted | 2 wide-body | 260 short tons/day |
| Daru | Gravel, part sealed | 1,450 m | None | No | C-130, reduced weight, dry only | 1 | 40 short tons/day |
| Kiunga | Sealed | 1,600 m | Drummed only | No | C-130, reduced weight | 1 | 35 short tons/day |
| Komavi | Grass / compacted laterite | 760 m | None | No | Light single and twin; rotary wing (observed) | 1 | Not measured |

Komavi has no apron, lighting or navigation aid, and the operator advises the surface is not serviceable for a period after heavy rainfall; the area records 7,600 mm of rainfall across 280 rain days per year, against 2,100 mm at Daru. Pavement classification numbers are not held.

**Ports.**

| **Facility** | **Reported parameters** |
|:---|----|
| Lae Port | Handles approximately half of all Papua New Guinea international cargo. Berths 180 m and 145 m; 11 m alongside; one 40 tonne mobile harbour crane; yard approximately 4,000 TEU. |
| Port Moresby (Motukea / Fairfax) | Principal southern-coast port. One 180 m berth; 10.5 m alongside. |
| Daru | Coastal wharf, 65 m; 3.5 m alongside; barge and landing-craft access; no crane above 15 tonnes. |
| Kiunga | River wharf at the head of navigation; Ok Tedi mine resupply terminal; 3,000 DWT barges transit year-round. |

**Fly River.** Navigable Daru to Kiunga, 510 river miles; controlling depth 4.5 m in the wet season and 2.4 m June through November; upriver transit 4 to 5 days, downriver 3. Above Kiunga the river takes shallow-draft workboats only, and no traffic at all within 20 miles of the Komavi area, which lies 190 air miles from Daru with no roads at all and 42 air miles from Kiunga.

**Ok Tedi commercial barge fleet.** Eleven self-propelled barges of 3,000 DWT and six tug-and-dumb-barge sets of approximately 1,200 tonnes at Kiunga and Daru; loaded draft 2.1 m in the dry season; utilisation against mine resupply approximately 85 percent. Charter terms for non-commercial use are not established.

**Bulk fuel.** Commercial JET A-1 tankage: Jacksons International 4,200 cubic metres, approximately 11 days of current offtake; Nadzab 1,600 cubic metres. Product arrives by coastal tanker on a nominal 14-day cycle. Kiunga holds 600 cubic metres of diesel and 90 of drummed JET A-1, both allocated to mine operations. Afloat: two fleet oilers of approximately 180,000 barrels each. No Defense Logistics Agency Energy contract or fuel support point exists in country.

**Classes of supply.** Class I: 21 days of operational rations at Guam and Okinawa against a notional 5,000-person force, none in country. Class IV at Guam and Port Hueneme. Class V: theater stocks at Guam and Okinawa, no ammunition holding area identified in country. Class VIII: unit assemblages, theater account at Yokosuka. Class IX: nothing forward of Guam.

**Contracting in Papua New Guinea.** No LOGCAP task order is active and no joint contracting support board has been convened; two contingency contracting officers are identified for deployment. The 2024 vendor base assessment found fuel distribution, ground transport in the Lae and Port Moresby corridors, potable water and stevedoring commercially available; no assessed vendor base exists for Western Province beyond the mine operator.

**Host-nation logistics.** The Papua New Guinea Defence Force maintains one engineer battalion at Lae with explosive ordnance disposal capability, and a Maritime Operations Element with three Balikpapan-class landing craft rated at 180 tonnes, 1.5 m beaching draft. Ammunition holdings are assessed at seven days of supply.

#### Ongoing actions

Theater distribution picture in assembly; requests for pavement data and for berth and yard availability; survey team requirements in preparation; engagement planning with the Ok Tedi mine operator.

#### Open items

Intratheater airlift and sealift allocation pending USTRANSCOM tasking. Survey team sourcing and clearance, barge charter terms, Class V holding area location, contracting board convening authority and fuel support arrangements — all pending.

## 5. J5 — Plans

#### Current posture

The joint planning group stood up at 231400Z JUN 2026 on receipt of the CJCS Warning Order, under J5 lead, and is in mission analysis preparation. An operational planning team is designated and partially manned; terms of reference await commander's planning guidance at 260500Z JUN 2026.

#### Data and holdings

- **Composition.** Twenty-one planners: J5 (7, including the chief of plans and the operational design lead), J3 (4), J4 (3), J2 (2), and one each from J6, Surgeon, Staff Judge Advocate, Comptroller and Public Affairs. Four of ten requested component planners have reported; the operational planning team is at eight of a planned 14.

- **Planning products held.** Theater campaign plan and Papua New Guinea country plan annex, revised 2025; a standing concept plan for noncombatant evacuation operations, last reviewed 2024 and not exercised since; 2024 infrastructure and access assessment. No time-phased force and deployment data exists and no joint operations area is defined.

- **Allied and partner coordination.** Australian Headquarters Joint Operations Command has offered two liaison planners, arriving 27 JUN 2026, and requested reciprocal US liaison; Australia runs a standing defence cooperation programme in Papua New Guinea with resident advisers at Murray and Igam Barracks. The Papua New Guinea Defence Force has nominated one planner from Army headquarters, with clearance in staffing.

- **Reachback.** Joint Staff J5 Pacific division; Joint Enabling Capabilities Command for planning augmentation, element requested and unsourced; USTRANSCOM Deployment and Distribution Operations Center; Defense Intelligence Agency.

#### Ongoing actions

Mission analysis framework in preparation and staff estimates in consolidation, of which this document is the first submission; facts, assumptions, constraints and restraints in compilation.

#### Open items

Commander's planning guidance scheduled 260500Z JUN 2026. Operational planning team terms of reference, component planner augmentation, Joint Enabling Capabilities Command sourcing and partner planner clearance — all pending.

## 6. J6 — Communications

#### Current posture

Theater communications are in peacetime configuration. A communications planning cell is open and an initial satellite access request has been submitted. No deployable communications package is alerted.

#### Data and holdings

- **Satellite footprint.** Wideband X-band and Ka-band coverage from two spacecraft reaching Papua New Guinea, look angles over Western Province 34 to 51 degrees; narrowband ultra-high-frequency from a single payload at 22 to 35 degrees, with terrain masking in the Fly headwaters valleys. Wideband apportionment for the Papua New Guinea area is 42 MHz; commercial leases run 12 to 18 days lead time. Rain fade is a planning factor at 7,600 mm of annual rainfall in the Komavi area.

- **Terrestrial infrastructure.** The Coral Sea Cable System lands at Port Moresby; the domestic Kumul submarine cable ring connects Port Moresby, Lae, Madang, Wewak, Vanimo and Kimbe, and does not serve Western Province. Terrestrial microwave serves the Kiunga–Tabubil corridor under mine operator ownership. Commercial power is intermittent outside Port Moresby and Lae.

- **Commercial telecommunications.** Two operators serve the country. Fourth-generation mobile coverage exists in Port Moresby, Lae, Madang and Mount Hagen; Western Province has second-generation voice and short message service only, at Daru, Kiunga and Tabubil, and the Komavi area has none. National mobile penetration is approximately 55 percent, internet penetration approximately 15 percent.

- **Coalition interoperability.** An accredited bilateral coalition network with Australia is in use at Camp H. M. Smith, Yokosuka, Hickam and Australian Headquarters Joint Operations Command. No accredited network exists with the Papua New Guinea Defence Force, which operates a signals squadron at Army headquarters with single-channel high-frequency and very-high-frequency equipment; no satellite capability is reported at battalion level or below, including the company at Kiunga.

- **Spectrum management.** Spectrum is regulated by the Papua New Guinea National Information and Communications Technology Authority; host-nation clearance is by application through Embassy Port Moresby, and the last routine application took 27 days. No joint restricted frequency list has been published.

#### Ongoing actions

Satellite access request in staffing; host-nation frequency clearance application in preparation; Western Province infrastructure baseline in compilation.

#### Open items

Satellite access approval and apportionment, host-nation frequency clearance, joint restricted frequency list, coalition network arrangement with the Papua New Guinea Defence Force and deployable package sourcing — all pending.

## 7. Surgeon — Health Service Support

#### Current posture

A health service support planning cell is open and the medical threat picture for Western Province is in compilation. No theater medical rules of eligibility are promulgated, no patient movement policy is set and no medical unit is alerted.

#### Data and holdings

- **Apportioned medical.** Fleet Surgical Team Nine, Sasebo, notice to move N+1, providing two operating rooms and 24 inpatient beds aboard USS TRIPOLI (LHD 7) when embarked.

- **Role of care.** Role 1 organic to deploying units; Role 2 afloat with the amphibious ready group; nearest Role 3 at US Naval Hospital Guam and Tripler Army Medical Center. Australia holds a deployable Role 2 within 17th Sustainment Brigade. Host-nation facilities are Port Moresby General, Angau Memorial at Lae, Daru General, Kiunga District and Rumginae Rural, the last two with no surgical capability beyond basic procedures and no blood bank. No medical facility of any kind exists in the Komavi area.

- **Evacuation chain and distances.** Komavi area to Daru, 190 air miles, no roads at all; Daru to Port Moresby, 275 air miles; Port Moresby to Lae, 200 air miles, none with a direct road. Daru to Kiunga is 165 air miles or 510 river miles; Lae to Guam, 1,400 nautical miles. Aeromedical evacuation is coordinated by the theater patient movement requirements centre; no aeromedical evacuation crews or en-route care teams appear on the US Force List for Planning. Casualty evacuation in the operational area is limited to Papua New Guinea Defence Force leased light helicopters and mine operator contract aircraft, none medically configured.

- **Endemic disease, Western Province.** Malaria holoendemic, year-round transmission of *Plasmodium falciparum* and *Plasmodium vivax*, chloroquine resistance documented, annual parasite incidence in the Middle and North Fly districts approximately 180 cases per 1,000 population. Dengue endemic at Daru and Kiunga. Scrub typhus (*Orientia tsutsugamushi*) in grassland and secondary regrowth in the Fly headwaters. Melioidosis (*Burkholderia pseudomallei*) in soil and surface water, wet-season peak. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis at high prevalence in the Daru area. Komavi ambient conditions: mean 27 degrees Celsius, 88 percent relative humidity sustained.

- **Preventive medicine.** No force health protection policy has been issued; existing theater guidance requires malaria chemoprophylaxis, permethrin-treated uniforms, bed nets and vector control. Preventive medicine detachment support is available at Okinawa and Guam; no preventive medicine unit appears on the US Force List for Planning. Immunisation currency across notice-to-move units is 61 percent for typhoid and 34 percent for Japanese encephalitis.

- **Blood.** Armed Services Blood Program support from Yokota and Okinawa; theater liquid group O holdings 620 units, frozen holdings at Guam 1,900. Daru and Kiunga hold no bank stock.

#### Ongoing actions

Medical threat assessment in compilation with the Navy Environmental and Preventive Medicine Unit; rules of eligibility and patient movement policy in drafting; Class VIII push-package composition under review.

#### Open items

Medical rules of eligibility, patient movement and evacuation policy, Class VIII push package release, preventive medicine detachment sourcing and the combined health support arrangement with Australia — all pending.

## 8. Engineer

#### Current posture

An engineering planning cell is open and base development data for Lae, Daru, Kiunga and the Komavi area is in compilation. No US engineer reconnaissance has been conducted since 2024. No engineer unit is alerted.

#### Data and holdings

- **Apportioned engineer force.** 84 EN BN, Hawaii, notice to move N+14; NMCB FIVE, Okinawa, notice to move N+7. The Papua New Guinea Defence Force engineer battalion at Lae holds explosive ordnance disposal capability. Australian engineer capability sits within 17th Sustainment Brigade.

- **Construction capacity.** 84 EN BN fields three construction companies with organic earthmoving, quarry and paving sections; sustained common excavation planned at 2,400 cubic metres per day dry and 900 under sustained rainfall. NMCB FIVE fields approximately 600 personnel and an 89-person air detachment deployable at 48 hours, with earthmoving planned at 1,800 cubic metres per day. A 32-person vertical platoon completes one pre-engineered building in nine working days.

- **Expeditionary airfield matting.** AM-2 matting at the Naval Construction Battalion Center detachment, Guam: 92,000 square feet; one complete expeditionary airfield package of 96,000 square feet at Port Hueneme. Planned installation rate is 9,000 square feet per day on a compacted subgrade of specified California bearing ratio, exclusive of subgrade preparation. Movement of matting stocks is by sealift or strategic airlift and is not currently scheduled.

- **Expeditionary airfield design criteria held by the planning cell.** Contingency airfield criteria applied by this staff are: C-17 semi-prepared assault strip, 1,065 m by 27 m at California bearing ratio 6 minimum; C-130 semi-prepared assault strip, 1,065 m by 18 m at California bearing ratio 6 minimum, reducible to 915 m for a single-ship emergency delivery at restricted gross weight; C-130 sustained-operations strip, 1,525 m by 27 m, surfaced. Rotary-wing landing zone, 50 m by 50 m cleared and level per aircraft, no bearing-ratio floor. STOL utility fixed-wing, 350 m unsurfaced. A grass or unsurfaced laterite runway loses an assessed 30 to 50 percent of dry-condition bearing ratio within 24 hours of heavy rainfall and is not restored without mechanical compaction.

- **Quarry and aggregate, Western Province.** Nearest tested hard-rock source to the Komavi area is the Ok Tedi crusher complex at Tabubil, linked to Kiunga by the mine-operated road, 85 miles; output is committed to mine operations. Alluvial gravel is available in the upper Fly and Ok Tedi river beds, quality untested. Laterite is present in the Komavi area, with no California bearing ratio testing conducted. The Daru coastal plain and Fly delta are alluvial silt and clay with no hard rock reported.

- **Water production.** NMCB FIVE holds two 3,000 gallon-per-hour reverse osmosis water purification units and four 1,500 gallon-per-hour tactical systems; 84 EN BN holds distribution and storage but no production above unit level. Surface water in the Fly headwaters is abundant year-round, with turbidity after rainfall regularly above 200 nephelometric turbidity units.

- **Other.** Unexploded ordnance from the 1942–1944 campaign remains a significant hazard nationwide, and off improved roads the ground is a sticky morass of mud for most of the year.

#### Ongoing actions

Base development baseline for Nadzab, Daru and Kiunga in compilation; request to Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Pacific for pavement data; engineer reconnaissance requirements in preparation.

#### Open items

Engineer reconnaissance team sourcing and clearance, pavement classification and California bearing ratio data for Daru, Kiunga and the Komavi area, a soil and aggregate survey, matting movement and customary land access arrangements — all pending.

## 9. Staff Judge Advocate

#### Current posture

One operational law attorney is assigned to the joint planning group and one to the crisis action team. No supplemental rules of engagement have been requested or approved for this operation.

#### Data and holdings

- **Authorities.** Presidential direction, per the Strategic Context, is to protect United States military personnel, citizens, contractors and physical property in Papua New Guinea, contain the situation to the immediate area and de-escalate the conflict, while pursuing peaceful settlement and not taking sides. The 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation, Article 5, commits the United States to protect and secure United States personnel in Papua New Guinea and provides the ability to cooperate in the defence of Papua New Guinea territory from foreign invasion. Interpretation of Article 5 as applied to the planning requirement has been requested from the Joint Staff Office of Legal Counsel.

- **Agreements in place.** 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation, including status protections for United States personnel; Torres Strait Treaty of 1978; October 2025 mutual defence treaty between Australia and Papua New Guinea; 1986 Treaty of Mutual Respect, Cooperation and Friendship, Articles 2 and 7, under which refugee status, joint border security operations and assurance against hot pursuit remain unresolved. An acquisition and cross-servicing agreement is in force with Australia, none with Papua New Guinea; force posture arrangements govern access at RAAF Darwin and RAAF Tindal.

- **Rules of engagement.** The standing rules of engagement remain in force with no supplemental measures approved. A draft package is in preparation covering self-defence of United States persons and property, protection of designated persons, and convoy security. The OPM is not designated a foreign terrorist organization by the United States.

- **Claims.** Single-service claims responsibility is not assigned and no foreign claims commission is appointed. Customary land accounts for 97 percent of the country, community-held and largely unregistered.

- **Detention and displaced persons.** No detention facility exists in theater and no detainee operations capability appears on the US Force List for Planning. Papua New Guinea is a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention with reservations, and the approximately 10,000 West Papuans in the Komavi area hold prima facie refugee status.

#### Ongoing actions

Draft supplemental rules of engagement measures in staffing; authorities and agreements annex in compilation; coordination with Embassy Port Moresby and the Australian Defence Force legal office.

#### Open items

Joint Staff Office of Legal Counsel interpretation of Article 5, supplemental rules of engagement approval, single-service claims designation, foreign claims commission appointment and implementing arrangements under the 2023 Agreement on Defense Cooperation — all pending.

## 10. Public Affairs and Information

#### Current posture

Public affairs operates under existing theater guidance; no guidance specific to Papua New Guinea has been issued by the Office of the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs. Media queries since 22 JUN 2026 total 31, all referred to the Department of State or answered from the standing travel advisory.

#### Data and holdings

- **Apportioned assets.** 5 Mobile Public Affairs Detachment, Washington, N+4; Combat Camera / 55 Signal Company, Maryland, N+3. Information-related capability on the same list: 7th PSYOP Group (USAR)(-), N+90; 5th PSYOP Battalion (Airborne), N+7; 364 CA Brigade HHC (USAR), N+90; 448 CA Battalion (USAR), N+90; 97th CA Battalion (Airborne), N+7.

- **Media environment.** Two national daily newspapers in English, a state broadcaster with national radio coverage and one commercial television broadcaster. Radio is the primary reach medium in rural areas, where 85 percent of the population resides. Working languages are English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu; more than 800 distinct languages are spoken. Internet penetration is approximately 15 percent, concentrated in Port Moresby and Lae; short-duration government restrictions on social media have been imposed previously. Regional coverage comes from Australian and New Zealand broadcasters and Indonesian state outlets.

- **Press posture.** Embassy Port Moresby is the release authority for country team messaging, and the travel advisory is the current public statement of record. No embed programme exists and no joint information bureau is established. Indonesian official statements are issued through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Jakarta.

#### Ongoing actions

Proposed public affairs guidance in preparation; daily media monitoring of Papua New Guinea, Australian and Indonesian outlets; translation requirement in compilation.

#### Open items

Public affairs guidance, joint information bureau location and manning, embed programme decision, translation and vernacular broadcast capacity, and release authority arrangements — all pending.

## 11. Provost Marshal and Force Protection

#### Current posture

Theater force protection condition is BRAVO, set 231000Z JUN 2026; United States military personnel at Embassy Port Moresby are at CHARLIE, set by the chief of mission on 23 JUN 2026. Random antiterrorism measures are in effect at Camp H. M. Smith and forward installations.

#### Data and holdings

- **Physical security in Papua New Guinea.** No United States-controlled installation exists in country. Military personnel permanently assigned number 11, all at Port Moresby, under chief of mission security authority. Exercise elements are 62 personnel at Igam Barracks, Lae, and 41 at Wewak, both under host-nation installation security with contract guard augmentation. Antiterrorism vulnerability assessments were last conducted for Port Moresby in 2024; none has been conducted for Lae, Daru, Kiunga or the Komavi area.

- **Host-nation security forces.** The Papua New Guinea Defence Force totals approximately 3,600 personnel, entirely voluntary, equipped and trained almost entirely by Australia. The Royal Pacific Islands Regiment fields one battalion at Port Moresby and one at Wewak, stated total 3,300, and companies at Vanimo and Kiunga; the Kiunga company numbers approximately 110 personnel with one 81 mm mortar section and no organic aviation.

- **Threat data.** OPM is reported at 2,500 to 3,000 committed personnel with at least 2,000 armed, holding small arms, rocket-propelled grenades and light mortars, and is assessed likely to blend in with displaced persons. Approximately 10,000 refugees are in the Komavi area, and unexploded ordnance remains a significant hazard nationwide.

- **Apportioned military police.** No military police, detainee handling or interpreter support units appear on the US Force List for Planning.

#### Ongoing actions

Antiterrorism vulnerability assessment requirements in preparation for Lae, Daru and Kiunga; review of random antiterrorism measures; coordination with the regional security officer at Embassy Port Moresby.

#### Open items

Vulnerability assessments for Lae, Daru and Kiunga, force protection condition setting authority for any deployed force, contract guard force sourcing, personnel recovery coordination cell designation and interpreter support — all pending.

## 12. Comptroller

#### Current posture

No contingency operation has been designated and no cost code assigned for SOUTHERN SHIELD. Costs to date are absorbed within current fiscal year operation and maintenance appropriations and captured manually. No emergency supplemental appropriation has been enacted.

#### Data and holdings

| **Authority** | **Basis** | **Fiscal year 2026 status and limits** |
|:---|----|----|
| Operation and maintenance, headquarters | Annual appropriation | 78 percent obligated at 25 JUN 2026 |
| Combatant Commander Initiative Fund | 10 USC 166a | \$9.4M allocated, \$6.1M committed; project and category limits apply; Chairman approval required |
| Overseas Humanitarian, Disaster and Civic Aid | 10 USC 2561 | \$14.2M allocated, \$11.7M committed; execution requires a chief of mission disaster declaration |
| Security cooperation, Papua New Guinea | 10 USC 333 | \$4.6M maritime security programme, fully obligated; changes require congressional notification |
| Traditional combatant commander activities | 10 USC 321 and 322 | \$2.8M allocated, \$1.9M committed |
| Acquisition and cross-servicing | 10 USC 2341–2350 | In force with Australia, annual order and transfer ceilings apply; none with Papua New Guinea |
| Unspecified minor military construction | 10 USC 2805 | Project ceiling \$6.0M; \$9.0M to correct a life-, health- or safety-threatening deficiency |
| Contingency construction | 10 USC 2804 | Requires a Secretary of Defense determination and congressional notification; none requested |

Transportation is funded through the transportation working capital fund unless a contingency designation directs otherwise. No host-nation support arrangement exists with Papua New Guinea.

#### Ongoing actions

Manual cost capture by directorate; cost code assignment request in preparation to the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense (Comptroller); initial cost estimate framework in preparation.

#### Open items

Contingency operation designation and cost code assignment pending, with component cost capture reporting to follow. Funding authority for construction in Papua New Guinea, Overseas Humanitarian, Disaster and Civic Aid execution, and contracting officer warrant coverage — all pending.

# Strategic Context — Operation STEADFAST MARINER

**Product Type:** Synthetic Strategic Guidance Compilation **Scope:** NSS / NDS / Africa Strategy excerpts relevant to the Gulf of Guinea counter-piracy crisis and Operation STEADFAST MARINER **Effective Date:** As of 09 February 2027 **Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E) **Reference frameworks:** DIME (instruments of national power); JP 1, JP 3-0, JP 5-0; UNCLOS Part VII (High Seas) Articles 100–107

## 1. Purpose

This document compiles the relevant strategic-guidance excerpts that condition the JFC’s Mission Analysis for Operation STEADFAST MARINER. The excerpts are synthetic but are constructed to be consistent with publicly available 2022 NSS / 2022 NDS / 2024 US Strategy Toward Sub-Saharan Africa structure and language patterns. They reflect the strategic environment as it would be characterized in an open-equivalent strategic guidance product as of February 2027.

## 2. National Security Strategy — Sub-Saharan Africa Excerpts (Synthetic, February 2027)

### 2.1 Overarching National Interests

The United States seeks an Africa that is open, democratic, prosperous, and free of malign influence. Sub-Saharan Africa is home to 1.2 billion people, more than half of whom will be under 25 by 2030. The region accounts for a growing share of global energy production (notably from Nigeria, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, and the Gulf of Guinea offshore basin) and is increasingly central to global supply chains for strategic minerals.

The United States maintains active diplomatic and security relationships with all 16 coastal and littoral states of West and Central Africa. Six of those states are signatories to the Yaoundé Code of Conduct (June 2013) regional maritime security architecture: Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, the Republic of Congo, and Angola. The Yaoundé Architecture is the principal multilateral mechanism through which African coastal states coordinate counter-piracy, counter-IUU fishing, and broader maritime security activity.

### 2.2 Strategic Priorities — Maritime Security in the Gulf of Guinea

In the Gulf of Guinea, the United States supports the Yaoundé Architecture and the African Union’s 2050 Africa’s Integrated Maritime Strategy (AIM 2050). The Gulf of Guinea remains the world’s most active piracy theater following the post-2012 suppression of the Horn of Africa piracy peak. Although coordinated international action — including EU NAVFOR–style coordinated maritime presence, French Mission CORYMBE, Spanish Operación PROSPERIDAD, Italian Operazione GABINIA, and the US Maritime Capacity-Building program — has reduced incidents from the 2018–2020 peak, the threat is controlled rather than eliminated.

The December 2026 drawdown of EU Coordinated Maritime Presence (CMP) contributions following budgetary reprioritization toward Eastern Flank deterrence has reduced coalition patrol density in the Gulf of Guinea by an estimated 35%. The post-drawdown coverage gap is concentrated in the Nigerian and Cameroonian EEZs — historically the highest-threat zones for kidnap-for-ransom (K&R) operations against merchant tankers. The 09 February 2027 coordinated attacks against three merchant tankers represent the largest single-day pirate event in the Gulf of Guinea since June 2020.

### 2.3 Strategic Priorities — US Energy Diversification and Atlantic-Basin Supply Chains

The United States imports approximately 10 percent of its crude oil from West African producers (primarily Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea, Angola), valued at approximately \$60 billion annually. West African crude provides supply diversification away from Persian Gulf and Russian sources and is particularly important for US Gulf Coast refiners that are configured for the light-sweet crudes typical of the West African offshore basin. Sustained Gulf of Guinea piracy raises maritime insurance rates, disrupts FPSO and oil-platform operations, and degrades the predictability of West African crude supply.

### 2.4 Strategic Priorities — Sub-Saharan African Partner Development

The 2024 US Strategy Toward Sub-Saharan Africa emphasizes African-led, African-owned security architectures over US-led intervention. The Yaoundé Architecture is the test case for that approach in the maritime domain. US engagement is structured to *enable* African coastal-state navies and law-enforcement organizations to conduct counter-piracy in their own EEZs, with US and European partner forces providing presence, capacity-building, intelligence support, and (where requested) direct kinetic support. The Operation STEADFAST MARINER concept must preserve the Yaoundé architecture’s primacy.

### 2.5 Integration of Instruments of National Power (DIME)

- **Diplomatic.** Department of State has activated bilateral consultations with Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and São Tomé. AU and ECOWAS notifications have been delivered. Coordination with EU External Action Service ongoing for European coalition contributions. UN Security Council briefing has occurred but no UNSCR is being sought — counter-piracy authority under UNCLOS is settled.

- **Information.** Strategic Communications coordinated through the US Embassy Abuja public affairs apparatus and the AFRICOM Strategic Communications cell. Narrative emphasizes US support for African-led maritime security; US is supporting role, not lead. Counter-narrative against possible pirate-network messaging via social media is being prepared.

- **Military.** USAFRICOM has been directed to plan and prepare to conduct multinational maritime security operations to (a) restore coalition patrol density, (b) recover hostages where feasible in coordination with host-nation forces, and (c) re-establish deterrent presence in the Gulf of Guinea while host-nation partners exercise primary law-enforcement jurisdiction. The President has authorized force-flow to position for execution.

- **Economic.** Treasury / OFAC consideration of targeted sanctions on identified pirate network financial enablers is underway but not yet announced. No broader West Africa economic measures contemplated.

## 3. National Defense Strategy — DoW-Specific Excerpts (Synthetic)

### 3.1 Pacing Challenge and Acute Threats

The 2022 NDS designates the People’s Republic of China as the pacing challenge for the Department of War, and the Russian Federation as an acute threat. The 2024 revision reaffirms both designations. Africa is identified as a region of increasing strategic competition — primarily through PRC and Russian malign activity (PRC infrastructure and basing footprint; Russian Wagner-descended private military presence in Sahel and Central Africa) — but not as a region of direct great-power conventional confrontation.

The 2024 NDS revision identifies maritime security in the African littorals as an enabling capability for the broader Africa Strategy, and explicitly cites the Yaoundé Architecture as a model for partner-led security architectures DoW is directed to support.

### 3.2 Force Allocation Priorities

Per the 2024 NDS implementation guidance:

1.  **First priority of effort:** Defending the homeland (USNORTHCOM, USSPACECOM, USCYBERCOM).

2.  **Second priority:** Deterring strategic attacks against the United States, allies, and partners (USSTRATCOM, regional CCMDs).

3.  **Third priority:** Deterring aggression while being prepared to prevail in conflict in the Indo-Pacific, with the Korean Peninsula and the Taiwan Strait as the two principal contingency drivers.

4.  **Fourth priority:** Deterring opportunistic aggression in Europe (USEUCOM, post-2022 elevated demand).

5.  **Concurrent:** Maintaining presence and partner-development capacity in CENTCOM, AFRICOM, and SOUTHCOM with rotating force contributions.

USAFRICOM is currently the fifth-priority CCMD for force allocation. Operation STEADFAST MARINER will be executed within rotating-contributions framework; no standing dedicated USAFRICOM major surface combatant force is apportioned.

### 3.3 NDS Direction Relevant to STEADFAST MARINER

- Maintain credible partner-development capacity in African littorals through rotating maritime presence.

- Operate as enabling element of African-led architectures (Yaoundé, ECOWAS, ECCAS) rather than as standalone US lead.

- Build interoperability with European partners through standing maritime security exercises (OBANGAME EXPRESS, GRAND AFRICAN NEMO, MULTINATIONAL MARITIME EXERCISE).

- Maintain ability to recover US persons in distress overseas without precommitting to direct kinetic engagement.

- Manage relationship with host nations to preserve future basing access and partnership equities.

## 4. Regional Strategy — 2024 US Strategy Toward Sub-Saharan Africa Excerpts (Synthetic)

### 4.1 Four Strategic Objectives

The 2024 US Strategy Toward Sub-Saharan Africa identifies four strategic objectives:

1.  Foster open and inclusive societies.

2.  Deliver democratic and security dividends.

3.  Advance pandemic recovery and economic opportunity.

4.  Support conservation, climate adaptation, and a just energy transition.

The “deliver democratic and security dividends” objective explicitly identifies maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea and the Horn of Africa as priority security partnerships.

### 4.2 Maritime Security Approach

The Strategy directs DoW to:

- Strengthen partner-nation maritime law-enforcement capacity through the Africa Maritime Law Enforcement Partnership (AMLEP) and parallel capacity-building programs.

- Coordinate US engagement with the Yaoundé Architecture rather than build parallel structures.

- Position US naval presence to demonstrate commitment to African partner-led security; presence visits, exercises, and capacity-building are weighted above kinetic operations.

- Where US persons are at risk, retain options for direct US action under appropriate authority.

### 4.3 Specific Direction on Gulf of Guinea

The Strategy directs sustained US engagement with the Yaoundé Architecture’s six original signatories plus the wider regional grouping. ICC Yaoundé and the two operational MMCCs (Douala in Zone D, Pointe-Noire in Zone A) are identified as the operational coordination centers US engagement should pass through. AMLEP funding through FY28 is identified at the \$45M/year level.

## 5. Strategic Communication Themes (Synthetic)

The following strategic communication themes are approved for Operation STEADFAST MARINER messaging:

1.  **African-led, US-enabled.** The operation restores coalition presence to a partner-led architecture; African coastal states retain primary jurisdiction and law-enforcement responsibility.

2.  **Hostage recovery without escalation.** Recovery of US and partner-nation hostages is a priority but is pursued in coordination with host-nation jurisdiction and existing diplomatic channels. The US is not invading any state.

3.  **Yaoundé Architecture endorsement.** US engagement reinforces, not displaces, the Yaoundé Code of Conduct framework.

4.  **Coalition continuity.** US engagement is alongside European partner naval contributions (UK, FRA, ESP, ITA, PRT); this is not unilateral US action.

5.  **Long-term partnership.** US engagement is part of a sustained Africa-Strategy commitment, not a one-off crisis response.

## 6. Cross-Reference to Planning Directive

The strategic guidance in this document is referenced in:

- CJCS EXORD SER 027-27 (07_CJCS_EXORD.md) §1 (Situation) and §2 (Mission).

- AFRICOM Linked EXORD SER 001-27 (08_AFRICOM_LINKED_EXORD.md) §1 (Situation) and §2 (Mission).

- NAVAF Component Linked EXORD (09a_NAVAF_Component_LINKED_EXORD.md) §1.

- CDR USAFRICOM Initial Planning Guidance (12_CIPG.md) §1 (Intent), §2 (Strategic Objectives), and §8 (Strategic Communication Themes).

- Annex C — Information (11_Annexes.md).

title: Regional Intel Summary
text:
# Regional Intelligence Summary — Operation STEADFAST MARINER

**Product Type:** Higher Headquarters Intelligence Background Paper **Date Range Covered:** January 2018 – February 2027 **Source Basis:** OSINT only — IMB Piracy Reporting Centre annual reports 2018–2027, Stable Seas Gulf of Guinea Maritime Security publications, RAND counter-piracy studies, Yaoundé Code of Conduct ICC publications, NAVAF intelligence support detachment products **Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E) **Cutoff:** 09 February 2027, 0600Z

## 1. Executive Summary

The Gulf of Guinea piracy threat has been controlled rather than eliminated since the 2018–2020 peak. Coordinated international maritime presence — EU Coordinated Maritime Presence (CMP), French Mission CORYMBE, Spanish Operación PROSPERIDAD, Italian Operazione GABINIA, UK Royal Navy Gulf of Guinea task element, US AMLEP capacity-building — combined with improved Nigerian Navy and Yaoundé Architecture coordination, drove a 70% reduction in attempted attacks from 2020 through 2025. The December 2026 EU CMP drawdown reduced coalition patrol density by approximately 35%. The 09 February 2027 coordinated attacks against three merchant tankers represent the largest single-day pirate event since June 2020 and a clear shift toward coordinated, higher-value targeting.

The primary adversary network is assessed as a Niger Delta-origin kidnap-for-ransom (K&R) organization with operational lineage traceable to the post-MEND (Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta) criminal milieu. Current-generation operations have shifted from oil-bunkering and cargo theft to coordinated K&R against merchant tanker crews. The network is composed of an estimated 4–6 active cells operating from coastal hides in the Niger Delta swamps, with on-shore logistical support from corrupt local officials and small-scale criminal networks. The network’s intent is assessed with low-to-moderate confidence; capabilities are well-characterized.

The principal coalition planning challenges are: (a) rapid rebalancing of patrol density to cover the post-EU CMP coverage gap, (b) recovery of 47 hostages including 4 US persons across three captured vessels with one vessel currently unlocated, (c) preservation of Yaoundé Architecture primacy in coastal-state EEZs while supporting host-nation forces, (d) management of pirate intent ambiguity — whether the 09 February event represents a one-off coordinated K&R or the opening of a sustained campaign.

## 2. Threat Pattern of Life — Gulf of Guinea Piracy, 2018–2027

### 2.1 Threat Evolution

|  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|
| Period | Characteristic activity | Key drivers |
| 2018–2020 (peak) | Coordinated K&R operations at scale; 130+ kidnapping incidents in 2020 alone; targets included tankers, supply vessels, fishing trawlers | Niger Delta militancy spillover; weak Nigerian Navy patrol coverage; high crude prices enabling ransom demand growth |
| 2021–2022 (initial reduction) | Quarterly incident counts cut by ~40%; some shift toward smaller fishing-vessel targets | Initial deployment of EU CMP, expanded Mission CORYMBE rotations, MOWCA coordination improvements |
| 2023–2024 (suppressed peak) | Incident counts at ~25% of 2018–2020 baseline; multiple network arrests including Nigerian Navy operations against Pirate Action Groups (PAGs) | Yaoundé Architecture maturation; Bonny Island and Forcados terminal security enhancements; coordinated coalition presence |
| 2025 (controlled) | Incident counts stable at low level; few successful K&R; trend toward opportunistic small-vessel targeting | Sustained coalition presence; improved Nigerian Navy capacity; some pirate-network displacement to Sahel hawala economy |
| Late 2026 (post-drawdown) | December 2026 EU CMP drawdown announced; coalition patrol density reduced ~35%; pirate-network communications intercept activity (assessed) increased | Budgetary reprioritization of EU member states toward Eastern Flank; opportunity-recognition by surviving pirate cells |
| **February 2027 (current)** | **09 February 2027 coordinated attacks against three merchant tankers; 47 hostages; one vessel unlocated** | **Assessed exploitation of post-drawdown patrol gap; shift toward coordinated higher-value targeting** |

### 2.2 The 09 February 2027 Event in Detail

At approximately 0420Z on 09 February 2027, three pirate skiffs operating in coordination boarded the Liberian-flag product tanker MV *AURORA STAR* (49,000 DWT, en route Lagos→Lomé with refined product cargo) at position 04°20’N 008°12’E in the Cameroon EEZ. Sixteen crew were taken hostage; the vessel was steered southeast toward the Niger Delta. AIS was spoofed approximately 30 minutes after boarding to indicate a position approximately 80 nm to the north-northwest. *AURORA STAR* has not been visually contacted since 0640Z; the assessed actual position is in the network of hides between the Brass River and Forcados River estuaries.

At approximately 0510Z, a second three-skiff team boarded the Maltese-flag product tanker MV *BENEDICT GALLOWAY* (38,000 DWT, en route Port Harcourt→Walvis Bay) at 04°08’N 007°56’E in the Nigerian EEZ. Eighteen crew were taken hostage; ransom contact was established on 09 February 2027 at approximately 1830Z via Nigerian intermediary. Vessel was abandoned by pirates at 1740Z and is now under Nigerian Navy custody at Calabar.

At approximately 0540Z, a third pirate team (assessed at 2 skiffs with 4–5 pirates each) boarded the Marshall Islands-flag chemical tanker MV *KINIPELA HOPE* (32,000 DWT, en route Bonny→Algeciras) at 04°15’N 008°22’E in the Equatoguinean EEZ. Thirteen crew were taken hostage; the vessel was released at 1120Z (under 6 hours after boarding) — atypical brevity, assessed as indicating either insufficient pirate manpower to maintain three simultaneous prizes or deliberate signaling.

The three vessels carried 47 crew total: 16 *AURORA STAR* (4 US persons, 7 Filipino, 5 Liberian); 18 *BENEDICT GALLOWAY* (released — all accounted for); 13 *KINIPELA HOPE* (released — all accounted for). Net hostage situation: 16 hostages aboard the unlocated *AURORA STAR*, including 4 US-flag-state mariners. ICRC notification of the four US persons is pending.

### 2.3 Coordination Indicators

The three attacks display coordination indicators not characteristic of opportunistic Gulf of Guinea piracy:

- Geographic dispersion across three EEZs (NGA, CMR, GEQ) within a 70-minute window argues for coordinated planning.

- AIS-spoofing technique on *AURORA STAR* is consistent across all three attacks (delayed, distance-shifted false position).

- Target selection (all product/chemical tankers, all 30,000–50,000 DWT class) suggests deliberate value-class selection rather than opportunistic interception.

- Brevity of the *KINIPELA HOPE* operation suggests planned exit, not interrupted operation.

### 2.4 Pirate Network Assessment

Assessed adversary: Niger Delta-origin K&R network, lineage to post-MEND criminal milieu (2009 amnesty cohort and their successors). Current generation operates as a loose federation of 4–6 cells, each with 15–25 active personnel, sharing logistics, intelligence, and ransom-negotiation infrastructure but executing independent operations.

Cell-level capability: - **Light infantry weapons.** AK-pattern rifles (mixed-origin, mostly older stocks routed via Sahel arms-trafficking), RPG-7 launchers, light mortars (60mm and 81mm — limited reports), GPMGs mounted on captured speedboats. - **Small-boat operations.** Modified fishing skiffs (12–14 meters, twin-outboard, capable of ~30 knots sustained); captured commercial speedboats and pilot vessels; mother-ship operations from fishing trawlers up to 200 nm offshore have been observed in 2024–2025. - **Communications.** Iridium and Inmarsat satellite phones (multiple per cell), end-to-end-encrypted messaging applications (Signal, Telegram, Wickr observed), VHF maritime radio (channel 16 monitoring + working channels). - **Maritime intelligence.** Commercial AIS-monitoring tools (mostly via public-internet aggregators); on-shore observation from port-area informants; corrupt-official intelligence streams. - **No cyber, space, or strategic capability.** No electronic warfare. No GPS denial. No cyber-influence campaigns. No remote sensing beyond commercial AIS.

Cell coordination is assessed as facilitated by 2–3 senior network figures who control ransom-negotiation infrastructure (typically via Lagos-area intermediaries and hawala networks) and provide top-level target-selection guidance. Senior figures rarely participate in attacks directly. Identities of senior figures are not confirmed in OSINT; one named individual (“ALATA-1,” likely pseudonym) has appeared in IMB reporting since 2023 but is not visually identified.

## 3. Adversary Strategic Posture (Pirate Network)

### 3.1 Most Likely Adversary COA (Most Likely)

The 09 February 2027 event is the opening of a sustained K&R campaign exploiting the post-EU CMP coverage gap. The network will conduct 2–4 additional coordinated attacks over the next 60–90 days, escalating to higher-value targets (15,000+ DWT crude carriers, FPSO support vessels, possibly LNG carriers) if the initial response is judged insufficient. Hostage demands will be staged: lower-value hostage releases in exchange for sub-million-dollar ransoms in the near term, building toward higher-value hostage demand cycles. **Confidence: moderate.** **Indicators:** continued AIS-spoofing reports; intercepted communications suggesting network coordination; observed pre-positioning of skiffs at hide locations.

### 3.2 Most Dangerous Adversary COA

The 09 February 2027 event is a network probing operation to assess coalition response capacity prior to a campaign against higher-value strategic infrastructure — specifically, an attempt to capture an FPSO support vessel or to seize an LNG carrier with the intent of denying the LNG supply chain or extracting a state-level ransom. The network may have, or be developing, contacts with state-actor proxies (assessed possibly Russian Federation-aligned given Sahel arms-trafficking patterns) interested in disrupting Western energy supply chains. **Confidence: low — limited reporting; significant strategic-consequence delta if true.** **Indicators:** evidence of pre-attack reconnaissance against FPSO or LNG infrastructure; weapons or comms upgrades inconsistent with K&R economics; political-messaging in hostage demands beyond ransom.

### 3.3 Alternative Adversary COA — One-Off Event

The 09 February 2027 event represents a one-off coordinated operation by the network to demonstrate continued capability post-coalition drawdown, intended to establish ransom-negotiation leverage rather than open a sustained campaign. After the *AURORA STAR* ransom is settled, network tempo returns to 2025–2026 controlled-baseline levels. **Confidence: moderate.** **Indicators:** rapid ransom-settlement negotiations; absence of further attacks within 30 days; intercepted communications suggesting the network considers the event “complete.”

### 3.4 Adversary Capabilities vs Intent Assessment (Kent Split)

**Capabilities (high confidence):** Pirate network capabilities are well-characterized through 6+ years of IMB reporting and Yaoundé Architecture intelligence sharing. Network can sustain 2–4 major coordinated K&R operations per quarter at current capacity; cannot sustain operations that require sophisticated EW or counter-naval capability; cannot threaten military vessels.

**Intent (low confidence):** Whether the 09 February 2027 event indicates a one-off, a sustained campaign, or a probing operation toward higher-value targets cannot be determined from current reporting. Three COAs (above) are presented with explicit confidence levels. The intent question is the principal J2 ambiguity in this scenario.

## 4. Coastal-State Posture

### 4.1 Nigeria

**Government:** President-elect’s administration (took office 29 May 2027 in scenario timeline; STEADFAST MARINER planning is occurring under outgoing administration). Inherited Yaoundé commitments and Nigerian Navy modernization program. Public commitment to counter-piracy is strong; private friction with US over basing access and SOFA arrangements.

**Nigerian Navy:** Eastern Naval Command at Calabar (RADM-equivalent, area of responsibility includes Bonny–Forcados sector — the primary pirate operating area). Western Naval Command at Lagos. Capability has materially improved since 2020: NNS *PROSPERITY*-class offshore patrol vessels, helicopter detachments, embarked Marines (Nigerian Navy Special Boat Service). Operating tempo is constrained by fuel and parts availability; mission availability of major surface units assessed at 65–70%.

**Posture on STEADFAST MARINER:** Welcomes coalition support; insistent on Nigerian primary jurisdiction in NGA EEZ; sensitive to public optics of foreign naval forces in Nigerian waters.

### 4.2 Cameroon

**Government:** Stable; long-running incumbent. Yaoundé Architecture original signatory.

**Marine Nationale Camerounaise:** Modest fleet (5 patrol vessels operational); coastal-defense role primarily. Hosts MMCC Douala (Yaoundé Architecture Zone D coordination center). MMCC Douala assessed as one of the more capable Yaoundé MMCCs.

**Posture on STEADFAST MARINER:** Strong supportive; offers port access at Douala for coalition operations; will second liaison officers to NAVAF MOC.

### 4.3 Equatorial Guinea

**Government:** Long-running incumbent; relationship with US is transactional. Hosts US oil-industry presence (Punta Europa LNG facility).

**Posture on STEADFAST MARINER:** Supportive but with bilateral concessions expected; access requires Foreign Ministry approval on case-by-case basis.

### 4.4 Gabon, São Tomé and Príncipe

Both Yaoundé signatories; modest naval capacity; supportive but not operationally significant contributors.

## 5. Coalition Posture

### 5.1 Standing Coalition Presence Pre-09 February 2027

- **US:** AMLEP capacity-building program; rotating SIXTH Fleet detachment for OBANGAME EXPRESS and GRAND AFRICAN NEMO exercises; no standing combatant presence.

- **France:** Mission CORYMBE — continuous since 1990; typically one FREMM-class or La Fayette-class frigate + one support vessel.

- **Spain:** Operación PROSPERIDAD — typically one BAM-class offshore patrol vessel since 2020.

- **Italy:** Operazione GABINIA — typically one PPA-class or FREMM-class frigate since 2020.

- **Portugal:** Periodic NRP frigate deployment (~3 months/year).

- **United Kingdom:** Royal Navy permanent Gulf of Guinea task element; typically OPV (Forth/Spey/Trent class) plus visiting frigate. **Note:** UK presence is independent of (formerly) EU CMP and continues unaffected by the December 2026 drawdown.

- **EU:** EU CMP (Coordinated Maritime Presence) — drawn down December 2026; previously coordinated FRA / ESP / ITA / PRT contributions plus periodic Greek and Romanian rotations.

### 5.2 Post-Drawdown Coverage Gap (December 2026 – Current)

The December 2026 EU CMP drawdown reduced standing coalition combatant presence in the Gulf of Guinea by approximately 35% (loss of periodic Greek, Romanian, and Danish rotations; reduced French operational tempo from continuous to ~75% coverage). UK presence is unaffected. National contributions (FRA / ESP / ITA / PRT) continue under bilateral arrangements but are reduced in tempo.

The Niger Delta operating area (Bonny–Forcados sector) — historically the highest-threat zone — has assessed coalition patrol coverage of approximately 40% of pre-drawdown levels. This coverage gap is the principal driver of the 09 February 2027 event.

### 5.3 Yaoundé Architecture Operational Status

- **ICC Yaoundé** (Inter-Regional Coordination Centre): Functional; provides daily fused operational picture to coastal states and partners; assessed as a coordination hub rather than a tasking authority.

- **MMCC Douala** (Maritime Multinational Coordination Centre, Zone D — Nigerian/Cameroonian/Equatoguinean/Gabonese coastal waters): Assessed as the most capable MMCC; effective at incident response coordination.

- **MMCC Pointe-Noire** (Zone A — Republic of Congo, Angola): Less capable; coordination quality varies.

- **Other MMCCs / coordination cells:** Variable capacity.

Yaoundé Architecture is voluntary, lacks enforcement mechanism, and depends on coastal-state political will. Coordination quality varies materially across zones. This is a designed-in inference point for the MA staff (#6 in 00_README.md).

## 6. Implications for the Operational Approach

The Regional Intelligence Summary supports the following analytic conclusions:

1.  **The 09 February 2027 event is qualitatively different from background Gulf of Guinea piracy.** Coordination across three EEZs, target selection consistency, and AIS-spoofing tradecraft suggest organized network action, not opportunistic incidents.

2.  **The coverage gap is the proximate enabler.** The pirate network is exploiting the post-EU CMP drawdown. Restoring coalition patrol density is necessary but may not be sufficient; sustained presence is required to deny the gap.

3.  **Pirate intent ambiguity is the binding J2 problem.** Three plausible adversary COAs (sustained campaign / probing operation / one-off event) have materially different operational implications. Intent-related CCIRs are the J2 priority.

4.  **Yaoundé primacy is a planning constraint, not a planning option.** US and coalition operations must support, not displace, host-nation primary jurisdiction in EEZ. The CIPG must articulate this constraint and its operational implications.

5.  **Personnel Recovery / Hostage Rescue (PR/HR) is a parallel mission set under PPD-30 with FBI as Lead Federal Agency.** The 4 US persons aboard the unlocated *AURORA STAR* are isolated US persons in non-state captivity. PPD-30 (24 June 2015) governs the US Government response: FBI HRFC is LFA; SPEHA leads diplomatic engagement; the military hostage-rescue option under JP 3-50 is the option of last resort with execution authority retained at the NCA. The MA staff must reason about (a) supported/supporting relationships between NAVAF (maritime security) and SOCAFRICA’s JSOTF–STEADFAST MARINER (PR/HR), (b) triggering conditions for shifting from FBI-led negotiation to military rescue, and (c) host-nation jurisdiction during any rescue. The standing counter-piracy mission remains the operation’s center of gravity; PR/HR is a parallel mission set, not a branch on it.

6.  **Coalition rebalancing is the J5 priority.** Allocation of finite UK / FRA / ESP / ITA / PRT / US patrol assets across coverage zones, plus the question of standing presence vs reactive surge, is the J5 planning load. Designed-in inference point \#1 (coalition rebalancing) is the principal J5 ambiguity in this scenario.

title: Adversary OOB
text:
# Adversary Order of Battle — Operation STEADFAST MARINER

**Product Type:** Adversary Network and Capability Inventory **Cutoff date:** 09 February 2027, 0600Z **Source basis:** OSINT — IMB Piracy Reporting Centre 2018–2027, Stable Seas Gulf of Guinea Maritime Security 2024–2026, Nigerian Navy public reporting, RAND Piracy Network Disruption studies, NAVAF intelligence support detachment composite assessments **Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

## 1. Adversary Strategic Command and Control

The adversary is a **decentralized criminal network**, not a state-aligned organization. There is no formal C2 structure analogous to a military OOB. The network is best modeled as a loose federation with three layers:

|  |  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|----|
| Layer | Function | Personnel | Identification |
| Senior network (“strategic”) | Target selection guidance; ransom negotiation infrastructure; financial enablement via Lagos-area intermediaries and hawala networks | Estimated 2–3 senior figures | Not visually confirmed in OSINT; one pseudonymous individual (“ALATA-1”) in IMB reporting since 2023 |
| Cell leaders (“operational”) | Cell-level tactical planning; on-scene command of K&R operations | Estimated 4–6 cell leaders (one per active cell) | Not confirmed |
| Cell members (“tactical”) | Skiff operators, boarders, on-shore logisticians, on-shore hostage handlers | Estimated 100–150 active personnel total across all cells | Partial identification via post-event captures (Nigerian Navy custody); most personnel rotate frequently |

Cell coordination is facilitated via: - Encrypted messaging applications (Signal, Telegram, Wickr observed) - Iridium and Inmarsat satphone calls (multiple per cell, rotated frequently) - Lagos-area intermediaries for ransom-negotiation communications with shipping companies - Hawala networks for ransom payment receipt and distribution

There is **no overhead political or governmental sponsor** identified in current reporting. The network is criminal-economic, not insurgent-political. (One adversary COA — see 02_Regional_Intel_Summary.md §3.2 — considers possible state-actor proxy contact; this is currently low-confidence reporting.)

## 2. Cell-Level Inventory (Estimated)

### 2.1 Cell ALPHA — Bonny Sector

- **Estimated strength:** 25–30 active personnel

- **Operating area:** Bonny–Forcados corridor, Niger Delta hides

- **Capability:** 4–6 modified fishing skiffs; 2–3 captured speedboats; 15–20 small arms; 2–3 RPG-7

- **Recent activity:** Attributed to MV *BENEDICT GALLOWAY* attack (09 February 2027)

- **Logistical base:** Coastal hide network in Brass River–Forcados River vicinity

### 2.2 Cell BRAVO — Calabar–Cameroon Border Sector

- **Estimated strength:** 20–25 active personnel

- **Operating area:** Eastern Niger Delta, Calabar approaches, Cameroon EEZ border region

- **Capability:** 3–4 modified fishing skiffs; 2 captured speedboats; 12–15 small arms; 1–2 mortars

- **Recent activity:** Attributed to MV *AURORA STAR* attack (09 February 2027). **MV *AURORA STAR* assessed currently held in Cell BRAVO hide network.**

- **Logistical base:** Coastal hide network west of Cross River mouth

### 2.3 Cell CHARLIE — Mid-Niger Delta

- **Estimated strength:** 20–25 active personnel

- **Operating area:** Mid-Niger Delta (Bayelsa coast), able to mount mother-ship operations to ~200 nm

- **Capability:** Includes one or two captured fishing trawlers used as mother ships; 6+ skiffs; broader arms inventory

- **Recent activity:** Attributed to MV *KINIPELA HOPE* attack (09 February 2027)

- **Logistical base:** Mid-Niger Delta hide network (south of Yenagoa)

### 2.4 Cells DELTA, ECHO, FOXTROT — Reserve / Reconstituting

Three additional cells assessed but not active in current reporting: - **DELTA:** Possibly reconstituting post-2025 Nigerian Navy captures; ~15–20 personnel - **ECHO:** Long-standing cell, currently low-tempo; ~15 personnel - **FOXTROT:** Younger cell, formed 2024–2025; ~10–15 personnel

Reserve cells could augment ALPHA/BRAVO/CHARLIE operations if the network is preparing a sustained campaign (MLCOA per §3.2 of Regional Intel Summary).

## 3. Weapons and Equipment

### 3.1 Light infantry weapons

|  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|
| Type | Estimated network inventory | Source |
| AK-pattern rifles (7.62 × 39 mm) | 80–100 units | Mixed-origin via Sahel arms-trafficking; older Soviet-bloc stock primarily |
| GPMG (PKM-pattern) | 4–6 units | Same |
| RPG-7 launchers (with assorted rounds) | 6–8 units | Same |
| Light mortars (60 mm / 81 mm) | 2–3 units, limited employment | Same |
| Pistols (mixed) | 30–40 units | Local-source |
| Improvised explosive devices | Limited use; pirate doctrine prefers intimidation to lethality | Local manufacture |

### 3.2 Small-boat platforms

|  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|
| Type | Network inventory | Performance |
| Modified fishing skiffs (12–14 m, twin outboard) | 15–25 units | ~30 kn sustained, ~300 nm range |
| Captured commercial speedboats | 4–6 units | 35–45 kn, ~200 nm range |
| Captured pilot vessels (occasional) | 1–2 units when held | 20 kn, longer endurance |
| Mother-ship trawlers (Cell CHARLIE) | 1–2 units | 12 kn, fuel + skiff support to 200 nm offshore |

### 3.3 Communications

|  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|
| Type | Use | Network inventory |
| Iridium satphones | Inter-cell and external comms | 8–12 active units rotated frequently |
| Inmarsat satphones | Same | 4–6 active units |
| Encrypted messaging (Signal/Telegram/Wickr) | Inter-cell coordination + ransom communications | Comprehensive |
| VHF maritime radio | On-scene during boarding ops | Each cell ~3–4 units |
| HF radio | Limited; on-shore base only | 2–3 units total |

### 3.4 Intelligence / sensing

- **AIS monitoring:** Comprehensive via public-internet aggregators (MarineTraffic, FleetMon)

- **Visual on-shore observation:** Port-area informants in Lagos, Port Harcourt, Calabar

- **Corrupt-official intelligence:** Variable but assessed as available across multiple coastal-state governments

- **No technical sensing capability:** No radar; no satellite imagery; no SIGINT capability

## 4. Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs)

### 4.1 Target selection

- Preferred targets: product tankers, chemical tankers, crude carriers in the 30,000–80,000 DWT class

- Target intelligence developed from AIS monitoring + port-area observation; targets typically selected 24–72 hours pre-attack

- Higher-value target ambitions noted but not consistently executed: FPSO support vessels, LNG carriers, oil-platform supply boats

### 4.2 Approach and boarding

- Skiff approach typically from quarter or bow; uses sun angle and sea-state to reduce visual signature

- Boarding via grappling hooks and ladders; takes 3–8 minutes from initial approach to control of bridge

- Crew typically corralled to bridge or messdeck; non-essential personnel restrained

- Master and chief engineer separated (high-value individuals for ransom negotiation)

### 4.3 Post-boarding

- AIS spoofing initiated within 30 minutes of boarding (delayed and distance-shifted false positions)

- Course altered toward Niger Delta hide network; transit times typically 12–36 hours depending on initial position

- Hostages transferred from vessel to coastal hide within 6–24 hours of arrival at hide network

- Vessel either retained for use (rare) or released after ransom negotiation (common)

### 4.4 Ransom negotiation

- Initial contact typically 24–72 hours post-event via Nigerian intermediary

- Negotiation cycle typically 30–90 days

- Recent ransom levels (2024–2026): US persons \$1.5–3M each; OECD-state mariners \$0.5–1.5M each; non-OECD mariners \$200K–800K each

- Payment via hawala or cryptocurrency (increasing trend); intermediaries take 10–20% of total

- Hostage release typically within 24–72 hours of payment confirmation

### 4.5 Reconstitution cycle

After major captures by Nigerian Navy or coalition operations, network cells typically reconstitute in 6–18 months, drawing on Niger Delta unemployed youth labor pool and pre-existing arms/equipment caches.

## 5. Network Vulnerabilities

|  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|
| Vulnerability | Exploitation method | Coalition capability fit |
| Coastal hide network (fixed locations) | Persistent HUMINT + ISR; raid execution | NAVAF + Nigerian Navy SBS combined ops |
| Ransom communications (intermediary nodes) | SIGINT on Lagos-area intermediaries; financial-intelligence on hawala flows | National-level SIGINT + Treasury OFAC coordination |
| Mother-ship operations (Cell CHARLIE) | Mother-ship distinctive AIS / radar signature | Coalition surface combatant patrol coverage |
| Skiff vulnerability outside hide network | Skiffs in open water are vulnerable to helicopter VBSS | NAVAF + UK / FRA / ESP / ITA / PRT embarked helo coordination |
| On-shore logistical support corruption | Coastal-state law-enforcement coordination | Yaoundé Architecture host-nation coordination |

## 6. Indicators and Warnings

The following I&W are recommended for CCIRs (see 13_CCIRs.md):

|  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|
| Indicator | Significance | Reporting threshold |
| New AIS-spoofing reports | Active pirate operation in progress | Immediate |
| Mother-ship signature on AIS / radar | Cell CHARLIE in offshore operating area | 1-hour reporting |
| Encrypted-messaging traffic spike between known network numbers | Pre-attack coordination | Daily fused report |
| Lagos-area intermediary observed contacting shipping company | Ransom negotiation in progress | 24-hour reporting |
| Hawala-network transaction inconsistent with normal pattern | Possible ransom payment | 24-hour reporting |
| Coastal hide observation (visual or thermal) | Hostage-handling activity | Immediate |
| Coalition partner contact with named senior network figure | High-confidence intent indicator | Immediate |

# Coalition Order of Battle — Operation STEADFAST MARINER

**Product Type:** Coalition Forces Apportioned and Allocated **Apportionment date:** 09 February 2027 (initial); refinement expected within 72 hours **Source basis:** OSINT — US Navy Force Structure documents, IISS Military Balance 2027, partner-nation public force-disposition statements, Yaoundé Architecture standing arrangements **Classification (synthetic):** UNCLASSIFIED // FOR EXERCISE / TRAINING USE ONLY (E)

## 1. US Forces Apportioned to USAFRICOM (for STEADFAST MARINER)

### 1.1 Major Surface Combatants and Maritime Patrol

|  |  |  |  |  |
|:---|----|----|----|----|
| Asset | Type | Home port | Apportionment | Notes |
| USS *FORREST SHERMAN* (DDG-98) | Arleigh Burke-class destroyer (Flight IIA) | Naval Station Norfolk | 1 × DDG apportioned 30 days | Currently on FDNF-E rotation; can redirect from Mediterranean transit |
| **BATAAN ARG (26th MEU embarked)** | Three-ship East Coast Amphibious Ready Group | Naval Station Norfolk | ARG apportioned 60 days (full rotation) | Standing II MEF / 2nd Fleet rotation; ARG composition below |
| └─ USS *BATAAN* (LHD-5) | Wasp-class amphibious assault ship | Naval Station Norfolk | ARG flagship | Embarks the 26th MEU Aviation Combat Element (MV-22B, CH-53E, AH-1Z, UH-1Y, MH-60S, F-35B det); ARG/MEU command element; Role 2E medical |
| └─ USS *FORT LAUDERDALE* (LPD-28) | San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock | Naval Station Norfolk | 60 days | **JSOTF SOF berthing/integration platform** under JSOTF tasking; embarks ½ MEU GCE (BLT element) + JSOTF SOF; Role 2 medical |

### 1.2 Special Operations Forces and Personnel Recovery / Hostage Rescue

The PR/HR mission set under JP 3-50 is led by Theater Special Operations Command, Africa (SOCAFRICA) through JSOTF–STEADFAST MARINER (constituted per the SOCAFRICA Component Linked EXORD at 09b_SOCAFRICA_Component_LINKED_EXORD.md, under AFRICOM Linked EXORD §3(b)–§3(c)). SEAL elements are the primary direct-action force for the military hostage-rescue option. The 26th MEU’s Maritime Raid Force is the supporting force, providing outer cordon, blocking, extraction security, and CASEVAC in support of the SEAL-led entry team. The “MEU(SOC)” designation was phased out in 2014; “TRAP” (Tactical Recovery of Aircraft and Personnel) is doctrinally for recovery of isolated military personnel (downed pilots) and is not the right framing for hostage rescue from a non-state network.

## 4. Coalition Forces — Host-Nation Partners (Primary Jurisdiction)

### 4.1 Nigerian Navy

- NNS *NIGERIA* (PROSPERITY-class OPV) — Eastern Naval Command, based Calabar

- NNS *UNITY* (former-USCG cutter, medium-endurance) — Eastern Naval Command

- 6 × small patrol craft and fast patrol boats — Eastern Naval Command coastal patrol

- **Status:** Primary jurisdiction within NGA EEZ; coordination via Eastern Naval Command HQ Calabar and MMCC Douala

### 4.2 Marine Nationale Camerounaise

- 1 × Ndiola-class patrol vessel

- 2 × Quartier-Maître-class patrol craft

- **Status:** Primary jurisdiction within CMR EEZ; coordination via MMCC Douala (which is co-located with Cameroonian naval headquarters)

- **Caveat:** Limited operating reach beyond ~120 nm; surge availability constrained

### 4.3 Other host-nation contributors

- Ghanaian Navy: 1 × patrol craft available for coordination (non-NGA EEZ)

- Equatoguinean coast guard: 2 × small craft; primarily Punta Europa security

## 5. Coalition Forces — Quiet / Implicit Support

> **Planner annotation (designed-in inference point \#6 — Yaoundé architecture limits):** Coordination quality varies across MMCCs. MMCC Douala is assessed capable; MMCC Pointe-Noire is variable. The Yaoundé Code of Conduct is voluntary and lacks enforcement mechanism. Coalition tasking must accommodate Yaoundé Architecture preferences without depending on it for decisive coordination. NAVAF MOC should expect to perform most fused-picture coordination directly, using MMCC Douala for tasking pass-through to coastal-state navies.

No quiet / implicit-support partners identified beyond the overt list. PRC maintains an independent Gulf of Aden-style presence but does not coordinate with Yaoundé Architecture and is not a STEADFAST MARINER partner. Russian Federation maritime presence in West Africa is minimal post-2022.
